title: What Your Procrastination Is Protecting
description: Putting something off is usually avoidance of a feeling rather than a shortage of discipline. This worksheet helps you find the feeling, then take one small step anyway.
intro_md: There is no score here and no verdict about your character. Delay is information. The useful question is not “why am I so lazy” but “what does starting this make me feel, and what does putting it off protect me from?”

fields.label: The task, named as specifically as you can — not “sort my life out”, but the actual next action
How long it has been waiting, and what you have been doing instead
What you tell yourself each time you decide not to start
Picture starting it right now. What shows up first — dread, boredom, resentment, shame, blankness?
Where that feeling sits in your body
If it could speak in one sentence, what would it say?

A time you did something imperfectly and it turned out fine anyway
A step so small it feels almost silly — open the file, write one line, find the phone number
When you'll do it. Day and time.
Afterwards: what actually happened, and how it compared with what you expected

title: Working With Intrusive Thoughts
description: A thought that arrives uninvited is not a plan, a wish, or a confession. This worksheet helps you notice one, step back from it, and decide what you do next.
intro_md: Intrusive thoughts are common — most people have them. They tend to run opposite to what you actually want, which is exactly why they alarm you. The aim here is not to work out what a thought means, or to argue it away. It is to let it be there without letting it steer. If a thought involves hurting yourself or someone else, or you cannot put it down, please talk to someone — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What you were doing when it arrived (time of day, where you were, who was around)
The thought, in a few words — a short phrase is enough, you do not need to write it out in full
How hard it landed, 0–100, and where you felt it in your body
Write it again starting with “I'm having the thought that…” — then read both versions and notice the difference
Name the shape of it without arguing with it (a doubt, a what-if, a worst-case image, an urge to check)
What it would cost you to leave this one unanswered
What you felt pulled to do — check, replay it, avoid something, ask someone whether it's true
What that gave you in the moment, and what it cost an hour later
What you could try instead the next time it shows up
What you were heading toward before the thought interrupted
One small thing you'll do now, whether or not the thought is still there
If this keeps happening: who you'd tell, and the one sentence you'd open with

title: Sort Your Worries and Book a Worry Time
description: Worry spreads across the whole day unless it is given a place. This log helps you write each worry down, sort it into something you can act on or not, and save the rest for a set worry time.
intro_md: Worry is not a sign that something is wrong with you. It is the mind trying to get ahead of trouble, and it works better with a container. This is not a test and there are no right answers. Over the week you will note worries as they arrive, decide whether each one has an action attached, and keep the rest for a short daily worry time you choose. Nothing here needs to be tidy or complete.

fields.label: The time of day you will give to worry — 15 to 20 minutes, not too close to bed, and the same time each day if you can
Where you will sit for it, and what you will do the moment it ends (make tea, walk to the mailbox, put music on)
One row for each worry as it arrives during the week. If there is a next action, name it; if there is not, save the worry for worry time
Which saved worries still felt urgent when you sat down with them, and which had gone quiet by themselves
For the worries you cannot act on, what they seem to want from you — certainty, a promise it won't happen, someone to say it will be fine
One sentence you can say to a worry that has no action attached, in your own words — not a slogan, something you would actually say
What you noticed about the split between worries with an action and worries without one — was it even, or leaning one way?
How the worry time itself felt by day five or six compared with day one
One worry from the “act on it” column that you will take the next action on, and the day you will do it
What you would like to notice next week when a worry shows up outside worry time

title: Your Panic Plan for Before, During and After
description: Panic is frightening and fast, which is why a plan written while you are calm helps. This guides you through what to prepare, what to do when it peaks, and how to recover afterward without adding shame.
intro_md: A panic episode feels like an emergency, and the body behaves as if it is one, even when nothing dangerous is happening. Writing a plan now, in a quieter moment, means the calm part of you gets a say later. This is not a test and there is nothing to get right; the plan can be short and it can change. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The early signs that panic may be on its way — a flutter in the chest, a change in breathing, a sudden need to leave
Places, times, or situations where it has tended to show up, and any that you have started to avoid because of it
What you want to remember about panic itself — for example, that it peaks and passes, usually within minutes, and has never actually harmed you
One thing you will do with your breath or your feet — slow the out-breath, press your heels into the floor, name five things you can see
A sentence you will say to yourself, written the way you actually talk, not the way a poster would
What you will not do, if you can manage it — for example, not leaving the room, not checking your pulse, not calling for reassurance
How you will know it is easing, and what you will let your body do next — shake, sit, drink water, keep going
What you tend to tell yourself after an episode, and a kinder, more accurate version of the same sentence
Something ordinary you will do within the hour so the day does not become about the panic
A person who could know about this plan, and the one thing you would want them to do or not do
Where you will keep a short copy of this — phone notes, wallet, bedside — and the three lines from it you would want to read first

title: Following the “What If” to the End
description: A catastrophic thought usually stops at the scariest frame and stays there. This walks you down each “and then what?” rung, rates how likely each step really is, and looks at how you would cope.
intro_md: Anxious thoughts tend to jump straight to the worst picture and then freeze the film there, so you never get to see what happens next. This worksheet asks you to follow one “what if” all the way down, one rung at a time, and to rate each rung honestly. It is not a test and there are no right answers. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The “what if” thought, written exactly as it arrives — for example, “what if I freeze during the presentation?”
How much you believe it right now (0–100%), and what happens in your body when you read it back
Follow the thought down. Each row asks “and if that happened, then what?” about the row above, until there is nowhere left to go
The final rung — the very worst end point the thought was pointing to — written out plainly in one sentence
Roughly combine the likelihoods: how likely is the bottom rung once every single step has to happen, one after another?
Suppose the bottom rung happened anyway. What would the first week look like, and what would still be true about you and your life?
Which rung was the one your mind had actually been stuck on, and what it felt like to keep climbing past it
Read the first thought again. How much you believe it now (0–100%), and what, if anything, shifted
One short thing to say to yourself the next time this “what if” arrives, drawn from what you found lower on the ladder

title: The Safety Behaviors Inventory
description: Checking, asking for reassurance and avoiding all bring relief in the moment and feed anxiety over time. This helps you list what you lean on, see what it costs, and choose one to set down this week.
intro_md: Safety behaviors are the small things you do to feel safer when anxiety is up: rereading the email four times, asking someone whether it will be fine, taking the long way around. They are not weaknesses; they are sensible responses to fear that have quietly started charging rent. There is no score here and no verdict. The point is to see the full list, notice what each one does for you, and pick just one to try living without for a week.

fields.label: Everything you do to feel safer when anxious, however small — rereading, over-preparing, checking locks, asking “are you sure?”, sitting near the exit
Pick the one you do most. What it seems to protect you from, and what your anxiety says would happen if you stopped
How long the relief tends to last, and what usually happens to the worry after that
What the behavior has quietly cost — time, closeness with someone, a belief that you could not have coped without it
The one safety behavior you will set down this week — the easiest to drop, not the hardest; small counts
The prediction: what your anxiety says will happen without it, as specifically as you can, and how sure you are (0–100%)
What you will do instead in the moment — stay put, wait ten minutes, write the urge down — and who, if anyone, you will tell
Each day you managed without it, a line about what actually happened, and what the urge felt like as it passed
At the end of the week, compare what happened with the prediction. What was different, and what does that tell you about the behavior?
The next one you might set down, when you are ready — no date needed yet

title: Your Seven-Rung Exposure Ladder
description: Avoiding something feared keeps the fear fresh. This ladder helps you break one avoided situation into seven steps, predict what will happen at each, do it, and write down what actually happened.
intro_md: Facing something a little at a time, on purpose and often, is one of the most reliable ways to shrink a fear, and it works best when you choose the steps yourself. This is not a test and there is no pace you are supposed to keep. Some rungs will take a day, some a month. What matters is the comparison between what you predicted and what really happened, because that is where anxiety starts to lose its grip.

fields.label: The situation you have been avoiding, in plain words — driving on the highway, eating in front of others, calling the clinic
What avoiding it has cost you so far, and what you would do more of if it stopped being an issue
The top of the ladder: what would it look like to be able to do this the way you would like to?
Seven steps from easiest to hardest, each a little harder than the last. Fill in the prediction before, the result after — the result column is the important one
When you will do rung one — day, time, and how long you will stay in the situation (long enough for the fear to start dropping)
What you will not do while you are there, so the step counts — no phone, no leaving early, no quiet checking
After a few rungs, what you have noticed about the gap between prediction and result
Which rung you will repeat before moving on, and which one you can now skip
A sentence about what you have learned that you would not have believed at rung one
The next rung, and the day you will take it

title: Where Anxiety Lives in Your Body
description: Anxiety is felt before it is thought. This helps you map where it sits — jaw, chest, stomach, hands — what each part is doing, and what it might be asking for right now.
intro_md: Most of us try to think our way out of anxiety, but the body is usually where it shows up first and where it eases first too. This is a slow, curious look at what your body is doing when anxiety is present, one area at a time. It is not a test and there are no right answers. If a part of you is tight or restless, that is information, and often it is asking for something quite simple.

fields.label: How anxious you feel right now (1–10), and where you first noticed it in your body when you read that question
The jaw, forehead, eyes and scalp — what they are doing right now, and what they tend to do when anxiety is high
If your jaw or forehead could ask for one thing, what would it be — to unclench, to look away, to stop scanning?
The chest, shoulders and breath — tight, fast, shallow, held, heavy — describe what you find without trying to fix it
What the chest and breath seem to be bracing for, and what they might be asking for instead — a longer out-breath, a hand resting there, room
The stomach, hands and legs — churning, buzzing, cold, restless, weak — and what they do when anxiety spikes
What these parts want to do that you usually stop them doing — run, shake, curl up, move — and whether you could allow any of it for a minute
Reading back over the map, the one area that seems to carry the most, and what it is asking for in one line
Something small you can offer that part today — warmth, stillness, a stretch, permission to rest
How anxious you feel now (1–10), and what you would like to notice in your body the next time it starts to rise

title: The Post-Event Replay, Reframed
description: After a social moment, the mind often runs a harsh replay of everything you got wrong. This helps you set what you feared people noticed beside the evidence for what they actually saw.
intro_md: The replay after a conversation, a meeting, or a party can be crueler than the event itself, and it tends to play from the inside — what you felt — rather than from where other people were standing. This is not a test, and it is not about deciding you did fine. It is about putting the fear and the evidence side by side and seeing how much of the replay is memory and how much is anxiety filling in gaps.

fields.label: The situation — where you were, who was there, and roughly how long it lasted
How anxious you felt during it (1–10), and the moment that stands out most now
What the replay says you did wrong, in its own words — went red, said something stupid, went quiet, laughed too loud
What you fear other people noticed and concluded about you, as specifically as you can
How many times the replay has run since, and what it does to your body each time
What was actually visible or audible from where others stood — not what you felt, but what a camera would have picked up
Anything anyone actually said or did afterward — a text, a wave, a follow-up, or nothing either way
What you noticed about other people’s slips during the same event, and how much you have thought about those since
Put the feared conclusion beside the evidence. How much of the replay is remembered, and how much is anxiety filling gaps?
A fairer one-sentence account of how the event went, written the way a kind observer would tell it
The next similar situation coming up, and one thing you will let yourself do afterward instead of running the replay

title: Leaving One Thing Unchecked
description: Not knowing is often more uncomfortable than bad news. This experiment helps you deliberately leave one thing unchecked, unplanned or unresolved, predict what will happen, and then see what actually did.
intro_md: A lot of anxiety is not about danger but about not knowing, and the usual answer — check again, plan every step, settle it tonight — brings relief that does not last. This is an experiment, not a test. You choose one small thing to leave open on purpose, write down what you expect, sit with the discomfort for a while, and then compare. Whatever happens, the result is useful information, not a grade.

fields.label: The one thing you will leave unchecked, unplanned, or unresolved this week — an email you won't reread, a trip you won't map out, a question you won't settle tonight
Why this one: small enough to try, uncomfortable enough to count
How long you will leave it — an hour, a day, until Friday — and how you will stop yourself quietly checking anyway
What your anxiety says will happen if you leave it, in its own words, and how sure it is (0–100%)
How uncomfortable you expect to feel at the start (1–10), and how long you expect the discomfort to last
What you noticed in the first ten minutes — urges, thoughts, where it sat in your body
What you did with the urge each time it came back, and what happened to it when you did not act
How uncomfortable it actually got at its peak (1–10), and roughly when it began to ease
What actually happened to the thing you left open, set beside what anxiety predicted
What you learned about not knowing that you could only have learned by doing it, not by thinking about it
A slightly larger thing you could leave open next, and when you will try it

title: Sensation, Story and the Cost of Checking
description: A twinge becomes a story fast, and checking — feeling for it, searching online, asking — brings relief that fades. This sheet helps you note each sensation, the story it tells, and what checking gives and costs.
intro_md: Bodies make noises, twinges, aches and flutters all day, and an anxious mind is very good at turning one of them into a story with a frightening ending. This is not a test, and it is not a way of deciding what a sensation means medically — that is a conversation for you and a doctor. It is a noticing sheet: what you felt, what your mind made of it, what checking gave you, and what it quietly took.

fields.label: Each time a sensation catches your attention, one row — the feeling itself, the story that followed, what you did to check, and what that gave and cost
The story that comes up most often, followed to its end — what the sensation is supposed to mean and what happens next
How many times this exact story has turned out to be true so far, and how many times the sensation has faded on its own
The kinds of checking you do — pressing, looking, searching online, comparing, asking someone — and which one is hardest to leave alone
How long the relief tends to last after checking, and what the worry does once the relief wears off
What the checking has cost this week — hours, sleep, a conversation that turned into reassurance, trust in your own body
One sensation this week that you will notice, name, and leave alone for an hour before doing anything about it
What you will do with that hour instead, and what you will say to the urge when it comes back
What you would like to notice next week about how sensations behave when they are given a little time

title: Mapping the Morning Dread
description: For some people the hardest part of the day is the first hour. This maps what happens between waking and leaving the house, where the dread peaks, and which small changes in the routine might ease it.
intro_md: Waking with a knot already in your stomach is common, and it is not laziness or a bad attitude. Morning dread usually has a shape — a particular moment, a particular thought — and shapes can be worked with. This is not a test and there are no right answers. You will map an ordinary morning step by step, find where the dread rises and falls, and try one small change to the sequence.

fields.label: What you first notice on waking — before you open your eyes, before you check your phone — thought, feeling, and where it sits in the body
What your first thoughts are usually about: the day ahead, something from yesterday, a general sense that something is wrong
Your morning from waking to leaving the house (or starting the day), one step per row — alarm, phone, shower, coffee, dressing, the door
The step where the dread is highest, and what is happening in your mind and body at that moment
The step, if any, where it eases even slightly, and what is different about that one
Which parts of the routine feed the dread — checking messages first, rushing, silence, skipping breakfast — and which parts help
One change to the sequence you will try for a week — phone after coffee, curtains open first, the same song, five minutes outside
What you expect to happen to the peak (1–10) if you make that change, and how sure you are
After a week, the actual peak on most mornings (1–10), and what surprised you about it
What you want to keep, what you will drop, and one thing you will say to yourself tomorrow morning at the hardest step

title: Your Stress Early-Warning Signals
description: Stress rarely arrives all at once; it sends signals first. This helps you name the ones your body, mood and behavior send, and draw a personal yellow line and red line so you can act sooner.
intro_md: This is not a test, and there is no score at the end. Most of us only notice stress once it has already taken over the week. The idea here is simpler: get to know the small, early signs that are yours in particular, so that next time you can spot them a little sooner. There are no right answers. Your signals may look nothing like anyone else’s, and that is exactly the point.

fields.label: The first places stress shows up physically — a tight jaw, shallow breathing, a knot in your stomach, headaches, waking at 4 a.m.
What changes in how you eat, sleep or move when the pressure is building, even slightly
The feelings that creep in first — irritability, flatness, a short fuse, tearfulness, a dread you cannot pin on anything
What you start thinking about yourself or other people when you are getting stretched — “nobody helps”, “I can’t keep up”
What you do more of under stress — snapping, scrolling, skipping meals, saying yes to everything, working late
What you do less of — calling friends, cooking, exercise, the things you usually enjoy
What a partner, friend or coworker would say they see in you before you admit anything is wrong
A time someone noticed before you did. What did they say, and how did you respond?
Your yellow line: the two or three signals that mean “pay attention now” — still manageable, but time to ease off something
Your red line: the signals that mean “stop and get help with this” — the point past which pushing on has never worked for you
What you will do the next time you cross yellow — one concrete move, like canceling one thing or telling one person
Who you will tell when you reach red, and the words you would use

title: Seven Days of Energy Drains and Refills
description: A one-week log of what takes your energy and what gives it back. By day seven, you will see patterns you could not see from inside a single tiring day, and you can pick one refill to protect.
intro_md: Tiredness is not a personal failing and it is not laziness; it is usually a ledger that has quietly gone into the red. This log is not about doing more or judging how you spend your time. For seven days, jot down what drained you and what put something back, however small. Then look at the week as a whole. There are no right answers, only your own pattern coming into view.

fields.label: How you would describe your energy right now, in a sentence — and what you think is draining it most
Your guess at what refills you. Write it down now so you can compare it with what the week actually shows.
One line a day, at bedtime if you can. Small things count on both sides — a rude email drains, a good coffee refills.
The drains that showed up more than once. Name them plainly — a person, a task, a time of day, a habit.
The refills that showed up, even tiny ones — a walk, a joke, ten minutes alone in the car
Which drains surprised you, and which refills you had been dismissing as not counting
How your guess from before the week compared with what you actually recorded
One refill you will make room for next week, and the day and time it goes in
One drain you can shrink by a small amount — leave a meeting early, batch the emails, say no to one request
What you will notice at bedtime next week to tell whether the change made a difference

title: A Burnout Map: What Each Part Is Protecting
description: Burnout tends to show up in three ways: exhaustion, cynicism and feeling ineffective. This walks you through each one and asks what it might be protecting you from, so you can respond with understanding instead of more effort.
intro_md: This is not a checklist for whether you are “burned out”, and there is nothing to score. Burnout is usually a reasonable response to too much for too long, and each part of it is trying to do something useful: exhaustion asks you to stop, cynicism keeps you from caring about what keeps hurting, and feeling ineffective lowers the bar so you can survive. Mapping them is a way of listening, not a verdict.

fields.label: How tired you are, described honestly — not just short on sleep, but the kind of tired that rest does not seem to touch
What your exhaustion stops you from doing, and what it might be trying to stop you from doing
The things or people you have gone cold on — the work, the clients, the family, the cause you used to believe in
Finish this: “If I let myself care about that again, I would have to feel…”
Where you feel you are no longer any good — and how that compares with what you actually got done this week
Finish this: “If I admitted I am still capable, then I would be expected to…”
Exhaustion is a brake. If it were not there, what would you keep doing, and for how much longer?
Cynicism is armor. What hurt was it fitted for, and when did you put it on?
Feeling ineffective lowers the bar. Whose standard was the old bar, and what has it cost you to keep reaching for it?
What each part would need in order to stand down a little — real rest for the brake, some safety for the armor, a fair standard instead of an impossible one
One thing you will hand back, pause or ask for this week, and who you will say it to
A sentence to say to yourself the next time the tiredness or the cold feeling shows up, that treats it as a message rather than a flaw

title: What I Can Put Down
description: Some of what is weighing on you is not really yours to carry, and some of it can be made smaller. This sorts your obligations into keep, shrink, delegate and drop, and gets you started on one of them.
intro_md: This is an inventory, not a test of how much you can handle. When everything feels heavy, it is hard to see that the load is made of separate pieces, and that not all of them have to stay exactly as they are. Nothing you write here commits you to anything. You are just laying the pieces out on the table and looking at them one at a time. There are no right answers.

fields.label: The obligations on your plate right now, big and small — the job, the school run, the aging parent, the committee, the friend who always needs you
Which of these you chose, which were handed to you, and which you simply drifted into
Take each obligation in turn. Be honest in the second column — “everyone” is rarely the real answer.
The items you marked “keep”. What makes them worth keeping — do they matter to you, or would you just feel guilty without them?
The items you could shrink. What would a smaller version look like — fewer hours, a lower standard, once a month instead of every week?
The items someone else could carry, and what stops you from asking — pride, guilt, a belief that they would do it wrong
The items you could drop entirely. What is the worst that would actually happen, and who would honestly mind?
The one item you will shrink, delegate or drop first — pick the easiest, not the most important
The exact words you will use to hand it over, scale it back or decline it, and who will hear them
When you will do it, and what you will do with the ten minutes or ten hours it gives back

title: A Recovery Day That Is Not a To-Do List
description: A day off often turns into chores, errands and catching up, and you end it as tired as you started. This helps you plan a day that actually restores you, and notice afterward what worked.
intro_md: This is not a schedule and there is nothing to complete. A recovery day is not a productive day in disguise, and it is not a reward you have to earn. It is a day whose only job is to leave you with slightly more than you started with. Plan it loosely before, notice how it goes during, and look back gently afterward. If you spend it doing nothing at all, that counts.

fields.label: What has worn you down lately — the kind of tired it is, and where you feel it
What you usually do with a free day, and how you feel at the end of it. Be honest about the laundry.
The things you are tempted to sneak in “because you have the time” — write them down here so they stay here
What actually restores you, as opposed to what merely distracts you — quiet, movement, people, water, making something, being outdoors
The one or two things you would genuinely like the day to include, held lightly rather than scheduled
What you will say to yourself, or to others, when the pull toward getting things done shows up
The date, and what you will do about your phone, your inbox and anyone likely to need you
Jot down as you go: what you did, whether it left you fuller or emptier, and any guilt that showed up
How you felt at the end of it compared with the end of a normal free day
What surprised you — what restored you more than expected, and what turned out to be a chore in disguise
The one thing from this day you could give yourself in a smaller dose during an ordinary week, and when

title: Your Coping Strategies, Audited
description: Everything you reach for under stress does something for you, even the things you wish you did not do. This lays them side by side — what each gives, what it costs — and helps you choose one swap.
intro_md: This is not a list of good habits and bad habits, and there is no score. Every coping strategy you have was learned because it worked at least once. The wine, the scrolling, the overworking, the long run, the phone call to your sister — each one gives you something. The only questions here are what it gives, what it costs, and whether a cheaper way to get the same thing might exist. There are no right answers.

fields.label: The things you do when the pressure is on, without editing the list — the helpful ones, the ones you are not proud of, the ones you barely notice
The one you reach for first, before you have even decided to. What is the trigger that sends you to it?
One strategy per row. Fill in the gives column before the costs column, and be fair to both.
What the “gives” column has in common — relief, numbness, control, company, a break from thinking. Name the need underneath.
The costs you had been quietly paying without adding them up — sleep, money, mornings, trust, self-respect
The strategies that give a lot and cost little. Why do you not reach for those first?
One strategy you would like to swap, and what it is really giving you that the replacement will have to give as well
The replacement — something that meets the same need, is available at the same moment, and that you would actually do
How you will remember the swap in the moment — a note on the fridge, a word on your phone, something moved out of reach
Afterward: the first time you tried the swap, what happened, and whether the need underneath was met

title: Pressure Versus Capacity: This Month’s Balance Sheet
description: Stress is the gap between what is coming at you and what you have to meet it. This puts this month’s pressures and your capacity on one page so you can see that gap and adjust either side.
intro_md: This is a balance sheet, not a test, and nothing here gets scored. Feeling overwhelmed is not a sign that you are weak; it usually means the pressure on you has outgrown the capacity you have available this month, and both of those things move. Writing them down side by side takes the vagueness out of “too much”. There are no right answers, and a month with a big gap is information, not a failure.

fields.label: What this month holds that other months do not — deadlines, visitors, a move, a school break, a medical appointment, an anniversary
The ongoing pressures that are always there underneath — the commute, money, a hard relationship, a demanding role
Your capacity this month — sleep, health, help at home, money, time off, people you can lean on, the parts of the month that are actually calm
What has quietly shrunk your capacity lately, and what has quietly added to it
Put pressures and capacity in the same table, one per row, so you can see both sides at once.
Looking at both sides, how big is the gap this month, in your own words — and is it wider or narrower than last month?
Which pressures are genuinely fixed, and which only feel fixed because you have not asked
One pressure you will reduce, postpone or share this month, and the first step
One piece of capacity you will add or protect — an early night, a boundary, a hand you accept
The date you will look at this sheet again to see whether the gap moved

title: Saying Out Loud That You’re Stretched
description: Telling a manager or a family member that you are at capacity is hard when you are used to coping quietly. This helps you decide what to say, say it plainly, and handle the reply.
intro_md: This is a script to draft, not a test to pass. Many people carry too much for a long time because saying so feels like admitting failure, or because they cannot find words that are honest without sounding like a complaint. You do not have to get the conversation perfect. You just need a clear ask, a plain sentence about how things are, and a plan for what you will do if the answer is not the one you hoped for.

fields.label: The person you need to tell — a manager, a partner, a parent, a friend — and what you are hoping will be different afterward
What has stopped you saying it so far — fear of looking weak, not wanting to burden them, the belief that it would not change anything
What it is costing you to keep coping quietly, for you and for them
The plain facts of how stretched you are — hours, sleep, what has slipped, what you have stopped doing — without softening or exaggerating
What you are asking for, specifically — a deadline moved, a task shared, an evening a week, someone else on the school run
Your opening sentence, in your own words. Something like “I need to tell you something I have been sitting on for a while.”
The two or three sentences that say how things are, using “I” and the facts from above rather than “you never” or “everyone expects”
The ask, said once, clearly, and then a pause. Write the exact words, and write “pause” after them.
The replies you are dreading — “we are all busy”, “you should have said sooner”, “I can’t do anything about that” — and one calm sentence for each
What you will do if the answer is no. Who else you could tell, what you could put down anyway, what you will not go back to doing.
When and where you will have the conversation, and how you will settle yourself in the minutes before
Afterward: what you actually said, how they responded, and what it was like to hear yourself say it out loud

title: Five Two-Minute Resets for a Day With No Free Hour
description: On the days when rest is out of the question, two minutes is still possible. This helps you plan five tiny resets into the gaps that already exist, and see whether they change how the day ends.
intro_md: This is not another thing to fit in, and it is not a test. Some days have no hour to spare, and telling yourself to “take a break” on those days only adds to the load. A two-minute reset is small enough to fit between one thing and the next: a few slow breaths at the sink, a look out of a window, feet flat on the floor for one song. Nothing here needs to be done well, only tried.

fields.label: The kind of day this is for — back-to-back meetings, a shift, a day with small children, a hospital day — and what it usually leaves you feeling by evening
The gaps that already exist, even if they are only ninety seconds — the kettle, the elevator, the walk to the car, the wait for a file to load
Things that settle you a little, fast — slow breathing, cold water on the wrists, stretching your neck, stepping outside, a photo you love, eyes closed in silence
What tends to derail a break, even a tiny one — picking up the phone, someone finding you, the feeling that you have not earned it
Five resets, each tied to a gap you already have. Fill the last column at the end of the day.
How you will remember each one — an alarm with a kind label, a sticky note, tying it to something you already do
What you will say to yourself if you miss two or three of them, so that missing one does not cancel the rest
How the day ended compared with a normal day of this kind — steadier, about the same, worse
Which reset you would keep even on an ordinary day, and the one you would swap for something else
One person you could tell about this, so that they know why you have gone quiet for two minutes

title: Rewriting Your Stress Story
description: Under pressure most of us repeat one sentence to ourselves — “I can’t cope”, “I have to do it all”. This helps you catch yours, check it against the evidence, and write a truer one to carry instead.
intro_md: This is not an exercise in correcting your thinking, and there is no right sentence at the end. The line you say to yourself under pressure was probably learned early and has probably kept you going more than once. It is not stupid and it is not the enemy. But it may be out of date, and it may be making the pressure heavier than it needs to be. The aim is a sentence that is truer, not just nicer.

fields.label: A recent moment when the pressure spiked — the email, the school call, the deadline moving, the third thing going wrong before nine
The sentence that ran through your head, word for word if you can — “I can’t do this”, “it’s all on me”, “if I stop, everything falls apart”
How your body responded to that sentence, and what you did in the next ten minutes
Who else in your life says or said a sentence like this — a parent, a boss, a coach — and in what tone of voice
A time when the sentence was true, or nearly true. What was happening then, and how old were you?
What the sentence does for you under pressure — keeps you moving, stops you asking for help, spares you from disappointing anyone
What it costs you — sleep, the ability to stop, the chance to be helped, the way you speak to yourself at midnight
The evidence the sentence leaves out — the times you did cope, the help that exists, the things that did not fall apart when you paused
A truer sentence. Not a slogan, and not the opposite of the old one — something you could say out loud without rolling your eyes.
Say both sentences slowly. What happens in your shoulders, your breathing and your urge to rush with each one?
Where you will keep the new sentence so it is there when the pressure spikes — a lock screen, a card in your wallet, a note on the monitor
The next time the old sentence shows up, what happened when you answered it with the new one — and what you would change about the wording

title: Seven Nights of Sleep, Written Down
description: A week-long log of when you went to bed, when you actually slept, what woke you and how rested you felt, so you can see your real pattern instead of the one you assume.
intro_md: This is a diary, not a test. Most of us guess at our sleep, and the guesses are usually gloomier than the record. For seven mornings, jot down roughly what happened — no stopwatch, no checking the clock through the night, just your best estimate over breakfast. At the end of the week you read it back and look for patterns. Nothing here is a verdict about you; it is simply information you did not have before.

fields.label: Fill in one row each morning, from memory and roughly. Guessing is fine; watching the clock all night is not the point.
For each night, note anything from the day before that might matter — caffeine after lunch, a late meal, alcohol, a screen in bed, exercise, an argument, a nap.
Read the week back. Which night felt best, and what was different about that day or evening?
Which night was roughest, and what surrounded it — not to blame anything, just to notice
How big is the gap between getting into bed and lights out? What fills it — a phone, a book, talking, staring at the ceiling?
Do the wake-ups cluster at a certain hour, or follow certain evenings? Write what you see, even if it is “no pattern at all”
Before this week, how would you have described your sleep in one sentence?
Now that you have the record, does that sentence still hold? What would you change about it?
One small thing the diary suggests trying next week — an earlier last coffee, lights out closer to bed time, the phone charging elsewhere
Which nights you will try it, and what you will look for in the diary afterwards

title: Build Your Wind-Down Hour
description: Plan the last sixty minutes before lights out in four fifteen-minute blocks, starting from what genuinely settles you rather than from anyone else’s idea of a perfect bedtime routine.
intro_md: There is no correct wind-down routine, only the one you will actually do. This sheet starts with how your evenings go now, then asks what settles you and what merely feels restful while quietly keeping you awake. From there you build the last hour before lights out in four short blocks. Keep it modest. An hour you can repeat on an ordinary Tuesday is worth far more than a beautiful one you manage twice.

fields.label: Walk through last night. From an hour before lights out, what did you actually do, in order?
Which parts of that hour left you more awake than before — a work email, the news, a game that was hard to stop?
Things that reliably settle you, even a little — a shower, stretching, a dull book, tidying one surface, talking to someone, a warm drink without caffeine
Things that feel like rest but tend to wake you up — scrolling, one more episode, reading about sleep at midnight. Be honest, not harsh.
Sixty to forty-five minutes before lights out. What happens in this block, and where in the house?
Forty-five to thirty minutes before. Ideally the screens are put down somewhere here — what takes their place?
Thirty to fifteen minutes before. The quieter, slower things go here — what are they for you?
The last fifteen minutes. What happens between the bathroom and the light going off?
The cue that starts the hour — an alarm with a kind label, the dishwasher going on, the dog’s last walk. Something outside your willpower.
What is most likely to derail it this week, and what you will do when that happens rather than abandoning the whole hour
The first night you will try it, and one thing to notice the next morning — how quickly you fell asleep, or simply how the hour felt

title: What Wakes You at 3 a.m.
description: Work out what tends to wake you in the small hours, what those thoughts look like by daylight, and a clear plan for what to do instead of lying there arguing with them.
intro_md: Thoughts at 3 a.m. are not the thoughts you would have at 3 p.m., even when the words match. The night removes distraction, adds tiredness and makes everything feel urgent and unsolvable. This sheet is not about stopping the thoughts; it is about knowing what to do when they arrive so the night does not become a fight. There are no right answers. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What tends to wake you — a thought, a full bladder, a sound, heat, or nothing you can name? And roughly what time?
The thoughts that show up once you are awake. Write a few of them down as they actually sound, not tidied up.
What you usually do next — check the phone, look at the clock, argue with the thought, plan, lie very still and hope
Take one of those thoughts. How does it look at 3 in the afternoon, with coffee and other people around?
What does the night add to it — no distraction, tiredness, the feeling that this must be solved right now?
What can genuinely be done about it at 3 a.m.? Usually the honest answer is nothing until morning. Write yours.
A sentence to write on a notepad by the bed so the thought is kept for morning — “Email Dana about the invoice. Not now.”
A phrase to say to yourself, in your own words, that admits the worry is real and still lets it wait
If you are still awake after what feels like twenty minutes, what you will get up and do — somewhere dim, something dull, no screens
What you will not do, and where the phone and clock will be so that choice is easy
What tells you it is time to go back to bed — heavy eyes, a yawn, the thought losing its grip
After the next 3 a.m. waking: what you did, how it went, and one thing you would keep

title: Bedroom and Evening Audit
description: Walk through light, noise, screens, caffeine, alcohol and temperature in your room and your evening, notice what is quietly working against you, and choose one change worth trying.
intro_md: Some of what keeps you awake is not in your head at all. It is a streetlight, a phone on the pillow, a coffee at four, a room two degrees too warm. This sheet walks through six ordinary factors and asks how each one actually is right now — not how it should be. You then pick one change. Only one. Nothing here is a judgment on how you live; it is a look around the room.

fields.label: One row each for light, noise, screens, caffeine, alcohol and temperature. Say how it really is on a normal night, whether it helps or hinders, and one possible change.
Which row surprised you, or was harder to answer honestly than you expected?
Which one have you known about for a while without changing? What has kept it in place — habit, comfort, someone else’s preference?
What is genuinely outside your control — a neighbor, a partner’s schedule, a baby, a thin wall — and what is still left to work with around it?
The one change you will try, described so plainly that tonight-you cannot misunderstand it
What would make it easy tonight — the charger moved now, the thermostat set now, the last coffee decided in advance
If the change affects someone else in the house, what you will say to them, in a sentence or two
After a week: what actually changed, if anything, and how you slept compared with before
Keep it, adjust it, or drop it and try the next row? Write what you have decided and why.

title: Why You Stay Up When You’re Tired
description: Map what the late hours give you that the day does not, what tomorrow pays for it, and how to bring some of that night-time freedom into daylight without a rule you will break.
intro_md: Staying up late while exhausted is rarely a discipline problem. More often the night is the only stretch of the day that belongs to you, and going to bed means giving it up. This sheet treats that as information. It asks what the late hours are giving you, what they cost, and whether any of it could be reclaimed earlier. There is no bedtime rule at the end, only a gentler stop.

fields.label: This week, roughly when you meant to sleep and when you actually did. A few nights is enough.
What you were actually doing in that gap — the specific show, app, task, snack, or simply sitting in the quiet
The moment you noticed you were tired and kept going anyway. What did you tell yourself?
Finish this: “The night is the only time I get to…”
What the day takes from you that the night hands back — privacy, choice, silence, not being needed by anyone
Who you get to be at midnight that you do not get to be at 2 p.m.
What tomorrow-you pays for it, honestly — the morning, the mood, the things that felt harder than they should have
The trade you are making, written as one plain sentence: “I give up X tomorrow to have Y tonight.”
One thing from the late hours that could happen earlier — twenty minutes of the show at eight, a closed door at seven, the walk before dinner
What you would need to protect it — a word with someone, a phone on silent, a lower bar for what counts as “time to myself”
A stop signal that is not a rule — “when this episode ends”, an alarm labeled with something kind, the kettle for the last drink
Tonight’s plan in two lines, and one thing to notice tomorrow morning

title: Naps and Daytime Rest Around a Hard Schedule
description: For shift workers, new parents and anyone whose nights are not their own, a way to find and protect real rest windows in the day, with or without actual sleep.
intro_md: If your sleep comes in pieces because of shifts, a baby, or caring for someone, the usual advice about eight unbroken hours can feel like a joke. This sheet works with the schedule you actually have. It looks for windows, decides what a nap or a rest could look like in each, and asks what you need from other people to protect them. Rest that is not sleep still counts here.

fields.label: Your schedule this week, as it really is — shifts, feeds, school runs, the hours nobody else can cover
When your longest stretch of sleep tends to happen, and roughly how long it is
The hour of the day when you are most wiped, and what you usually push through it with
For each day, find one window where rest is possible even if sleep is not. Afterwards, note whether you took it and how it went.
A short nap of around twenty minutes usually leaves you clearer; ninety lets you finish a full cycle. Which suits your windows, and what will wake you?
What makes the room dark and quiet enough — a mask, earplugs, a fan, a towel over the curtain rail, the baby monitor turned down but not off
What counts as rest when sleep is not possible — lying down with eyes closed, sitting in the parked car, ten minutes on the floor with the door shut
What you need from someone else to make even one window happen, and who that person is
The words you will use to ask — plain, specific, without apologizing: “Can you take the 6 to 7 feed on Tuesday so I can lie down?”
The one window this week you will protect no matter what, and what you will notice about the rest of that day

title: The Fear of Not Sleeping
description: Set the fears about a bad night next to what bad nights have actually cost you, and find a calmer sentence to reach for when sleep will not come.
intro_md: Worrying about not sleeping is one of the most reliable ways to stay awake, which is unfair. This sheet does not tell you the worry is silly. It asks you to write the fear down, then check it against your own record of bad nights and the days that followed. Most people find the days were harder than usual and still happened. There is no score, and no right amount of sleep here.

fields.label: What you tell yourself when you cannot sleep — “I’ll be useless tomorrow”, “I can’t cope on less than seven”, “this is going to become a thing”
Where that worry shows up in your body once it starts — the jaw, the chest, the legs that will not settle
What you do to try to force sleep, and honestly how well that works
Bad nights you remember. For each, note roughly how much you slept, what you feared for the next day, what the day was actually like, and the real cost.
Read the table back. What do you notice about the gap between the feared cost and the real one?
Things you have done on very little sleep that turned out fine enough — a shift, a drive, a hard conversation, a whole first year of a child’s life
Rewrite the sentence from the first box into something you could actually believe at 2 a.m. — not cheerful, just accurate
What a friend who sleeps badly and still manages would say to you about tomorrow
What you will do when sleep will not come — rest still counts. Lying quietly in the dark is not the same as failing.
The next bad night: before you get up, predict tomorrow’s cost out of ten. At the end of that day, write the real number beside it.

title: Anchor Your Mornings
description: Choose one wake time you can keep every day, plan where your morning light will come from, and track a week of it to see what steadier mornings do to your nights.
intro_md: If you want to move your sleep, the morning is the easier end to hold. A wake time that stays the same and daylight soon after it are two of the steadiest signals your body listens to. This sheet helps you pick an anchor you can actually keep — including on weekends and after a bad night — and plan where the light comes from. It is a plan to try, not a rule to fail.

fields.label: Your wake times this week, weekdays and weekend. How far apart are the earliest and the latest?
What the first thirty minutes after waking usually look like — phone in bed, straight to the kids, coffee in a dark kitchen?
How much actual daylight you get before noon on a normal day, and where
The wake time you could keep seven days a week, even after a rough night. Choose the one you can hold, not the one you admire.
What you would have to give up on weekends to keep it, and whether that trade seems worth a month’s trial
Where the light will come from within an hour of waking — a walk, the porch with coffee, breakfast by the brightest window, the bus stop
How long, realistically. Ten minutes outside beats thirty minutes planned and skipped.
Fill in each morning. In the evening, note how sleepy you felt at bedtime.
What is most likely to get in the way — a late night, rain, a sick child — and the smallest version of the anchor on that day
What you will look for after the week: falling asleep faster, waking before the alarm, evenings feeling different

title: Which Kind of Rest Are You Missing
description: Take stock of seven kinds of rest — physical, mental, sensory, creative, emotional, social and spiritual — to see which are running low and why more sleep alone has not fixed your tiredness.
intro_md: Tiredness is not always a sleep problem. You can sleep eight hours and still wake depleted because the rest you are short of is a different kind — a break from noise, from deciding, from being needed, from performing. This sheet lists seven kinds of rest and asks how full each tank is right now. There is no score to add up. The point is to notice which one you keep reaching past.

fields.label: One row each for physical, mental, sensory, creative, emotional, social and spiritual rest. Rate how full each feels, then what drains it and what refills it for you.
The two lowest rows. Does that match how you would have described your tiredness before you filled it in?
Which kind of rest do you never think about? Sensory and emotional rest are the ones most people forget exist.
Which tank is actually fairly full? Is it possible you keep topping up that one because it is easy, while the low one stays low?
What you reach for when you are tired — scrolling, sleeping in, snacks, a show — and which kind of rest, if any, it actually gives you
Why more sleep on its own has not been enough lately, in your own words
The one kind of rest you will top up this week, and what refills it, from your table
A ten-minute version of that — a walk without earbuds, a door closed, a page of drawing, a conversation with someone who asks nothing of you
When it will happen, on which days, and what you will notice about your tiredness afterwards

title: The Nights Before a Big Day
description: A before, during and after plan for the nights leading up to an interview, exam, flight or difficult conversation, so the pressure to sleep well does not become the thing that keeps you up.
intro_md: The night before something important is often the worst night to try to sleep, precisely because it matters. This sheet plans backwards from the big day: the night two days out, which counts more than people think, the night before, and the morning itself. It also looks at what you have already managed on poor sleep. It is not a promise of a perfect night, just a way to take the pressure off one.

fields.label: What is coming, when, and what feels at stake in it
What nights before big days have been like for you in the past — the pattern, if there is one
Finish this: “If I don’t sleep well the night before, then…”
Something important you got through on a poor night’s sleep, and how it actually went
Two nights before is the one that matters most and the one nobody worries about. What is the plan for that evening and lights out?
The evening before: what you will do, what you will avoid, and when the phone goes away. Keep it ordinary, not special.
If you are awake at 1 a.m., what you will do — rest with eyes closed, get up for a dim, dull twenty minutes, read the sentence below
What will be set out so the morning takes care of itself — clothes, documents, the route, breakfast
How the morning starts, step by step, so there are no decisions to make before you are properly awake
A sentence to carry into the day, whatever the night was like — “I have done hard things tired before”
Afterwards: how you slept, how the day actually went, and the one part of this plan you would keep for next time

title: A Transcript of Your Inner Critic
description: The voice that tells you you’re not enough is easier to answer once you’ve written down exactly what it says. This worksheet helps you catch it word for word, work out whose voice it borrowed, and write a reply.
intro_md: This is not a test, and there are no right answers. The inner critic is not proof of anything about you — it is a habit of speech, usually learned early, that believes it is keeping you safe. Writing its lines down takes some of the power out of them. You will finish by answering it in your own voice, which may feel strange at first. That is fine.

fields.label: A recent moment when the critic got loud — a mistake, a message you sent, a mirror, a meeting
Write down what it said, as close to word for word as you can, in the second person: “You always…”, “Nobody…”
Its tone. Is it sneering, tired, panicky, cold? Does it shout or mutter?
Whose voice does it sound like — a parent, a teacher, a coach, an ex, a version of yourself at a certain age?
The earliest time you can remember hearing something like this said to you or about you
Finish this: “If I stopped listening to the critic, it is afraid that I would…”
fields.section: What it is trying to prevent

fields.label: What it thinks will happen if it goes quiet — that you’ll get lazy, get hurt, get found out, get left?
fields.section: What it is trying to prevent

fields.label: Is there a grain of something useful under the cruelty — a real wish to do well, to be liked, to be safe?
fields.section: What it is trying to prevent

fields.label: Now write a reply, in your own voice, as you would to a frightened person who is being rude to you. Firm, not cruel.
One sentence from that reply short enough to say under your breath next time it starts
Read the transcript and the reply aloud. Which one sounds more like a grown-up? Which one would you rather listen to?
Next time you hear the critic this week, what will you notice first — the words, the tone, or the feeling in your body?

title: The Good Enough Experiment
description: Perfectionism promises that extra effort will keep you safe, but rarely gets tested. This worksheet helps you do one ordinary task at about 80 percent, predict the fallout, and then record what actually happened.
intro_md: This is an experiment, not an exam. Nobody is going to grade the result, including you. The idea is simple: pick one low-stakes task, do it deliberately less than perfectly, and find out what really follows. Some people discover that no one notices. Some discover that they feel worse than expected, which is also useful information. Either way, you learn something you cannot learn by thinking about it.

fields.label: The task you’ll do at about 80 percent — an email, a meal, a report, tidying a room. Pick something with low stakes.
What 100 percent would look like for this task, honestly: the rereads, the extra checks, the time it usually eats
What 80 percent will look like instead. Be concrete: one draft and send, twenty minutes and stop, no second coat.
Before you start, what you expect will go wrong, and how bad you think it will feel (1–10)
Who you imagine noticing the difference, and what you imagine them thinking
Day and time you’ll do it. Write it down like an appointment.
While you were doing it: the moment you most wanted to go back and fix, polish, or check. What did you do instead?
Prediction versus result. Fill in the left column before, the right two after.
Did anyone notice? If so, what did they actually say — not what you read into their face
How long the discomfort lasted, and what it was like an hour later
What the extra 20 percent usually buys you, now that you have seen what happens without it
The next task you’ll try at 80 percent, and one thing you’ll do differently this time

title: Unpacking One Shame Moment
description: Shame makes you want to disappear, which is exactly why it stays hidden. This worksheet walks you slowly through one recent moment — what set it off, what you believed about yourself, who you hid from, and what you needed.
intro_md: Go gently here. Shame is the feeling that something is wrong with who you are, not just with what you did, and it thrives on silence. Writing it down is a way of breaking that silence in private, on your own terms. This is not a confession and there are no right answers. Pick one moment, recent enough to remember clearly, and small enough to look at without being flooded.

fields.label: The moment, in a few plain sentences. Where you were, who was there, what happened.
What set it off — a look, a comment, a silence, a mistake, being seen doing something ordinary?
What shame felt like in your body: heat in the face, a drop in the stomach, wanting to shrink or leave
Finish this: “In that moment, what I believed about myself was that I am…”
How old that belief feels. Is it new, or is it one you have carried for a long time?
Who you hid from afterward — someone in the room, someone you would normally tell, or yourself
How you hid: went quiet, made a joke, changed the subject, left, replayed it alone at night
What you were afraid they would see if you hadn’t hidden
What you actually needed in that moment — to be reassured, to be told it was human, to be left alone kindly, to laugh with someone
Who in your life could have given you that, if they had known
Imagine a friend describing this exact moment to you. Write what you would say to them, word for word.
One person you could tell a small version of this story to this week, and the first sentence you would use

title: Your Evidence File
description: Low self-esteem runs on a filter that keeps the misses and drops the rest. This worksheet has you collect seven days of small things you did competently or kindly, so the record is finally complete.
intro_md: This is not a brag sheet and there are no right answers. Most people find it surprisingly hard at first, because the filter has been running for years and the evidence feels too small to count. Count it anyway. Holding a door, answering an email well, noticing someone was tired — it all goes in. You are not deciding whether you are a good person. You are just keeping better records.

fields.label: Before you start: how you would describe yourself on a bad day, in a sentence. Keep it — you will read it again at the end.
What usually happens when you do something well — you forget it, explain it away, say anyone could have done it?
One row a day for a week. Anything done competently or kindly, however small. Fill it in before bed.
Which entry was hardest to write down, and what you told yourself while writing it
A pattern you notice across the seven rows — a quality that keeps showing up under different names
Read your bad-day sentence again. Does the table agree with it? Where exactly do they disagree?
What someone who only had this table, and nothing else, would conclude about you
One entry you would be willing to let yourself feel a little good about. Sit with it for a minute and write what that was like.
Where you will keep the file next week — a note on your phone, a page in a notebook — and when you will add to it

title: The Comparison Detox
description: Comparing yourself to other people is automatic, and it almost always uses a picture with half the details missing. This worksheet helps you name who you compare yourself to, on what, and what you never get to see.
intro_md: There are no right answers here, and comparing is not a flaw — every human mind does it. The trouble is that it compares your whole life, including the parts only you can see, against the edited version of someone else’s. This is a chance to lay the comparisons out in daylight, fill in what is missing from the picture, and decide what you would rather do with that attention.

fields.label: The people you find yourself measuring against most often — a sibling, a colleague, a friend, someone online you have never met
Where you usually see them: in person, on a screen, in your memory, in what other people tell you about them
One row per comparison. Be specific about what you compare, and honest about what you cannot see.
Pick the comparison that stings most. What do you actually know about that person’s week — sleep, money, health, worries, what they gave up?
What you are comparing against them — your unfiltered inside, or the version of you that other people see?
Something in your life that someone else might be comparing themselves to right now, without you knowing
What the comparing gives you — a push to try harder, a reason to stay small, a way to feel bad that at least feels familiar?
What it costs you in an ordinary week: time, mood, the ability to enjoy what you have
One feed, habit, or situation you will reduce or step away from for the next seven days
fields.section: A week with less of it

fields.label: What you’ll do with the attention you get back — something you want to get better at for its own sake, not to catch up with anyone
fields.section: A week with less of it

fields.label: At the end of the week: what changed, and which comparison came back first
fields.section: A week with less of it

title: The Rules I Live By
description: Most of the pressure you feel comes from rules you never chose out loud — the shoulds and musts running in the background. This worksheet helps you write them down, find where they came from, and loosen one on purpose.
intro_md: This is not a test and there is nothing wrong with having rules. Some of yours have served you well. The problem is the ones that were handed to you before you could refuse them, that no longer fit, and that punish you every time you fall short. Writing them out is the first step to deciding which ones are still yours. Nobody is asking you to throw them all away.

fields.label: The shoulds and musts you hear most often in your own head. Write at least five, in their exact wording: “I should always…”, “I must never…”
The rule that is loudest right now, and what happened this week when you broke it or nearly did
For the loudest rule: where it came from. A person, a household, a school, a job, a hard time when it kept you safe
Who else lived by this rule, and how it worked out for them
What the rule is protecting you from — being criticized, being needy, being ordinary, being caught off guard?
What keeping it costs you — in rest, in honesty, in relationships, in things you don’t try
What you would think of a friend who broke this rule. Be honest: is it the same standard you hold yourself to?
The one rule you are willing to loosen. Not abolish — loosen. Rewrite it with a “sometimes”, a “usually”, or an “unless”.
What you predict will happen the first time you act on the looser version
A specific situation this week where you will try the looser rule, and what you’ll do differently in it
Afterward: what actually happened, how it felt, and whether the old rule was right

title: The Self-Talk Swap
description: You would never coach anyone the way you talk to yourself. This worksheet puts your harshest sentences next to what a good coach would say instead, so you can hear the difference and practice one swap.
intro_md: There are no right answers here, and the goal is not to replace harsh talk with empty cheerleading. A good coach is honest. They notice what went wrong, they want you to improve, and they know that contempt makes people worse at things, not better. This is about tone and intent, not pretending. Write the harsh sentences exactly as they sound; you will not be graded on them.

fields.label: The things you most often say to yourself after a mistake, a slow day, or a look in the mirror. Get the actual wording.
Picture someone you respect — a coach, a mentor, a steady friend — saying those same sentences to a person they cared about. What happens in you?
One harsh sentence per row, then the coach’s version. The coach can be direct, but never cruel.
columns: What a good coach would say

fields.label: Read the coach column aloud. What is different about it — not just the words, but what it assumes about you?
Which swap felt fake or too soft, and how you could make it truer without making it meaner
What the harsh version believes about how people change, and whether that has ever actually worked on you
The one swap you will practice this week. Write both sentences here so you can find them fast.
Where you will meet the harsh sentence this week — the situation, the time of day — and how you will catch it
At the end of the week: how many times you caught it, what you said instead, and what changed, if anything

title: Strengths in Context
description: Listing your strengths can feel hollow when you don’t believe them. This worksheet asks for five qualities and, for each, a real moment when it actually helped someone — so the strengths come with evidence attached.
intro_md: There are no right answers and no tidy list of approved virtues. A strength here is anything about you that has been useful to another person: patience, noticing, humor, stubbornness, the ability to sit with someone who is upset. If you cannot think of five, ask someone who knows you, or start with what people thank you for. The moments matter more than the labels.

fields.label: What people tend to thank you for, come to you for, or say “you’re good at that” about — even if you brush it off
A quality in you that has caused trouble sometimes but has also, in the right place, been exactly what was needed
Quality one, named in a word or two, and a specific time it actually helped someone — who, when, what you did
Quality two, and a specific time it helped someone
Quality three, and a specific time it helped someone
Quality four, and a specific time it helped someone
Quality five, and a specific time it helped someone
Which of the five moments was hardest to write, and what got in the way — modesty, doubt, the feeling it didn’t count?
Which quality shows up most in the moments, and where in your life it is currently going unused
A situation coming up this week where one of these five qualities could help someone. Which one, and how?
Afterward: what you did, how the other person responded, and whether you let yourself notice it

title: The People-Pleasing Pattern
description: Saying yes when you mean no usually feels like kindness in the moment and resentment later. This worksheet looks at one recent yes, what you actually wanted, what you feared, and one honest sentence to try.
intro_md: This is not a test, and wanting people to be happy with you is not a flaw. It is a skill that once kept you safe or loved. The trouble starts when it runs on its own and costs you things you never agreed to give. Look at one recent example with curiosity rather than blame. There are no right answers, only patterns worth knowing.

fields.label: Something you said yes to recently that you did not want to do — a favor, a plan, extra work, a conversation
How you said it. The exact words if you can: “Sure, no problem”, “Of course”, “I’d love to”
How fast you answered, and what your body was doing while you said it
What you actually wanted to say, in plain words, to nobody but yourself
What you gave up by saying yes — time, rest, money, a plan of your own, a bit of self-respect
Finish this: “If I had said no, I was afraid that they would…”
Finish this: “…and if they did that, it would mean that I am…”
Has that feared thing ever actually happened when you said no? What really happened instead?
Where you learned that keeping people happy was your job. Who taught it, and what happened when you didn’t.
Who you say yes to most automatically, and who you can already be honest with. What is different about them?
Write the honest sentence you could have said instead. Short, warm, no long excuse: “I can’t take that on this week.”
A request likely to come up in the next seven days, and the sentence you will use. Afterward, note what they actually said.

title: Receiving a Compliment
description: When someone says something kind about you, the reflex is to deflect it. This worksheet is a seven-day practice in letting compliments land — noticing what you do with them, and trying a simple thank you instead.
intro_md: There are no right answers here, and deflecting praise is not a character flaw — for many people it is manners, or safety, or both. But a compliment that bounces off never gets a chance to do its work. For one week, you will track the kind things people say, what you did with them, and how it felt to try receiving them. It will feel awkward. Awkward is fine.

fields.label: What you usually do when someone compliments you — argue, deflect, return it fast, joke, explain it away, change the subject
The last compliment you remember getting, and what you said back. Then what you thought about it later.
What you are afraid happens if you just accept it — seeming arrogant, owing them, being found out later?
The practice: say “thank you”, full stop, then let two seconds pass before saying anything else. Write it out in your own words so it is yours.
What you will do with your face and body while those two seconds pass
One row per compliment, for seven days. Include tiny ones — “nice job”, “that was helpful”, “you look well”.
Which compliment was hardest to receive, and what it was about — the thing praised, the person, or being seen at all
Whether anyone reacted badly to a plain thank you. If not, what does that tell you about the fear?
Read the compliment column on its own, as if it were about someone else. What kind of person does it describe?
One compliment from the week you will keep. Write it here in the exact words, and who said it.
Where you will see it again — a note, a phone screen — and the next person whose compliment you will practice receiving

title: Planning a Hard Conversation
description: Before a conversation you have been dreading, get clear on what you want the other person to know, what you want to happen, and how you will open — so nerves don't decide for you.
intro_md: Some conversations get rehearsed in the shower for weeks and never happen. This is not a test of courage and there is no right way to do it. It is a place to think slowly before you talk, so that when the moment comes you are not improvising from fear. You can write the whole thing out and still decide the timing isn't right. That is allowed.

fields.label: Who it's with, and what it's about — in one plain sentence, the way you'd tell a friend
How long you've been putting it off, and what has happened each time you nearly started it
What you are afraid will happen if you say it, and what you're afraid will happen if you never do
The one thing you most want them to understand by the end. Not everything — the one thing.
What you want them to know about how you feel, in plain words — hurt, worried, tired, unsure
Anything you want to own from your side, said the way you'd want to hear it
The outcome you are hoping for — a change, an apology, an answer, or simply being heard
What would count as a good enough result, even if it's not the whole thing you hoped for
Your first sentence, word for word. Short, warm, and about you — “I've been wanting to talk about something that's been on my mind.”
When and where — a time with no rush and no audience — and how you'll ask whether it's a good moment
The signs it's going wrong — raised voices, silence, old arguments creeping in — and what you'll say to pause it
What you will do afterwards no matter how it went — a walk, a call to someone kind, a note about what you learned

title: Replaying an Argument in Slow Motion
description: After a fight, go back through it one line at a time — what was said, what you meant, what you heard, and what you actually needed — so the next one can go differently.
intro_md: Arguments move fast, and most of what matters gets lost in the speed. This is not a way to work out who was right, and there are no correct answers here. It is a slow replay, done alone and afterwards, to notice the gap between what was said and what was meant. Be as honest about your side as you would like them to be about theirs.

fields.label: Who it was with, when, and what it was supposedly about — the surface topic
How it started. The first sentence or look that tipped it from a conversation into a fight
How it ended — someone left, someone went quiet, someone gave in, it fizzled out
The line of yours that landed worst, as close to word for word as you can remember
The line of theirs that landed worst for you, as close to word for word as you can remember
What you actually meant by your line — the worry or hurt underneath the words
What you heard in their line — the message you took from it, which may not be what they meant
What they might have meant instead, if you give them the same benefit of the doubt you'd want
What you needed in that moment — to be taken seriously, to be left alone, to feel like you were on the same side
What you think they needed, going by what they did rather than what they said
One sentence you could have said at the tipping point that named the need instead of the complaint
Something you'd like to tell them about this argument now that it has cooled, if anything

title: A Script for Making Repair
description: After a rupture — a snapped reply, a missed moment, a bigger hurt — this helps you write what you'll say to reconnect: the apology, the ownership, and the ask, in your own words.
intro_md: Every close relationship has ruptures. What matters more is whether they get repaired. This is not a test of how sorry you are and there is no perfect apology. It is a place to draft what you'll say before you say it, so that you go in with something to offer rather than hoping the right words arrive. Write it plainly. Then read it out loud.

fields.label: The rupture, in a sentence or two — what you did or didn't do, without the reasons yet
What it cost them, as far as you can tell — how they looked, what they said, what changed afterwards
What was going on for you at the time — tired, scared, cornered. This is context, not an excuse.
The part that is yours, said without a “but” — “I snapped at you in front of your sister.”
The part that isn't yours, which you are choosing to leave out of this conversation for now
Your opening line — how you'll ask for a few minutes, e.g. “I've been thinking about Tuesday and I'd like to make it right.”
The apology itself, in one or two sentences. Name the thing, name the effect, then stop.
What you'll do differently, small and specific enough that they could notice it happening
What you'll ask them — “Is there anything I've missed?” or “What do you need from me?”
What you'll say if they aren't ready to talk or are still angry — and how you'll leave the door open
