How you'll look after yourself if the repair doesn't land the first time
When you'll say it, and the first four words you will actually open with

title: Mapping the Company You Miss
description: Loneliness is rarely one thing. This helps you sort out which kind of company you're missing — someone to do things with, someone who gets it, someone who needs you — and find one reachable step for each.
intro_md: Feeling lonely does not mean something is wrong with you, and it is not the same as being alone. This is not a test and there are no right answers. It is a map of the particular kinds of company you are short of. Some gaps are easier to close than others; the point is to see them clearly. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: When the loneliness is loudest — Sunday evenings, after work, at school pickup, in a full room
What you tend to do with it — scroll, work late, sleep, text someone and then delete it
The things you would do more of if you had company for them — walks, movies, a gym, a meal out
Who, from anyone you know even slightly, might say yes to one of those — and the one step that would ask them
The part of your life you'd like to be understood without having to explain it from scratch
Where people who share that live — a group, a forum, a colleague, someone you've drifted from — and one step toward them
Who or what could use what you have to give — a neighbor, a younger relative, a cause, an animal
The step that would put you in their path this month, however small it is
Of the three steps above, the one that feels most possible, and the day you'll take it
What you'd like to notice about the loneliness a week after taking it — not that it's gone, but any shift at all

title: Listening Without Fixing
description: A practice log across five conversations where your only job is to listen — no advice, no solutions, no “have you tried”. You note what you wanted to say and what happened when you didn't.
intro_md: Most of us listen with a fix half-formed before the other person has finished. This is not a test of your patience and there is no score. It is a small experiment, run over five real conversations, where you try only to understand and notice how hard that is. The urge to fix is not a fault; it usually comes from caring. Here you set it down for a few minutes and see what happens.

fields.label: How you usually respond when someone brings you a problem — jump in, reassure, suggest, change the subject, go quiet
What you think would happen if you just listened and said almost nothing. Your honest prediction.
One row per conversation. Fill it in as soon afterwards as you can, while the urge to fix is still fresh
The moments the fix was hardest to hold back — and what was going on in you at that point
What people did when you didn't fix — kept talking, went deeper, found their own answer, asked for advice
How it compared with your prediction above, and anything that surprised you
Two or three things you said that kept the door open — “that sounds hard”, “what was that like”, “tell me more”
What you'll say when someone actually wants advice, so you can offer it without it becoming the default
One person you'd like to listen to this way next week, and what you'll say to yourself when the fix rises

title: Keeping Friendships Alive
description: Friendships drift when nobody means them to. This helps you name who you'd like to be closer to, what has kept you from reaching out, and one small, specific message for each of them.
intro_md: Adult friendships rarely end; they thin out. This is not a test of how good a friend you have been and there are no right answers. It is a plan for tending a few relationships you'd like to keep, in steps small enough to actually happen on a busy week. Reaching out after a long silence is almost always more welcome than it feels.

fields.label: The friendships that have gone quieter than you'd like, and roughly how long since you last properly talked
What has gotten in the way — time, distance, awkwardness about the gap, waiting for them to go first
One row per person. Make the reach-out small enough to send today — a photo, a question, a “thought of you”
What you're afraid a message might land as — needy, out of the blue, too late — and what you'd think if a friend sent you the same
A sentence that names the gap lightly if you need one: “It's been ages and that's on me — how are you?”
One small habit that would keep this going — a monthly call, a standing walk, a message on the commute
How you'll remember to do it — a calendar reminder, a note on the fridge, one friend-day each week
The first message you'll send, to whom, and when. Then come back and write what happened
What you'd like to notice about yourself the next time a friend goes quiet on you

title: The Resentment Ledger
description: Resentment is often a need that was never asked for out loud. This helps you write down what you've been keeping score of, and what it would sound like to ask for it directly.
intro_md: Keeping score is exhausting and very human. This is not a test of your generosity and there is no verdict here. Resentment is information: usually a need you have been meeting silently, expecting the other person to notice. Writing the ledger out is not about presenting a bill. It is about finding the ask that has been hiding inside each entry and deciding what to do with it.

fields.label: Who this resentment is with — a partner, a parent, a roommate, a colleague, a friend — and how long it's been building
How it shows up — sharpness, silence, doing things with a sigh, mentally rehearsing speeches
One entry per row. Be specific: not “they never help”, but “I've done every school pickup since March”
columns: What I do about it now

fields.label: Which entries they could reasonably know about, and which you have never actually said out loud
Which single entry, if it were resolved, would ease most of the rest
Anything on the list that is really about someone else, or about an older story, rather than this person
The one ask you'll make first, written the way you'll say it — plain, about your need, without the tally attached
What you'll do if the answer is no or not now, so that it doesn't just go back on the ledger
When you'll make the ask, and what you'd like to notice in yourself in the days after

title: Building “I” Statements
description: Turn complaints into statements the other person can actually hear. Six rows to practice the shape — when you…, I feel…, because…, what I'd like… — with the situations that matter to you.
intro_md: An “I” statement is not a magic phrase, and this is not a test of getting the grammar right. It is a shape for saying something hard without an accusation attached, so the other person hears the feeling instead of bracing for the blame. It can feel stilted at first; that is normal. Practice it here with real situations until it starts to sound like you.

fields.label: Three things you've said recently, or wanted to, that begin with “you” — “you never listen”, “you're always late”
What tends to happen when you say them that way — for you and for them
One situation per row. Describe the behavior, not the person: “when you look at your phone while I'm talking”, not “when you ignore me”
Read each “I feel” — is it a feeling (hurt, left out, worried) or a verdict in disguise (“I feel like you don't care”)?
Read each “what I'd like” — is it specific enough that they would know when they had done it?
The row that felt most true when you read it back, and why that one
Which statement you'll try first, with whom, and when — ideally not in the middle of the thing itself
After you've said it: what happened, and how it compared with the “you” version
How you'll make the shape sound like you rather than a script — the words you'd swap in or out

title: What You Need Versus How You've Been Asking
description: Underneath most conflict is a need that's fine and a strategy that isn't working. This helps you separate the two, so you can keep the need and try a different way of meeting it.
intro_md: Needs — to feel safe, to matter, to rest, to be included — are not the problem. The trouble is usually in the strategies we use to get them met: hinting, withdrawing, going quiet, doing everything ourselves. This is not a test and there are no wrong needs. It is a way of seeing which strategies have been standing in for a direct ask, and choosing something else for one of them.

fields.label: A recent situation where you didn't get what you wanted from someone, and what you did about it
How that went — for you, and as far as you can tell, for them
One need per row. Needs are short and universal — rest, respect, company, to be trusted. Strategies are what you do to get them.
columns: How I've been trying to get it

fields.label: The strategy you rely on most, and where you learned it — many of them made good sense once
Any need you've been meeting through one person only, when it could come from more than one place
The need on the list you'd find hardest to ask for out loud, and what makes it hard
The one different strategy you'll try this week — the words, the person, the day
What you'll watch for afterwards to know whether the need got met, apart from whether you got your way
A sentence to remember when the old strategy rises: “The need is fine. I can ask for it a different way.” Or your own.

title: New Place, New People
description: Just moved or started a new job? Building a life from scratch takes deliberate steps. This helps you plan where you'll go, who you'll say hello to, and how you'll get through the awkward first weeks.
intro_md: Arriving somewhere new means losing your background hum of familiar faces all at once, and it is normal to feel it for months. This is not a test of how outgoing you are and there is no right pace. It is a practical plan for putting yourself in the same rooms as the same people often enough that strangers turn into faces, and faces into names.

fields.label: What changed — the move, the job, the ending — and how many weeks in you are
What you left behind that you miss most — not just people, but the ease of knowing where things are and being known
Who you still have, even at a distance, and how often you are actually in touch
Three places you could go every week where the same people would also be — a class, a run club, a coffee shop, a volunteer shift
The one you'll start with, and the day and time you'll go for the first four weeks
What you'll say to one new person the first time — something small and about the place, not about you
What you expect to feel just before you say it, and how you'll get yourself through those ten seconds
What you'll tell yourself in week three, when you've shown up and nothing much has happened yet
Small comforts that make a new place feel like yours — a route you like, a shop where they know your order, a corner set up your way
Three months from now — one thing you'd like to be true about your week here that isn't yet
Someone from your old life you'll tell how it's going, and when you'll do that

title: Where Your Boundaries Leak
description: A boundary that keeps slipping usually slips in the same place every time. This inventory walks through six areas of your life — time, energy, body, money, information, digital — so you can see exactly where the leaks are.
intro_md: This is not a test of how good you are at boundaries, and there are no right answers. Most people have one or two areas that hold firm and others that give way without anyone noticing, including them. The point of this inventory is simply to look. Where does your time go without your say-so? Who gets to your energy, your body, your money, your information, your phone? Naming the leak is most of the work.

fields.label: Go through the six areas — time, energy, body, money, information, digital — one per row, and note where each one gives way, with whom, and what it costs
Of the six, which leak bothers you most right now, and what happened the last time it leaked
What you usually tell yourself in that moment — “it's easier”, “they'd be hurt”, “it's not worth the fuss”
Where in your body you feel it when you let this one slide
An area where your boundary already holds well, even if it is small — the door you close, the money you don't lend
What makes that one easier — is it the person, the rule, or the practice you've built up?
If the leaking area were sealed, what would a normal Tuesday look like? Be concrete — the hours, the phone, the money
What you're afraid would happen if you sealed it, and who you're afraid it would happen with
One leak you'll close this week, and the exact words or action that closes it — “I stop answering at 7”, “not this month”
Who you'd tell about it, so it feels a little more real
Next week: which leak you'll look at once more, and what you'll notice about it

title: Five Ways to Say No
description: Most of us have a clear no inside and a padded one that comes out. This script sheet lets you write both for five real situations, then look at the gap between them and what it costs you.
intro_md: There is no right way to say no, and a soft no is not a failure. Sometimes the padded version is the kind one, and sometimes it is the one that leaves you doing the thing anyway. This sheet is a place to write both versions side by side, without judging either, so you can see how far apart they are and decide which one you'd like to move toward.

fields.label: Five requests you find hard to refuse — a favor, extra work, a visit, a loan, a plan you don't want to join
Read the two no columns aloud. Which situation has the widest gap between the no you want and the no you'd say?
What gets added in the softer version — apologies, reasons, offers, a maybe? Name the padding here
What the softer no has cost you before — the thing you ended up doing, the resentment, the time
Who in your life said no plainly, and how it landed on you as a child or younger adult
Who taught you that a bare no was rude, dangerous, or selfish, and how they taught it
Pick one situation and write a no that is honest but still kind — shorter than your padded one, warmer than your blunt one
Say it out loud three times. What changed in your voice or body by the third?
The one situation you'll answer with the middle version next time it comes up, and roughly when that might be
Afterward: what you said, how they responded, and whether the thing you feared actually happened

title: The Over-Explaining Tracker
description: When you justify a choice at length, you are usually asking permission you don't need. Over one week, this tracker records what you explained, to whom, and the one sentence that would have done the job.
intro_md: Explaining yourself is not a flaw. It often started as a way of staying safe with someone who needed reasons before they would let you be. This is not a test, and there is no right amount of explaining. For one week, simply notice when a two-sentence answer became a paragraph, who it was for, and what the short version would have been. The pattern tends to show itself by day four or five.

fields.label: The last time you caught yourself over-explaining — what you were justifying, and how long you went on
What you were hoping the explanation would get you — agreement, forgiveness, not being thought of as difficult?
Each day, log one moment you explained more than you needed to. The last two columns are the sentence you could have said and how strong the urge was
Look down the “to whom” column. Who gets the longest explanations, and what do you expect from them if you keep it short?
Anyone in the week who got the short version easily — what's different about them, or about you with them?
Finish this sentence: “If I don't explain, they will think I am…”
Take your favorite one-sentence version from the table and say it aloud. What does your body do when the sentence ends and you don't add more?
A sentence you can keep ready for the silence after a short answer — “that's the whole reason”, or simply a breath
One person you'll give the one-sentence version to next week, and what you'll notice in the seconds after
What you'll do with your hands or your breath in that pause, instead of filling it

title: What Happens After I Hold It
description: The fear of holding a boundary is usually built on a prediction that has never been tested. This experiment has you write the prediction first, hold the line once, then record what actually happened.
intro_md: This is an experiment, not a test, and there is no result that counts as failing. You will pick one boundary you have been reluctant to hold, write down in detail what you expect to happen if you hold it, then hold it once and come back to write what actually happened. The two pieces of writing are the whole point. Predictions made in fear tend to be very specific and very wrong, but you can only find that out by checking.

fields.label: The boundary, stated in one plain sentence — “I leave at nine”, “I don't lend money”, “I'm not discussing my weight”
With whom, and in what kind of moment it usually comes up
How many times you've let it go rather than hold it, roughly, and what letting it go looks like
Write exactly what you expect them to say or do, word for word if you can. Don't soften it
How you expect to feel in the first ten minutes, and how confident you are in that prediction (1–10)
What you expect to be true about the relationship a week later
The worst version of the outcome, in one sentence, and how likely it honestly feels (1–10)
When and where you'll hold it, and what you'll say. Date, place, the actual words
Something you'll do for yourself in the hour afterward, whatever happens
What they actually said or did, word for word if you can remember it
How you actually felt in the first ten minutes, and how you felt a day later
Put the prediction and the result side by side. What did your fear get right, and what did it get wrong?
One sentence you'll remember the next time this boundary comes up, based on what actually happened rather than what you feared

title: The Guilt After a Boundary
description: Guilt after saying no does not mean you did something wrong. It means a rule got broken. This sheet helps you find the rule, work out where it came from, and decide whether it is actually yours.
intro_md: There is no right answer here and nobody grading your conscience. Guilt is a signal that some rule has been broken, and the only question worth asking is whose rule it was. Some of the rules we carry were handed to us by people who needed us to be easy, and we kept them long after those people stopped watching. This sheet is a slow look at one bout of guilt, so you can decide what to keep.

fields.label: The boundary you held, and who it was with
The guilt as it actually arrived — a thought, a stomach drop, a need to text and take it back? Describe it plainly
How long it lasted, and what you did with it — apologized, undid the boundary, sat with it?
Finish this sentence: “A good person would have…”
Finish this sentence: “If I say no, then I am…”
Now write the rule you broke as a single flat sentence, the way it would sound on a sign — “Never let anyone be disappointed in you”
Who first taught you this rule, and what they needed from you at the time
What happened, back then, when you broke it
Would you hand this rule to a child you love? If not, what would you tell them instead?
If the rule is yours and you'd keep it, write it in your own words. If it isn't, write the rule you'd rather live by
The next time this guilt arrives, one sentence you'll say to it — not to argue, just to name whose voice it is
Something you'll notice in the next week about how long the guilt lasts when you don't act on it

title: Six Asks, Lowest Stakes First
description: Asking for what you need is a skill that builds from small to large. This builder has you write six asks, from the easiest to the one you've been avoiding, and make each one specific enough to say.
intro_md: This is not a test of how assertive you are, and nobody needs to make all six asks this month. The idea is to build a ladder. The bottom rung is something you could ask for today with barely a flutter; the top rung is the one you've been carrying around unspoken. Writing them all out, in order, makes the big one look less like a cliff and more like a few more steps.

fields.label: Things you've been needing and not asking for — more help at home, a raise, an answer, quiet, to be visited. Just list them
What usually happens instead of asking — you hint, you do it yourself, you wait, you go quiet?
Order your asks from lowest stakes to highest. Write the exact words you'd use, not a summary of them
Look at your exact words in each row. Cross out, in your head, any apology or reason that comes before the ask itself. What's left?
For the highest-stakes ask, what you fear the answer will be, and what you'd do the next day if that answer came
For the same ask, what a yes would actually change in your week
The lowest-stakes ask, when you'll make it, and what you'll do with your face and hands while you wait for the answer
Afterward: what you said, what they said, and how it compared with what you expected
Which ask you'll climb to next, and one thing from the first ask that will make the second one easier

title: A Boundary With One Difficult Person
description: Some people need a boundary written down before you can hold it in the room. This sheet helps you set one with a specific person: what you'll allow, what you won't, and what you'll do if it's crossed.
intro_md: This is not a plan to change the other person, and nobody is grading how much you allow. A boundary with a difficult person works best when it is specific: this topic, this tone, this hour, this amount. Write it as plainly as you can, including what you will do when it is crossed, because it probably will be. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Who this is, and the relationship — parent, ex, boss, sibling, neighbor, friend
The specific thing they do that you've had enough of — not “they're difficult”, but the comment, the drop-in, the request, the tone
What it costs you afterward — hours, sleep, a bad mood you take home, money
What you're genuinely fine with from this person — the contact, topics, or help you're willing to keep giving
The conditions under which you'll allow it — daytime only, in public, with someone else there, once a month
The line, in one sentence you could say out loud — “I won't discuss my marriage with you”, “I'm not lending money again”
How you'll tell them, if you're going to — the words, the setting, and whether it's said once or repeated each time
The first thing you'll do the moment they cross it — end the call, change the subject, leave the room, say the sentence again
What you'll do if they cross it a second time in the same conversation, and a third
What you'll do with your own reaction afterward — who you'll call, where you'll go, how you'll get the adrenaline out
Someone who knows this boundary exists and can remind you of it when you wobble
The first time you expect to need this, and the one sentence you'll have ready

title: Your Digital Availability Plan
description: Being reachable at all hours is a choice most of us never made on purpose. This plan helps you decide when you're available, on which channels, and who gets through when you're not.
intro_md: This is not about going offline or being hard to reach, and there are no right hours. It is about choosing your availability rather than defaulting to always. Most of us answer work messages in bed and family messages in meetings because nobody ever asked us where the edges were. This sheet asks. You'll set hours, sort channels, and decide who can reach you outside those hours, then try it for a week and see what breaks.

fields.label: The first thing you check when you wake and the last thing before sleep, and roughly how many minutes each
Which channels ping you — work email, work chat, texts, group chats, social apps, calls — and which one you resent most
The last time a message outside working hours changed your evening, and what it was
The hours you'll be reachable for work on a weekday — a start and an end, for example 8:30 to 6
The hours you'll be reachable for friends and family, if different, and what weekends look like
One stretch each day that is nobody's — no phone at all — even if it's twenty minutes
For each channel, what you'll do with it outside your hours — muted, off, notifications silenced, phone in another room. Be specific about the settings
Which channel you'll turn off entirely, or delete, and what you'll lose by doing so
The short list of people who can reach you at any hour, and how they'll do it — a starred contact, a particular ringtone, a call not a text
What you'll tell everyone else, in one sentence — an email signature, a status, or just something you say when asked
The day you'll start, and the two or three settings you'll change that morning
What you expect to be hardest — the urge to check, someone's reaction, feeling out of the loop
At the end of the week: what actually happened when a message waited, and what you'd adjust

title: The Taking Up Space Log
description: Shrinking in a room happens in seconds and is easy to forget by evening. This one-week log catches those moments — meetings, groups, family tables — and pairs each one with a sentence for next time.
intro_md: This is not a log of failures and there is no right amount of space to take. Sometimes going quiet is the wise choice. The point is to notice the moments when you made yourself smaller without deciding to — laughed off your own idea, let someone finish your sentence, gave up your chair — and to write one thing you could say next time. Not a speech. One sentence.

fields.label: The rooms where you shrink most — a particular meeting, a friend group, the family table, a class, a chat thread
What shrinking looks like on you — talking faster, trailing off, “sorry, quick thought”, agreeing to end it, going to make the tea
Each day, one moment you made yourself smaller. The last column is one plain sentence you could say next time, not a speech
Look at the “who was there” column. Is there a person, or a kind of person, in most of the rows?
What you believe would happen if you took the space — the interruption, the eye-roll, the silence. Write the fear specifically
A time someone else took that same space in that same room, and what actually happened to them
How you sit, stand, or hold your hands when you're shrinking, and what the opposite would look like — feet flat, shoulders down, hands still
Something you can do with your body before you speak that takes two seconds — a breath, a hand on the table
The one sentence from your log you'll actually say this coming week, and in which room
How you'll finish the sentence — with a full stop, not a question, not “if that makes sense”
Afterward: what you said, what the room did, and whether you'd say it again

title: After a Boundary Is Crossed
description: A boundary that gets crossed is not proof it was wrong to set. This sheet walks you through what happened, what it cost, what you'll restate, and what you'll do differently next time.
intro_md: There is no verdict on whether you should have held firmer. Boundaries get crossed; that is part of having them. What matters is what you do in the days after, when the temptation is either to give up on the boundary or to give up on the person. This sheet looks at what happened, what it cost, and how you'll say it again. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The boundary as you originally set it, in the words you used at the time
How it was crossed — what they did or said, when, and whether it was a slow lean or a straight step over
What you did in the moment — went along, went quiet, argued, left — without judging it
What it cost you that day — time, money, sleep, a plan, your mood
What it cost in the week after, including anything you said yes to that you wouldn't have otherwise
What you've been telling yourself since — “I should have”, “it's not worth it”, “they'll never change”
The boundary, said again. Keep the original if it was right; tighten it if the crossing showed a gap. One sentence
How and when you'll say it to them — face to face, a message, next time it comes up — and whether you need to say it at all
What you'll leave out this time — the apology, the explanation, the “I know it's hard for you”
The early sign that the boundary is about to be crossed, and what you'll do at that moment rather than afterward
One thing you'll do for yourself, or ask someone for, so that the next crossing costs less
A sentence to say to yourself the next time this happens — something steadier than “I should have”

title: Everything That Went With It
description: A loss is rarely one thing. This helps you name the person or thing you lost, and then the routines, roles, futures and small daily details that quietly disappeared alongside it.
intro_md: When something is gone, people grieve the obvious part and feel ambushed by the rest — the empty side of the sofa, the errand you no longer run. This is not a test and there are no right answers. It is a place to see the whole shape of what you lost, so none of it has to be grieved in secret. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Who or what you lost, in your own words — a name, a job title, a house, a friendship, a version of your health
When it ended, or when you understood it had. Some losses have a date; some arrive slowly
Daily or weekly things you did with or because of them — the Sunday call, the walk, the shared commute, cooking for two
Which of those routines you have stopped, and which ones you still half-do out of habit
Who you were to them, or in that place — partner, caregiver, colleague, the one who knew the way. Which of those roles has nowhere to go now
Plans and futures that quietly ended too — the trip, the retirement, the child's first day, the conversation you were saving
The details nobody else would think to grieve, and how each one lands when you bump into it
Reading back over all of this, what surprises you about how much was tied to this one loss
One small part of what you lost that you could deliberately keep — a routine, a recipe, a phrase, a place you still go
One person you could show this page to, or one line from it you could say out loud this week

title: A Letter to Who or What You Lost
description: Grief often holds words that never got said. This gives you a quiet place to write them — to a person, a pet, a home, a former life — with no need to send it anywhere.
intro_md: This is a letter nobody has to read but you. It is not a test of how well you are grieving, and there is no correct thing to say. You can be angry, grateful, unfinished, or all three in one paragraph. Write in whatever order the words come. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Who or what this letter is to, and how you want to address them — a name, a nickname, “dear old house”
What you are hoping the letter might do — say goodbye, argue, thank, explain, catch them up, or just keep talking
Where you are writing this, and whether it is somewhere you can be interrupted. It is fine to stop and come back
Start with what has happened since. The ordinary news you would have told them first
What you miss most, in specifics — a sound, a habit, the way a particular day used to go
What was never said, or never finished — an apology, a thank-you, a question, the thing you were saving for later
What you are angry about, if anything. Being angry at someone you loved, or at a loss you did not choose, is allowed here
What you want them to know about how you are carrying on, even on the days you are not carrying on well
How you want to sign off. Take your time with the last line
Read it back once. What you notice in your body, and what surprised you on the page
What you would like to do with it — keep it, read it somewhere that mattered, share it with one person, or write another one next month

title: Seven Days of Grief Waves
description: Grief tends to arrive in waves rather than a steady line. Over one week you log what set each wave off, how strong it was, how long it lasted and what helped, so the pattern becomes visible.
intro_md: Waves are not setbacks. They are how grief moves, and most people find they get no less real but somewhat more familiar. This log is not a measure of progress and it will not tell you whether you are grieving correctly. It is a week of noticing, so that next week you have a little more information about what steadies you. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The loss this week is about, and roughly how long it has been
What you expect the waves to look like — when in the day they usually come, what tends to set them off
One row per day. Fill it in that evening, or right after a wave passes, whichever is easier
The triggers you expected, and the ones that surprised you — a song in a store, a form asking for next of kin
Any pattern in the timing — mornings, late nights, after work, weekends, the moment you stop being busy
What actually helped, as opposed to what you assumed would. Be honest if the answer was “nothing, it just passed”
How the strongest wave ended. What was happening in the minute it began to ease
One thing from the “what helped” column you could have ready before the next wave — a person's number, a place to sit, a jacket to walk in
One trigger you might gently prepare for rather than avoid, and how
A sentence to say to yourself mid-wave, written now while you are steady

title: Planning for a Hard Date
description: Anniversaries, birthdays and other marked days can loom for weeks. This helps you plan the next one — before, during and after — so the day is shaped by you rather than dreaded.
intro_md: A hard date does not have to be survived by accident. Some people want to mark it; some want to be somewhere else entirely; many want both by the afternoon. None of those is the right way. This is a plan you can change, and the point is to walk into the day with a few decisions already made. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The date that is coming, what it marks, and how far away it is
What you notice as it gets closer — sleep, irritability, an urge to fill the calendar, or a numbness you cannot name
If you have been through this date before, what the day was actually like — not what you feared, what happened
What helped last time, and what you would not repeat
What you will tell the people around you, and by when — “the 14th is my mother's anniversary, I may be quiet”
Anything to arrange ahead — time off, a place booked, a person on standby, food in the fridge, the phone on silent
How you would like to mark it, if at all — a visit, a candle, their favorite meal, a walk, doing nothing on purpose
One person you could be with for part of the day, and one hour you might prefer to be alone
A backup plan if the morning is worse than expected — something small, kind and already decided
How you will let yourself land on the next day — a slower start, a check-in call, no big decisions
A note to your future self to read the morning of the date, written now

title: What People Said, and What Helped
description: People say a lot after a loss, and not all of it lands well. This helps you sort what helped from what hurt, and name what you actually wish someone would say to you.
intro_md: Most people around a loss are doing their best with very little practice, and some of what they say still stings. Writing it down is not about grading them. It is about noticing what you needed to hear, so you can ask for it more directly and let the clumsier remarks go. There are no wrong entries here. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The remarks that have stuck with you since the loss, kind and otherwise
The one thing someone said or did that you keep coming back to. What made it work — the words, the timing, or just that they showed up
Things people did without saying much — the dropped-off meal, the text with no question in it — that turned out to matter
The remark that stung most, and what you think the person was actually trying to do
The kinds of comment you have learned to expect — “at least”, “everything happens for a reason”, “you're so strong” — and how you would like to answer them now
Write the sentence you have been waiting to hear. Exactly as you would want it said
Who in your life is most likely to be able to say something close to that, if you told them
One sentence you could send or say this week that tells someone what helps — “you don't have to fix it, just mention her name”
How you might respond, kindly or briefly, the next time a well-meant comment misses

title: Carrying Them Forward
description: Grief does not require letting go. This helps you find concrete ways to keep a bond alive — a recipe, a habit, a place, a phrase — so the person or thing you lost stays part of your days.
intro_md: You do not have to “move on” from someone to move forward. Often the bond changes shape rather than ending — it lives in a dish you cook, a route you walk, a phrase you say. This is not a set of instructions and there is no right amount of remembering. It is a place to choose, on purpose, what you carry. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Who or what this page is about, and one thing that was unmistakably theirs — a way of laughing, a rule about coffee, a garden
Something they made, cooked, said or did that you would recognize anywhere
A value or a way of treating people you learned from them, whether or not they knew they were teaching it
A recipe or a meal — theirs, or one you shared — you could make, and an occasion to make it
A habit of theirs you could take up, even in a small way — the morning walk, calling people back, reading the paper cover to cover
A place that holds them, and how often you could realistically go there
A phrase, saying or joke of theirs you could keep using out loud, and who would understand it
One story about them you would like someone else to know, and who you could tell it to
Where their name could still be said — a toast, a birthday, a child's question, a form that asks who inspired you
The one way of carrying them forward you will start with, and when. Small and specific — Sunday, their pancakes, their radio station
How you will notice it is helping, or what you will do if it turns out to hurt more than it holds for now

title: A Loss Nobody Sent Flowers For
description: A breakup, a job, a home, your health, a friendship — losses without a funeral still need grieving. This helps you take one seriously, name what it cost, and give it the room it deserves.
intro_md: Some losses come with casseroles and time off. Others — the relationship that ended, the layoff, the house you had to leave, the health you counted on — come with a shrug and “at least”. Grief does not check whether anyone died first. This is not a comparison with anyone else's loss. It is permission to treat yours as real. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What ended, and when. Say it plainly — the marriage, the job title, the apartment, the friend, the future you assumed
What it gave you that you did not fully notice until it was gone — structure, identity, money, a place to be on Tuesdays, someone who knew your history
How you have described this loss to other people so far, and how that differs from how it actually feels
Things you or others have said that made it smaller — “it was just a job”, “you'll meet someone”, “people move all the time”
Anything about this loss that carries shame, blame or a sense that you chose it, and so should not be sad about it
Whether any part of you is relieved too. Relief and grief sit together more often than people admit
If this loss had come with a ceremony, what would it have included — who would be there, what would be said, what would be kept
A way to mark the ending that fits its size — a last visit, a box packed with care, a meal with one person who understood what it meant
The parts of yourself that went quiet with this loss, and which of them you would like back
One person you could tell, this week, that this has been a real loss for you — and the first sentence you would use
One thing you will do to take care of the grieving part of you in the next seven days, as you would for a bereaved friend

title: If Only: Guilt After a Loss
description: Grief often brings a loop of if-onlys. This helps you write each one down, next to what you actually knew at the time, and hear what a kind witness would say about it.
intro_md: If-only thoughts are grief trying to find a version of events where the loss could have been prevented — and where you had more power than you did. They are painful, common, and not proof of anything. This is not a trial, and it does not decide whether you are guilty. It puts each thought next to what you actually knew then. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The loss these thoughts circle around, and how often the if-onlys come — every night, only when tired, at random
The one that comes most often, word for word, as it sounds in your head
One row per if-only. Fill the middle columns with what you knew and could do at the time, not what you know now
columns: What I was dealing with then

fields.label: What most of the if-onlys have in common — a single moment, a decision, a thing you said or did not say
How much of what you now know was actually available to you at the time. Be precise about hindsight
Whether any of these thoughts are doing a job — keeping you connected, keeping you busy, keeping you from feeling something else
Picture someone who saw everything you did and did not do, and who is on your side. What they say about the whole picture, not one moment
What you would say to a close friend who brought you the same if-only about their own loss
One if-only you might be able to set down, even a little, and what you would put in its place — a fact, a memory, a sentence
A sentence to say to yourself the next time the loop starts, written now

title: Who I Am Now
description: Loss changes who you get to be. This reflection sorts the roles that ended, the ones that remain and the ones quietly beginning, so you can see yourself clearly without pretending nothing changed.
intro_md: When a person, a job or a home is gone, part of your identity goes quiet too — you were a partner, a son, the one on that street. This is not a test of resilience and it will not tell you who to become. It is an honest look at the roles you have, had, and might be growing into. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The roles that ended with this loss — partner, caregiver, employee, neighbor, the person who always drove. Name each one
Which of those roles you were proud of, and which you were tired of, even if it feels disloyal to say so
What each ended role used to fill in an ordinary week — hours, purpose, being needed, a reason to get dressed
The roles you still hold — friend, parent, colleague, the one who knows the dog's schedule. Include the small ones
Which remaining role has been carrying you lately, and which has felt like too much
One role you have been neglecting since the loss that you would like to return to, gently
Anything new you have found yourself doing since — handling the bills, cooking for one, being the person others check on
A role you can feel the edges of but cannot name yet. Describe it rather than labeling it
Something about the person you are becoming that the person you lost would recognize, and something they would be surprised by
Finish this sentence for today, not forever: “Right now, I am someone who…”
One small thing you could do this week that belongs to who you are now, not who you were

title: Asking for Help This Month
description: Grief makes ordinary life heavier and asking for help harder. This turns what you need this month into a short, practical list, matched to people who could give it, with the words to ask.
intro_md: People around a loss often say “let me know if you need anything” and mean it, then wait for instructions that never come. This is not a test of how independent you are. It is a list — rides, meals, paperwork, someone to sit with you — and a way to hand it to the people who have already offered. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The practical things that have piled up or gone undone since the loss — bills, forms, the yard, groceries, school pickups, the dog
The things you are managing but at a cost — the ones that leave you wrung out or in tears in the car
The non-practical help you need too — company on a Sunday, someone to say their name, a person who will let you not talk
Match each need to a person. One row per need; a person can appear more than once, and “nobody yet” is an honest answer
People who have said “anything you need” and whom you have not taken up on it. What has stopped you
Anyone outside your circle who could carry a piece — a neighbor, a coworker, a service, a faith community, a grief group
What makes asking hard for you right now — not wanting to be a burden, not knowing what to say, pride, exhaustion
Write the actual words for one ask, as a text or a sentence — “Could you take the kids Thursday after school? I have the lawyer at four”
How you will let someone help imperfectly — the wrong brand, a slightly late ride — without taking the task back
The one request you will make in the next three days, who you will ask, and when
What you will notice about how it felt to be helped, so you can decide whether to ask again

title: Replaying One Anger Episode in Slow Motion
description: Anger moves fast, which is why it is hard to learn from in the moment. You slow one recent episode down frame by frame — trigger, body, thought, action, wish, cost — so the next one has more room.
intro_md: Pick one episode, recent enough that you can still feel its edges. This is a replay, not a trial. There is no score and no verdict on whether you were right to be angry; anger is information about something that mattered to you. You are looking for the moments that went by too quickly to notice, because those are the only places a different choice could ever fit.

fields.label: What happened, in two or three plain sentences, the way a camera would have seen it
The exact trigger — the sentence, tone, look, delay or object that tipped it. Be precise: “the third time he sighed”, not “his attitude”
The first sign in your body, before you knew you were angry — heat in the face, tight jaw, a held breath, a change in your voice
How long between that first body signal and the point where you acted? A second, ten, a minute?
The thought that arrived with the heat, in its own words — “here we go again”, “nobody listens to me”, “they think I'm stupid”
Underneath that thought, what did the moment seem to mean about you, or about how you are treated?
What you actually did or said, including anything you are not proud of. Plain description, no commentary
What you really wanted in that moment — to be heard, to be left alone, for it to stop, to be taken seriously
Did what you did get you what you wanted? Fully, partly, or did it get you something else?
What the episode cost — the mood afterward, the look on their face, the apology owed, the hour lost, the thing said that can't be unsaid
Looking at the replay, the one frame where a different move was possible — usually right after the first body signal. What would that move be?
One sentence you would like to be able to say at that frame next time, written out in full

title: Seven Days of Irritability
description: Irritability is rarely about the thing that set it off. For one week you log each flash and look underneath — tired, hungry, hurt, scared, unheard — so the pattern shows up on paper first.
intro_md: This is a log, not a test, and nobody is grading you on how many entries it has. Snappishness gets treated here as a messenger with a badly worded message. Fill in a row whenever you notice the edge in your voice or the eye-roll in your chest, then come back after seven days and read the whole week at once. The last column is the one that matters.

fields.label: What your irritability usually looks like from the outside — short answers, sighing, the door a bit too firm, going quiet, correcting people
Your guess, before logging anything, about what is usually underneath it. You'll check this guess at the end of the week
One row per flash of irritability. For “what was underneath”, choose from tired, hungry, hurt, scared, unheard, overloaded — or add your own
Which word showed up most in the “what was underneath” column, and did it match your guess from before?
Any times of day, days of the week, or people that appear more than once in the log
Look at the rows where the heat was highest. What was the real, unspoken need in each — food, rest, being listened to, feeling safe?
The rows where what you did made things better, if any. What was different about those?
One thing you could give yourself earlier — a snack at three, ten minutes alone after work, an earlier night — that would take the edge off before it arrives
A phrase for the people around you that names what is underneath, such as “I'm not angry at you, I'm running on empty”. Write yours
The one signal you'll watch for next week that tells you the edge is coming

title: Your Own Anger Thermometer
description: Everyone's anger climbs differently. You build a 1–10 scale in your own words, with a body sign and a concrete move at 3, 6 and 9, so you can act while you can still choose.
intro_md: A thermometer is only useful if it is calibrated to you, so this one uses your body, your words and your history rather than anyone else's. There are no right numbers here and no target to hit. The aim is simply to know where you are on the scale early enough that a move is still possible, because by 9 most of us have very few moves left.

fields.label: What 1 feels like — the you that is genuinely at ease. What is your body doing, what is your voice like?
What 10 looks like, based on the worst it has actually been rather than a guess. What did you do, say or nearly do?
Roughly how long it takes you to climb from 1 to 8 on a bad day — seconds, minutes, or does it build over hours?
The body sign that tells you you're at 3 — a slight tightness, a change in your breathing, a sharper tone you can just hear in yourself
The move that fits at 3, when you still have all your options — name it, ask for a minute, slow your speech, check whether you are hungry or tired
The body sign at 6 — hot face, clenched hands, the urge to interrupt, a feeling that words are speeding up
The move at 6, when you can still leave cleanly — a sentence you can say to buy space, and where you go with that space
The body sign at 9 — the point where you know from experience that the next thing out of your mouth will not be one you choose
The one move you can still make at 9, kept deliberately simple: leave the room, close your mouth, put the phone down, walk
Who else could know your scale, so they can say “you look like a 6” without it being an accusation? What would you want them to say?
Where you'll keep a copy of your 3, 6 and 9 moves so they are there when you need them, and the number you'll check in with tonight

title: The Rule That Got Broken
description: Behind most anger is a rule about how things should go. You find the rule, check whether the other person ever knew it, and decide if it is one you want to keep, say out loud, or loosen.
intro_md: Anger usually means a line was crossed. The trouble is that many of our lines are invisible, even to us, until someone steps over one. This is not a test of whether your rules are reasonable, and it is not about whether you were entitled to be angry. It is a look at the rulebook you carry, so that fewer of its pages are secret from the people you live and work with.

fields.label: The thing that made you angry, described plainly and without the adjectives you'd use to a friend
Finish this: “People should…” or “They should never…” — the rule that was broken, in one sentence
Where the rule came from — a parent, a hard experience, a household you grew up in, a job that punished mistakes
How strictly you hold yourself to it, honestly. Are you ever the one who breaks it?
Had you ever said this rule out loud to the person, in plain words? Or was it something they were meant to just know?
What rule do you suspect they were following instead? Most people are keeping to a rule of their own, not breaking yours on purpose
If they had known your rule, what do you think they would actually have done differently, if anything?
Other unspoken rules that tend to get you angry when broken. Look for the ones you've never actually said
columns: Who I expect to follow it
Have I said it out loud?

fields.label: For the rule that got broken: keep it and say it out loud, keep it just for yourself, or loosen it? What would loosening it look like?
If you're keeping it, the sentence you'll use to tell the person — a request, not a verdict. Write it exactly as you'd say it
One of your rules you'd like to quietly retire this month, and what you'll notice when someone breaks it and you let it go

title: A Time-Out Plan You Both Agree To
description: Walking away mid-argument only works if the other person knows you're coming back. You and a partner or housemate agree the signal, where you go, how long, and how you return, before you need it.
intro_md: This plan is written together, ideally on an ordinary evening when nobody is angry. A time-out is not storming off and it is not the silent treatment; it is a pause you have both agreed to in advance, with a return built in. There is no right length and no perfect signal. Whatever the two of you can actually remember at a 7 out of 10 is the right answer. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What usually happens when an argument between you goes past the point of being useful. Describe the last one briefly, from both sides if you can
What each of you does now when it gets too hot — one leaves, one follows, one goes quiet, one keeps going. Say it without blame
The word, phrase or gesture either of you can use to call a time-out, agreed by both. Short, a bit neutral, and impossible to mistake for an insult
What the other person agrees to do when they hear it — for example, stop talking, not follow, not text during the break
Where each of you goes, separately, and what you'll do there that actually lowers the heat rather than rehearses the argument
How long the break lasts — twenty minutes is often the minimum to settle, so agree a time you can both bear and a maximum
What is off the table during the break: driving angry, drinking, calling people to take sides, leaving the house without saying so
Who comes to find whom, and the first sentence spoken on return. Something like “I'm back, are you ready to try again?”
What happens if one of you is not ready yet — a second, longer break, or a set time to pick it up tomorrow
Each time the plan gets used, note how it went. Review together after five uses
Both of you, in your own words: what you're each agreeing to. Sign it, date it, and say where the plan will be kept

title: From Resentment to Request
description: Resentment is anger that has settled in and stopped asking for anything. Six rows take each grudge from what you're angry about to what you'd like instead to how you'd actually ask for it.
intro_md: Resentment is a request that was never made, or was made once and then buried. It is not a character flaw; it is usually the residue of not wanting a fight. This converter is not about deciding whether your grievance is fair. It takes each one and asks what it wants, then finds words that could be said out loud without starting a war. You only need to say one of them.

fields.label: The people or situations you feel a low, steady anger toward at the moment. Names are fine; nobody sees this but you
How the resentment shows itself — a tone, keeping score, doing the thing yourself with a sigh, a story you tell others about them
One resentment per row. In the last column, write the request the way you would actually say it — specific, one thing, no history lesson
Read the “how I'd ask” column back. Cross out any “you always” or “you never”, and any request that is really a punishment in disguise
For each row, could the other person actually do what you're asking? If not, what smaller version could they?
Which row have you never said out loud in any form, and what has kept it silent — fear of the reaction, not wanting to seem petty, giving up?
The single request you'll make this week. Pick the one most likely to be heard, not the one that hurts most
When and where you'll ask — not mid-argument, not by text at midnight. A calm moment with time to spare
What you'll do if the answer is no. Resentment grows fastest where a “no” is treated as the end of the conversation
The request in full, in your own voice, ready to say. Read it aloud once before you use it

title: Where Your Anger Goes Instead
description: Some people never get angry out loud, but the anger still has to go somewhere. You trace where yours ends up — body, sarcasm, silence, over-helping — and try one small, safe way to let it show.
intro_md: If people describe you as easygoing and you privately know that isn't quite true, this is for you. Not getting angry out loud is a skill you learned for good reasons, and nobody here is asking you to start shouting. But anger that has no exit finds one anyway. This is a map, not a diagnosis, and there is no right amount of anger to have. You're just finding out where yours has been living.

fields.label: What happened in the house you grew up in when someone got angry. Who was allowed to, and what it cost the ones who weren't
The sentence you learned about anger — “it's not worth it”, “nice people don't”, “it only makes things worse”. Write yours
The last time you felt anger and said nothing. What did you do with the next ten minutes?
In your body — headaches, a tight jaw, stomach trouble, exhaustion, grinding teeth at night. Which of these do you know well?
In your words — sarcasm, jokes with an edge, agreeing and then not doing it, being “fine” in a tone that says otherwise
In what you do — going quiet for days, over-helping until you're depleted, tidying furiously, being late, forgetting the thing they asked
Who gets it in the end. Often it is not the person you were angry at but someone safer — a child, a partner, a colleague, yourself
What you have lost by keeping it in — a friendship that faded, a job you stayed in too long, something you never asked for
Imagine you had said, calmly, “that made me angry” the last time it was true. What do you predict would actually have happened?
One low-stakes place to let a little of it show this week — “I'm annoyed about that, actually” to someone who can take it
What you'll notice in your body afterward, and one kind sentence to say to yourself if it feels awful the first time

title: When the Anger Is at You
description: Anger pointed inward — at your own mistakes, your body, your past — rarely fixes anything, but it feels like discipline. You separate what you're angry about from the voice doing the shouting, and find a fairer verdict.
intro_md: This is for the anger you turn on yourself: the harshness after a mistake, the contempt for a habit, the fury at your own body or history. It is not a test of whether you deserve it. Self-directed anger often started as an attempt to keep you safe or in line, and it can be looked at like any other anger — what set it off, what it wants, what it costs. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The thing you are angry at yourself about right now, named plainly — the missed deadline, the thing said at dinner, the money, the years
What you actually did or didn't do, described as a neutral witness would, without the adjectives
What the anger says to you, word for word, including the names it calls you. Write it down exactly, however ugly
Whose voice does it sound like? Who spoke to you in that tone first, and when?
What the anger says it is trying to achieve — make you better, stop you doing it again, punish you before someone else does
What happens to you after a round of it — do you fix the thing, or do you go flat, hide, avoid, or do the thing again?
How long you have been angry at yourself about this one, and whether the anger has changed anything in that time
What you would say to a friend who had done exactly the same thing and told you about it in the same words
What was actually true at the time — what you knew, how tired or scared you were, what you were trying to do. Not excuses, context
The fair sentence: what you did, what it cost, and what you're responsible for. No more, no less
If there is a real repair to make — an apology, a payment, a doctor's appointment — what is it, and when?
One sentence to say to yourself the next time the voice starts, written in the tone you'd use with someone you actually wanted to help

title: What Actually Cools You Down
description: Everyone has been told to count to ten. You test what really lowers your heat — cold water, walking, silence, a specific person — rate each one before and after, and keep only what works for you.
intro_md: Advice about calming down is plentiful and mostly untested on you. This is an experiment, not a test: for a week or two, whenever you are hot, try one tool from your list and note the temperature before and after. Some “obvious” methods will turn out to make things worse, and something odd will turn out to work. There is no right toolkit, only yours, and you build it from evidence rather than from what you're supposed to do.

fields.label: Every calming-down method you've ever been advised to use, whether or not you've tried it — breathing, counting, walking, punching a pillow, talking it out
The ones you already suspect don't work for you, and what they do instead — venting that winds you up, breathing that feels like being managed
Things that have cooled you down by accident — a cold shower, a dog, a particular song, sorting something, a person who doesn't try to fix it
Before testing, pick the three you expect to work best and the one you expect to be useless. Write them here so you can check later
One row per test. Rate your heat honestly before you start and again ten minutes after. Try at least five different tools
What surprised you — a method that worked better than expected, or a favorite that did nothing?
Which tools work when you are at a 4 but are useless at an 8? Most toolkits need something for each
Any tool that lowered the number but left you feeling worse in another way — numb, ashamed, hungover, further from the person
Your top three, in order, with the heat level each one is for. Write them so they'd make sense on a card in your wallet
Where the tools live so they are reachable when you need them — cold water needs a tap, a walk needs shoes by the door, a person needs their number
The next likely hot moment this week, and which tool you'll reach for first

title: An Apology Without a But
description: After losing your temper, a good apology names what you did, its impact, and what you'll do next time — and stops there. You draft yours here so it comes out clean instead of turning into round two.
intro_md: This is for the morning after. A real apology is short, specific and has no “but” in it, which is harder than it sounds when you still believe you had a point. You may well have had a point; it goes in a different conversation. Nothing here is a verdict on you as a person. Losing your temper is something you did, and this is about repairing it, not about being forgiven on the spot.

fields.label: What you actually did, in plain words and in the first person — “I shouted”, “I slammed the door”, “I called you selfish”. No “things got heated”
The parts you'd rather leave out because they are the most embarrassing. Those are usually the parts they remember most
What you saw on their face or heard in their voice, and what you think it was like to be on the other end of you
What it may have cost them since — sleep, trust, walking on eggshells, a story they now tell themselves about you
Every “but” you're tempted to include: they started it, you were exhausted, they know how to push your buttons. Write them all here, and then leave them here
The point you still think is fair, in one sentence, and when you could raise it later, separately, once the repair has had time to land
What you'll do differently next time it gets hot — concrete and checkable, like “I'll say I need twenty minutes and go outside”, not “I'll try to stay calm”
What you're asking of them, if anything, that would make next time easier. Keep it small, and keep it for after the apology
The whole apology in three to five sentences: what you did, its impact, what you'll do next time. Read it back and cut any “but”, “if” or “you”
What you'll do if they are not ready to accept it — they are allowed to still be hurt. A sentence for that moment, such as “I understand”
When and where you'll say it, in person if you can, and what you'll do with yourself in the hour afterward

title: Your Personal Grounding Menu
description: Grounding works best when it's yours. You try senses, movement, temperature, and naming, rate how far each one brought you back, and build a short menu you can reach for without thinking.
intro_md: Grounding is not a trick for making feelings go away. It reminds your body that it is here, now, in this room, and not back there. What works is personal — cold water for one person, naming dog breeds for another — so this sheet is for trying things and keeping what helps. There are no right answers here. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: How you usually know you have drifted out of the present — for example, sounds go far away, hands feel numb, time skips
A moment in the last week when something small brought you back — a cold drink, a dog, a song. What was it?
Try each one when you are only a little unsettled, not in the middle of the worst of it. Rate how far it brought you back.
Five things you can see right now, described in detail — colors, edges, how the light falls
Something to touch that you could carry — a stone, a key, a piece of fabric. What does it feel like between your fingers?
A smell or taste that reliably says ‘now’ to you — mint, coffee, a certain soap
A way to feel your feet — pressing into the floor, walking a hallway, stepping outside. Describe it.
Cold or warm — running cold water over your wrists, holding ice, a hot mug. Which one, and what happened when you tried it?
A category you can list out loud — dog breeds, streets near your childhood home, blue things in the room. Which one works best?
One sentence that tells you where and when you are — for example, ‘It's Tuesday, I'm in my kitchen, the door is locked, and I'm 34.’
Your top three from the table, in the order you would reach for them
Where the menu will live so you can find it without thinking — phone lock screen, wallet, fridge — and who you might show it to

title: Triggers and Glimmers Log
description: A week-long log of what pulls you out of the present and what pulls you back in, so you can plan around the triggers and put the glimmers in your path on purpose.
intro_md: This is a log, not a test. Over a week, you'll notice what pulls you out of the present — a tone of voice, a smell, a crowded room — and what pulls you back in. The second half matters as much as the first. Nobody needs to know what a trigger connects to; only what it is today, and what helps. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What it looks like for you when something pulls you out of the present — in your body, your breathing, what your mind does
What a glimmer is for you — the small things that make you feel briefly safe or okay: a warm mug, a familiar voice, sunlight on a wall
Each day, jot one moment that pulled you out and one that pulled you back. Short notes are fine.
columns: What I noticed in my body

fields.label: Any patterns in what pulled you out — times of day, places, tones of voice, being tired or hungry
Which of the triggers surprised you, and which you already knew about
Which glimmers showed up more than once? Were any of them things you could arrange on purpose?
Which pulled you back fastest — a person, a place, something you did with your hands?
One trigger you could soften or plan around next week — for example, headphones on the bus, leaving a door open, eating before the meeting
One glimmer you will put in your path on purpose this week, and when
A sentence you could say to someone close to you about what helps you come back

title: Finding Your Window of Tolerance
description: Helps you learn your own signs of being too revved up or too shut down, what a steady middle feels like for you, and what brings you back in each direction.
intro_md: Everyone has a range where they can think, feel, and choose at the same time. Above it, you're revved — racing, braced, on guard. Below it, you're shut down — foggy, far away, flat. Neither is a failing; both are your body trying to protect you. This sheet helps you learn your own signs and your own way back to the middle. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What too much looks like for you — racing thoughts, snapping, can't sit still, heart pounding, scanning the room
The earliest sign, the one that shows up before anyone else would notice
What shutdown looks like for you — foggy, far away, heavy, can't answer, can't feel much of anything
The earliest sign of that — the one you could catch if you were looking for it
A recent moment when you felt steady enough to think, feel, and choose. Where were you and what was happening?
How your body feels when you're in the window — breathing, shoulders, jaw, how the room sounds
What settles you when you're revved — slower things: a long exhale, cold water, walking, a weighted blanket, a quiet room
What wakes you when you're shut down — brighter things: standing up, music with a beat, a strong taste, talking to someone, stepping outside
Something that helps in one direction but makes the other worse — for example coffee, lying down, being alone
What a person who cares about you could do or say that helps, and what they should not do
One thing to notice this week — the earliest sign in either direction — and what you'll try the moment you see it

title: Safe-Enough Places and People
description: A map of the places and people where you can breathe a little easier, what makes them safe enough, and a place you can carry in your mind when the real ones are out of reach.
intro_md: Safe enough is a lower bar than safe, and a more honest one. This is a map of the places and people where your shoulders come down a little — including a place you can go to in your mind when the real ones aren't available. Nothing here is scored, and no one is grading your choices. Include small things. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Safe enough doesn't mean perfect. What does ‘I can breathe here’ feel like in your body?
What tends to make a place feel unsafe to you — no clear exit, noise, being watched, being cornered, certain smells
Places, real and reachable, where you feel safe enough. Include small ones — a car, a shower, a corner of a library.
People you feel safe enough with — and what they do, exactly, that lets you settle: they don't push, they let silence sit, they text back
People who are fine in small doses, and what the dose is — an hour, a phone call, in a group but not alone
A person you could call at 2 a.m., or a line you could call if there isn't one right now
A place you can go to in your mind — real or imagined. Describe it so you could walk around it: light, temperature, sounds, what's underfoot.
An object, a photo, or a phrase that stands for that place and fits in your pocket
The next time you notice you're not safe enough, what is the first thing on this map you'll reach for?
One place or person you'd like to add to this map over the next month, and one small step toward that

title: After a Nightmare or a Bad Morning
description: A plan you make on an ordinary day for a bad night or a bad morning — what to do in the first minutes, how to get up, what to skip, and who to tell.
intro_md: A nightmare or a bad morning can hijack a whole day. This is a plan you make on an ordinary day for a hard one: what you'll do in the first minutes, how you'll get up, what you'll skip, who you'll tell. You will never be asked what the dream was about, and there is no right way to do this. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What a bad night or morning looks like for you — a jolt awake, dread before you open your eyes, not wanting to move. No need to describe the dream.
What you usually do in the first hour afterward, and how that tends to go
Three things you'll do before getting out of bed to tell your body it's now — lights on, feet on the floor, say the date aloud, touch the wall
A sentence to say to yourself, out loud if you can — for example, ‘That was a dream. I'm in my room. It's morning.’
What to do with the dream — write one line, tell no one, tell someone, let it go. Whatever you choose is allowed.
Your bad-morning routine, shorter than your usual one — water, shower, something warm, open the blinds. List the steps in order.
What you'll skip or postpone on a bad morning without apology — the news, email, the hard conversation
Who you could tell, and what you'd say — it can be as little as ‘rough night, go easy on me today’
Something kind and ordinary planned for the afternoon or evening — a walk, a show, food you like
What you'll put by the bed tonight so the plan is ready — water, a lamp within reach, a note with your sentence, warm socks
One thing to notice next time — did the plan shorten the bad part, even a little?

title: What Your Body Needs Right Now
description: A slow head-to-feet check-in that asks each part of your body what it needs right now, and helps you offer one small thing in return. You never have to say what happened.
intro_md: This check-in asks your body what it needs, not what happened to it. You move slowly from head to feet, notice what's there, and ask each area what it would want if it could speak. You can skip any area you'd rather not visit today, stop at any point, and there is nothing to get right. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Where you are right now, and one thing that makes this an okay place to do this — a locked door, a blanket, a window
Anything you want to set down before you begin — the phone, a task, a worry you'll come back to. Name it and set it aside for ten minutes.
Move slowly from the top down. For each area, what do you notice, and what would it ask for if it could? Skip any area you'd rather not visit today.
columns: Area (head, jaw, shoulders, chest, belly, hands, legs and feet)

fields.label: The area that most wanted something. What did it ask for — warmth, stillness, movement, to be left alone, to be held?
An area that felt easy or neutral. Rest your attention there a moment. What is that like?
If an area wanted something you can't give right now, what's the nearest thing you can give?
One thing you'll do in the next ten minutes for the area that needed it most — a stretch, a hand on your chest, a hot drink, socks
How your body feels after, in a sentence — it's fine if the answer is ‘the same’
A time this week you'll check in like this again, and a two-word cue that will remind you — for example ‘feet first’
One thing your body asked for today that you'd like to give it more often

title: Choices I Have Today
description: For days when everything feels decided for you. You find the small, real choices that are still yours — what you eat, how you move, what you let in — and make one on purpose.
intro_md: Some days everything feels decided for you. When that happens, it helps to find the choices that are still yours — not the big ones, the small, real ones: what you drink, which door you use, what you say no to. This is not about pretending you have control you don't. It's about noticing the control you do. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What feels out of your control today — the big things and the ordinary ones. Write them down; don't argue with them yet.
What happens in your body when you feel like nothing is up to you — heavy, frozen, frantic, blank
What you'll eat or drink next, and how — hot or cold, standing or sitting, alone or with someone
What your body does next — stay, stand, stretch, shower, go outside, lie down. Which one?
What you let in — which sounds, which screens, which people — and which you'll keep out for now
Something you must do today. What's one thing about how you do it that is yours — the order, the pace, the music, the breaks?
What you'll say no to, or not answer, today — even something tiny, even just for now
Something you'll do slightly differently than usual, simply because you can — a different route, a different mug
How you'll speak to yourself today when something goes wrong — choose one sentence now, before you need it
Who you tell about today, and what you keep private. Both are choices.
Pick one choice from this page to make on purpose today. Afterward, note whether it was as small as it looked.

title: A Pacing Plan for a Hard Week
description: Plan a hard week before it arrives: what you'll do less of, what stays because it holds you up, where rest goes, and who knows, so you don't have to push through.
