intro_md: Some weeks you can see coming — an anniversary, a hearing, a visit, a season. Pacing means deciding in advance what you'll do less of, what stays because it holds you up, and who will know. It's the opposite of pushing through. This is not a schedule you have to keep; it's a sketch you're allowed to change. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What makes this week hard — an anniversary, a court date, a visit, a season, or nothing you can name. Just say what you know.
What usually happens when you push through a week like this at full speed
What you'll do less of this week — fewer plans, shorter days, fewer people, less news
What stays no matter what, because it holds you up — meals, medication, walks, the dog, one text a day
What you'll do a little more of — sleep, warmth, quiet, time with one safe person
Sketch the week, lightly. Leave gaps. Nothing in this table is a promise.
Who knows it's a hard week, and what exactly you've told them — you don't owe anyone the reason
The sentence you could send someone so they can help without asking questions — for example, ‘Rough week. Don't need details, do need company Thursday.’
What you'll do if the week turns out harder than planned — the pared-down version of the plan
At the end of the week, what you'll ask yourself — not ‘did I cope’ but ‘what helped, what didn't, what would I keep?’
One thing from this week's plan you'd keep for ordinary weeks too

title: What a Fair Witness Would Say
description: Takes the self-blaming sentence in your head and looks at it with what you actually knew and could do at the time, then lets a fair witness write a more accurate one.
intro_md: Self-blame often arrives as a single sentence that has been repeating for years. This sheet takes that sentence and looks at it with what you actually knew and could do at the time — not what you know now. You will not be asked to describe what happened, only to be fair to the person you were. There is no verdict here. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The self-blaming sentence, word for word, as it sounds in your head — ‘I should have…’, ‘If I hadn't…’, ‘It's my fault because…’
When it shows up loudest — at night, after a reminder, when things are going well
What the sentence does for you, if anything. Sometimes blame feels safer than the alternative — that it wasn't in your control at all.
What you actually knew at the time — not what you know now, not what you've learned since. Only what you knew then.
How old you were, how tired, how scared, how alone, and how much power you had in that room
What the sentence assumes you could have done. Was that actually available to you, in that body, on that day?
Anything you did that helped, however small — staying quiet, getting through, calling someone later, surviving it. Write it down.
Picture someone fair — not a soft friend, not a harsh judge — someone who saw everything and has no stake in it. What do they say about the sentence?
Whose responsibility the fair witness would name instead of yours, or alongside it
A fairer sentence, written by the witness. It doesn't have to be kind yet. It has to be accurate.
What you'll do the next time the old sentence shows up — read the witness's sentence, say it out loud, put a hand on your chest, text someone
One person you could read the witness's sentence to, if and when you're ready

title: My Crisis and Support Plan
description: A practical plan for a hard night: your warning signs, what helps, the people and numbers you'd actually use, how to make the space safer, and one reason to get through tonight.
intro_md: This is a plan you write on a steadier day, for a night that isn't. It's practical — your warning signs, what helps, who to contact, how to make the space safer, and one reason to get through tonight. It isn't a test, and filling it in doesn't mean anything is wrong with you; it means you're looking after yourself. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The early signs that things are sliding — not sleeping, not answering, not eating, the same thought looping, wanting everything to stop
The signs other people would notice before you do — going quiet, canceling, saying ‘I'm fine’ in a certain voice
What you can do on your own, right where you are — cold water, going outside, a show you've seen ten times, holding something, a shower
Places that help — somewhere with people around but no demands, like a café, a library, a store, a friend's couch
What has helped before, even once, even a little
People you can contact and what you'd say. Include the number. It's fine if the message is just ‘can you talk?’
Professionals and lines — a therapist, a doctor, a crisis line. In the US, 988 is there by call or text any time. Write down the ones you'd actually use.
The one person or line you'll try first, and the one you'll try if that doesn't answer
Anything you can put out of reach, hand to someone, or lock away tonight so a bad hour has less to work with
Who could hold it for you, and what you'd say when you hand it over
One reason to get through tonight. It can be small — the dog, tomorrow's coffee, a person, a thing you haven't finished. Only tonight.
Where this plan will live so you can find it fast, and one person who will have a copy

title: Design a Tiny Habit
description: Big habits fail because they ask too much on a bad day. This helps you shrink one habit until it is almost too small to skip, attach it to something you already do, and track a first week.
intro_md: This is not a test of willpower, and there is no right answer about which habit you pick. A tiny habit is one that takes under a minute and can survive a day when you are tired, late, or fed up. The point of the first week is not to be perfect. It is to find out where the habit fits, how it feels, and what gets in its way, so you can adjust it rather than abandon it.

fields.label: The habit you would like to have, in plain words — “floss”, “stretch in the morning”, “write a few lines”
Why it matters to you right now, not why it should matter to anyone
Every version of this you have tried before, and roughly how long each one lasted
The smallest version that still counts — one tooth, one stretch, one sentence. Make it take under a minute
If that still feels like too much on a rough day, shrink it again. Write the even smaller version here
Something you already do every day without deciding to — pouring coffee, sitting down at your desk, brushing your teeth
Your recipe, in one line: “After I [anchor], I will [tiny behavior]”
How you will mark it as done the moment it happens — a quiet “nice”, a fist pump, a tick on this sheet. Pick something that feels good, not silly
Tick each day you did the tiny version. A note on what made it easy or hard is more useful than a perfect row
columns: What made it easy or hard

fields.label: Which days it happened easily, and what those days had in common
If the anchor was wrong, a different daily moment that might fit better
The version you will carry into next week — same tiny size, or one notch bigger if it felt easy

title: Why I Stopped Last Time
description: Most habits do not fail from laziness; they end at a specific week, for a specific reason. This helps you look honestly at one abandoned habit and find what it actually needed to keep going.
intro_md: Stopping is not a verdict about you. It is a record of what happened when a habit met real life, and that record is full of useful information. There are no right answers here and nothing to be ashamed of. You are not being asked to restart anything today. You are only being asked to look closely at how one habit ended, so that the next attempt starts from what you know instead of from a fresh burst of hope.

fields.label: The habit you dropped — walking after dinner, the language app, cooking on Sundays, the journal
When you started it, and what was going on in your life that made it feel possible
The best stretch — how long it lasted, and what it felt like while it was working
What changed around the time it stopped — a trip, a cold, a new job, a bad week, nothing you can name
The first day you missed. What you told yourself that day, as exactly as you can remember
How many missed days it took before you quietly stopped calling it a habit
The sentence you now say about that attempt — “I never stick to anything”, “I just got busy”
A kinder and more accurate sentence. What actually got in the way, in plain words
The size it was at. Would a much smaller version have survived that week?
Who knew you were doing it, and whether anyone would have noticed if you stopped
What it was competing with for that time slot, and which one usually won
One thing you would change — the size, the time, the place, telling someone, a plan for missed days
One thing you would keep exactly as it was, because it worked
A sentence to say to yourself on the first missed day next time, written now while you are calm

title: The Friction Map
description: The habits you keep are often the easiest ones, not the ones you want most. This helps you map what makes a wanted habit hard and an unwanted one easy, then change one small thing on each side.
intro_md: This is not about trying harder. It is about noticing how your day is arranged, because the arrangement decides more than your willpower does. Every habit has a path of small steps in front of it. When the path is short and clear, the habit happens. When it is long or cluttered, it does not. There are no right answers here — only an honest look at the paths, and one small change to each.

fields.label: The habit you want more of, and the habit you want less of. Name both plainly
Where and when each one usually happens, or fails to happen
Every step between deciding to do it and actually doing it — finding the shoes, clearing the table, opening the app. Then what could make each step shorter
columns: One way to make it easier

fields.label: The single step where you most often give up, and what you are usually feeling at that point
What is already set up so that this habit needs almost no effort — the snacks in view, the app on the home screen, the remote within reach
What it gives you in the moment. Be fair to it; it is doing a job
One step you could add in front of it — a drawer, a logout, a rule about the room it happens in
The one change that makes the wanted habit easier, chosen from the table. Small and physical beats big and mental
The one change that makes the unwanted habit a little harder. It only needs to add a pause, not a wall
When you will make both changes. Day, time, and what you need to buy, move, or delete
What you expect to happen, so you can compare it with what does
After a week: what changed, what did not, and which swap deserves to stay

title: What the Scrolling Is For
description: Reaching for your phone is rarely about the phone. This helps you notice what you are avoiding when you pick it up, what it gives you, what it quietly costs, and one rule you can actually keep.
intro_md: This is not a lecture about screen time, and there is no right amount to aim for. Your phone is doing something for you every time you reach for it, and the aim is to find out what. Once you can see the feeling underneath the reach, you have a choice about how to answer it. Notice without judgment. The pickups you log here are information, not evidence against you.

fields.label: For one day, jot down a few pickups that were not for a task. What was happening just before, and what you were feeling
The moments of the day when you reach for it most — waking, waiting, after work, in bed, mid-task
The feeling you are usually stepping away from — boredom, loneliness, a hard task, a conversation, being alone with your thoughts
What you would be doing in those moments if the phone were in another room
What you genuinely get from it — company, a laugh, a break, feeling connected, a sense of being informed
The apps or feeds that leave you feeling better afterward, and the ones that leave you feeling worse
What the scrolling tends to take — sleep, the first hour of the morning, the middle of a book, time with someone in the room
How you usually feel when you finally put it down, in a word or two
One thing you keep saying you have no time for, and whether the hours might be here
One rule small enough to keep this week — no phone at the table, charger outside the bedroom, one feed deleted. Write it as a sentence you can say aloud
What you will do instead in the moment you would normally reach — the answer to the feeling, not just a ban on the phone
At the end of the week: how often the rule held, and what happened in the gap it left

title: For Days You Don't Feel Like It
description: Motivation shows up after you start, not before. This helps you build a plan for the days it never arrives, with a minimum version of the habit and a sentence to get you moving anyway.
intro_md: There is nothing wrong with you on the days you do not feel like it. Nobody feels like it most of the time; people who keep habits have simply stopped waiting for the feeling. This is not a pep talk and there are no right answers. It is a plan you write while you feel calm, for a version of you who is tired and unconvinced. Make it easy for that person. They are the one who has to use it.

fields.label: The habit this plan is for, and how often the “not today” feeling shows up around it
What “not feeling like it” is actually made of for you — tiredness, dread, resentment, wanting comfort, a blank flatness
What you usually do instead on those days, and how you feel about it by bedtime
A time the motivation did show up partway through, once you had already started
What waiting costs you over a month — the missed days add up to what?
The smallest version that still counts on a bad day — two minutes, one page, one street, putting on the shoes
The point at which you are allowed to stop with no guilt, and whether you will tell yourself that in advance
What has to be ready the night before so that starting takes no decisions — clothes out, file open, bag by the door
A person you could message with “doing it now” who will not mind, and might send one back
What you will do in the first thirty seconds, so precisely that you do not have to think
A sentence to say to yourself in the moment — “Just the shoes”, “I don't have to want to”, “Start and see”. Choose one you can actually hear yourself saying
The next day you expect to not feel like it. Mark it, and plan to use the minimum version on purpose

title: A Habit Stacking Week
description: You already have routines that happen without effort. This helps you attach one or two new habits to those routines, run the pairing for a week, and keep the stacks that fit.
intro_md: You do not need new discipline to add a habit; you need a slot. Your day already has fixed points — the kettle, the commute, the moment you sit down after work — and each one can carry a small extra behavior. This is not a test, and a stack that does not fit is not a failure. It is a pairing that needs a different slot. Aim small, keep the ones that stick, and let the rest go.

fields.label: Things you do every day without deciding to — coffee, unlocking the door, feeding the cat, plugging in your phone. List as many as you can
The two or three that happen at the same time and place almost every day
The new habit you want to add, shrunk to under two minutes
The routine it will follow, written as a sentence: “After I [routine], I will [habit]”
A second stack if you want one — keep it separate from the first so they do not compete
Each day, note whether the stack happened, and what got in the way if it did not
The days the routine itself did not happen. If it is not daily, it is not a good anchor
Whether the habit felt natural after its routine, or like an interruption. Describe the moment of switching
A better slot for anything that felt forced
The stack you will keep exactly as it is, and the one you will move or drop
The next routine you could stack onto once this one feels automatic — not yet, just noted

title: Riding Out an Urge
description: Urges rise, peak, and pass whether or not you act on them. This log helps you watch that happen for any habit you are cutting back — drinking, spending, snacking, checking — and find what helps you wait.
intro_md: This is not a sobriety pledge, a budget, or a diet, and it will not judge what you are cutting back or why. It is a log of urges, kept so you can see them clearly. An urge feels permanent while it is happening, but it has a shape: it climbs, it peaks, and it comes down, usually within twenty minutes. Watching that shape a few times, whatever you decide to do, changes your relationship with it.

fields.label: The habit you are cutting back on, and what “cutting back” means for you right now — fewer nights, a limit, a pause, none for a month
What it gives you in the moment. Be honest and fair; it is doing something for you
What made you decide to cut back, in your own words rather than anyone else's
When the urge usually shows up — a time of day, a place, a person, a feeling that comes first
What the urge sounds like in your head — “just one”, “I deserve it”, “it doesn't count today”
Each time an urge shows up, note it. Whether you acted on it or not, write it down — the log is for watching, not for grading
How long the urges actually lasted, compared with how long they felt like they would last
What helped you wait, on the times you waited — moving rooms, a glass of water, texting someone, doing the thing you were avoiding
What happened on the times you acted on it, and how you felt an hour later
What you will do in the first two minutes of the next one — one physical action, not a plan to resist
Someone you could tell that you are cutting back, and what you would ask them for

title: Three Votes for Who You're Becoming
description: Every small action is a vote for the kind of person you are. This helps you name the person you are becoming, notice the votes you have already cast, and choose three more for this week.
intro_md: This is not about becoming someone else, and there is no right person to pick. Most of us describe ourselves by what we have failed to do — “I'm not a morning person”, “I'm bad with money”. Those are also just votes, counted over years. You do not need a majority. You need a few new votes, small enough to cast this week, for the person you would rather be. The identity follows the evidence.

fields.label: The kind of person you would like to be, in a short phrase — someone who moves every day, someone who shows up, someone who finishes things
What that person does on an ordinary Tuesday. Small, specific, visible things
How that person handles a bad day, because that is where the identity is really decided
Something you did in the last month that this person would also have done
The sentence you currently use to describe yourself in this area, and how long you have been saying it
Evidence against that sentence — any time at all that you acted differently
Vote one: an action so small it is hard to argue with. When and where
Vote two: a different action, or the same one on a different day
Vote three: the one you will cast on the day you least feel like it
What you will say to yourself if a vote does not get cast — a missed vote is not a vote for the other side
At the end of the week: which votes you cast, and the one moment you felt most like the person you named
A new sentence about yourself that the week's evidence would support, even slightly

title: The Restart Plan
description: A missed day only ends a habit if you decide it does. This helps you replace “I blew it” with a plan for the next hour, so a slip stays a slip instead of becoming the end.
intro_md: A slip is not a relapse and a relapse is not a verdict. Everyone who has ever kept a habit has also broken it, often more than once. What separates a habit that lasts from one that ends is not the missed day; it is what happens the day after. This is not a test and there are no right answers. Write it while you are steady, so that the version of you who has just slipped has something to read.

fields.label: The slip, described plainly and without adjectives — what you did or did not do, when, and for how long
What was going on that day. Tiredness, a hard conversation, a party, a bad week, nothing in particular
The sentence that shows up after a slip — “I've ruined it”, “I always do this”, “what's the point now”
What that sentence gives you permission to do next. Be honest — usually it is permission to stop
What you would say to a friend who had the same slip and said the same sentence
How many days you kept the habit before the slip, written as a number
Whether one missed day changes that number, or just adds a gap to it
The very next opportunity to do the habit — not Monday, not the first of the month, the next real chance
The smallest version you will do at that opportunity, so that restarting is easier than the original habit was
One thing to change so the same slip is less likely, if there is one. If there is not, say so and move on
A short note to the you who has just slipped, to read before the story starts. Three or four sentences, kind and practical
Where you will keep this note so you can find it in the moment — phone notes, the fridge, a bookmark

title: Month-End Habit Review
description: A month is long enough to see which habits fit your real life. This helps you look back on each one, work out what helped and what got in the way, and decide what to keep, drop, or shrink.
intro_md: This is a review, not a report card. Nothing here is scored, and a habit that did not stick is not a failure; it is a habit that was the wrong size, in the wrong slot, or simply not the right one for this month. Take it one habit at a time and be as fair to yourself as you would be to a friend reading their own list. The goal is a shorter, better list for next month, not a longer one.

fields.label: What kind of month it was — steady, chaotic, sick, traveling, heavy at work. The habits lived inside that
The habits you were trying to keep this month, all of them, including the ones you forgot about
One row per habit. A rough count is fine; the last column is your honest first instinct
The habit that happened most easily, and what made it easy — the time, the place, the size, who knew about it
The habit you are quietly proud of, even if it was small
The habit that fell away first, and the week it went. What was happening then
Whether it was too big, badly placed, or a habit you wanted to want rather than actually wanted
Any habit you are dropping for now, with no guilt attached. Say it plainly
The habits you are keeping as they are, and the ones you are shrinking to a smaller version
One thing you will not add, even though it is tempting
The date you will do this review again, and where this sheet will be so you can find it

title: A One-Minute Check-In, Three Times a Day
description: A week of sixty-second pauses — morning, midday, evening — to notice your body, your mood, the thought on top, and what you need. You build the habit of checking in before the day runs off with you.
intro_md: This is a small practice, not a test. Three times a day, for a week, you stop for about a minute and answer four quiet questions: what is my body doing, what is my mood, what thought is on top, and what do I need right now? There are no right answers and nothing to improve. You are simply taking a reading, the way you might glance at the sky before leaving the house.

fields.label: The three moments you'll use each day — for example just after waking, at lunch, and when you close the laptop
What you expect to find over the week. A guess is fine — “probably tense all day” or “honestly, no idea”
For each check-in, jot four short things: body (tight jaw, hungry), mood (flat, jittery), the thought on top, and what you need right now
The time of day when your body was most often carrying something — and what it was carrying
A mood that showed up more than you expected, and one that showed up less than you expected
The thought that was on top most often. Write it out in its own words, as it sounded
What you most often needed, and how often you actually gave it to yourself
A check-in that changed what you did next — even slightly, like drinking water, stepping outside, or sending a text
The one check-in time you'll keep next week, and what will remind you to stop for it

title: One Meal, Fully Tasted
description: A single-meal reflection for eating with your attention on the food instead of a screen. You slow down for one sitting and notice appetite, taste, texture, and the moment you have had enough.
intro_md: Pick one meal — not a special one, just the next one. Eat it without a screen if you can, and a little slower than usual. This is not a diet sheet and there is nothing to get right; you are not counting anything or judging what is on the plate. You are simply paying attention to something you do every day and mostly miss. Fill in the first part before you eat and the rest afterward.

fields.label: The meal, where you are eating it, and what you would normally be doing while you ate it
How hungry you are right now, in your own words — “ravenous”, “not really, just habit”, “could go either way”
What you notice with your eyes and nose before tasting anything — color, steam, a smell you usually skip past
The first bite, described as if to someone who has never eaten this — texture, temperature, where the taste lands
How the taste changed between the first bite and the fifth, if it changed at all
Where your mind went while you ate, and how many times you caught it and brought it back to the plate
The moment you noticed you had had enough — or that you didn't notice, and what that was like
How you feel in your body now — full, comfortable, heavy, still hungry, satisfied, restless
One thing you tasted today that you have eaten a hundred times without ever really noticing
How this meal differed from the way you usually eat, in plain terms — slower, quieter, more, less, the same
One meal this week you'll eat this way again, and the one small thing you'll change — phone in another room, sitting down, the first three bites slow

title: Thoughts as Weather
description: A sheet for spotting the mind's habits — planning, replaying, judging, comparing — and naming them as passing weather rather than orders to follow. You practice noticing a thought without climbing aboard it.
intro_md: Thoughts arrive the way weather does: you do not choose them, and you cannot stop them, but you also do not have to walk out into every storm. This sheet is not about clearing your mind, and there are no wrong thoughts to have. It is about learning to name the kind of thought that has shown up — planning, replaying, judging, comparing — and letting it pass while you stay where you are.

fields.label: A thought that is on top right now, or was earlier today, written down as it actually sounded in your head
Which family it belongs to — planning, replaying, judging, comparing, worrying, or something else you can name
How long it has been circling, and roughly how many times today it has come back around
The kind of weather your mind makes most — replaying old conversations, planning three steps ahead, comparing yourself, judging what you just did
The time of day or situation when that pattern rolls in most reliably — in bed, in the shower, scrolling, after a meeting
What usually happens when you follow it — where it takes you and how you feel an hour later
Try saying it silently: “Planning is happening” or “Here is the comparing again.” Write what shifted, even slightly, when you named it
Where the thought sits in your body when you don't chase it — throat, chest, forehead, restless legs
What is actually here, in the room, right now — three things you can see, hear, or feel against your skin
The one pattern you'll practice naming this week, and the short phrase you'll use for it
Something you'll notice about the weather next time it comes — how long it lasts, whether it passes quicker once named

title: The Walking and Noticing Log
description: A log for five to seven short walks where the point is not exercise or getting somewhere, but noticing — feet, air, sound, the mind's wandering. You gather what you found and what pulled you back.
intro_md: A walk you take with your attention on it is a different walk from one you take with your attention in your phone. This log is for a handful of walks, any length, anywhere — to the mailbox counts. There is nothing to achieve and no right amount of noticing; your mind will wander every single time, and noticing that it wandered is the practice, not a failure of it.

fields.label: Where you tend to walk already, and what usually has your attention while you do — a podcast, a worry, the next thing on the list
One thing you'll leave behind or turn off for these walks, if anything — headphones, the phone in a back pocket
After each walk, jot the essentials. Under “What I noticed”, be specific — the sound of gravel, cold on your ears, a color you had never seen on that street
The sense that came alive most often — feet on the ground, air on skin, sounds, smells, what you saw
The place your mind went most, and how far into the walk it usually left
The thing that most reliably brought you back — a bird, a step, a smell, remembering this log
A walk that felt different from the others, and what was different about it
One walk you'll take this week with nothing in your ears, and the single thing you'll pay attention to for its first minute
A phrase to use when you notice you've drifted — “back to the feet”, “here I am”, or your own

title: The Autopilot Audit
description: A look at the stretches of an ordinary day you don't remember living — the commute, the shower, the scroll. You map where you were absent and pick one stretch to be present for.
intro_md: Most of a day happens without us. We arrive at work and cannot recall the drive; we finish a meal and do not remember eating it. That is not a flaw — autopilot is how the mind saves effort. But it is worth seeing where it runs, because those stretches add up to a life. This is an audit, not a judgment. There is nothing to fix. You are simply finding out where you actually are during your own day.

fields.label: Walk back through yesterday in six or seven chunks — waking, commute, morning work, lunch, afternoon, evening, bed. Be honest about what is blank
The stretches you couldn't remember at all, and roughly how many hours of the day they add up to
What autopilot was doing for you in those stretches — resting, hiding from boredom, getting through something unpleasant
The stretch where you were most present yesterday, and what made that one different from the rest
Something that probably happened in a blank stretch that you would have liked to notice — a conversation, the weather, a taste
A person you were with during autopilot, and what they might have noticed about you
The single stretch you'll choose to be present for tomorrow — the shower, the first coffee, the walk from the car. Keep it short
What being present in that stretch will actually look like — no phone, one sense to follow, a question to hold
Afterward: what you noticed in that stretch that you would normally have slept through
Whether you want to keep that one stretch for the rest of the week, or try a different one next

title: A Difficult Feeling, Allowed
description: A step-by-step sheet for staying with a hard feeling instead of pushing it away — recognize it, allow it, look at it with curiosity, and offer yourself some care. In plain words, at your own pace.
intro_md: This is for a feeling you would rather not have — the one you have been outrunning all week. You will not be asked to fix it or explain it away. The steps are simple: recognize what is here, allow it to stay, look at it with some curiosity, then be kind to the person feeling it. Go slowly. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The feeling, named as best you can — not just “bad”, but sad, ashamed, furious, lonely, scared, or a mix of several
What set it off, or what you were doing when you first noticed it was there
What you have been doing to keep it at arm's length — busyness, scrolling, snapping at people, sleeping, staying late
Try saying to yourself, “This is here. It is allowed to be here for now.” Write down what happens when you do — resistance, relief, tears, nothing at all
What you are afraid would happen if you stopped pushing it away and just let it sit
Where it lives in your body right now — chest, throat, stomach, shoulders — and whether it is heavy, tight, hot, or hollow
What the feeling believes. Finish this: “This feeling is telling me that…”
What it might be asking for — rest, to be heard, an apology, to grieve something, to be left alone for an hour
What you would say to a close friend feeling exactly this. Write it to yourself, using your own name if that helps
One small kind thing you can do for yourself in the next hour — a hand on your chest, a warm drink, telling someone
What you'll say to yourself the next time this feeling shows up, before you reach for the usual escape

title: Gratitude, With the Details
description: Not a list of things you are grateful for, but one of them looked at closely — the sounds, the light, the faces, the exact moment. Specifics are what make gratitude land instead of skimming past.
intro_md: You may have tried writing three things you are grateful for and found it went flat after a week. That is because lists skim. This sheet asks you to pick just one thing and go slowly into it — what it looked like, sounded like, who was there, what your body did. There is no right thing to choose and nothing too small. A good cup of coffee described properly beats a vague “my family” every time.

fields.label: One thing from the last few days you were glad of. Not a category like “my health” — a moment, an object, a specific person doing a specific thing
Why this one, out of everything that happened — what made it stick with you
What you could see — the light, the colors, the expression on someone's face, the exact place you were standing or sitting
What you could hear, smell, taste, or feel on your skin — a voice, rain, warmth, the weight of something in your hand
What your body was doing in that moment — shoulders dropping, a laugh, breath slowing, leaning in
Who made this possible, including people you never met — the friend who called, whoever grew the tomatoes, whoever built the bench
What it might have cost them, or what they had to choose, for this to reach you
The feeling this brings up when you sit with it for a minute now — warmth, tenderness, an ache, missing someone
What this one moment tells you about what you actually value, beneath the busy version of your life
One person you could tell about this, in a sentence or two, this week — and the words you might use
Something to look for tomorrow that might be like this — the same kind of light, the same kind of kindness

title: Being Here With Someone
description: A plan-and-reflect sheet for one conversation where you give someone your full attention — no phone, no rehearsing your reply. You prepare, have the conversation, then notice what changed when you were fully there.
intro_md: Most of us listen while doing something else: checking a screen, planning what to say next, drifting off. This sheet is for one conversation, with one person, where you decide to be entirely here. It is not a technique for getting something from them, and there is no performance to grade afterward. Fill in the first part beforehand, then come back to the rest the same day while it is fresh.

fields.label: Who it will be with, and when. An ordinary conversation is better than a big one — dinner, a phone call, the school pickup
What usually takes you away when you talk with this person — your phone, planning your reply, an old irritation, tiredness
What you'll set aside for this one — phone face down in another room, the urge to fix, the story you already know
One thing to keep noticing while they talk — their eyes, their hands, the pauses, your own breath
What you'll do when you notice you've drifted — a quiet “back”, feeling your feet, looking at their face again
What they said that you would probably have missed — a detail, a change in tone, something they almost didn't say
How many times you caught yourself leaving, and what pulled you away each time
What it felt like in your body to just listen without preparing an answer — restless, calm, oddly moving
Anything they did differently once they had your full attention — slowed down, said more, softened, looked at you
One thing you learned about this person today that you didn't know this morning
The next conversation you'll do this with, and the one distraction you'll leave at the door

title: Setting Down a Busy Mind at Night
description: An end-of-day sheet for a mind that won't stop. You write out what you're carrying, decide what can wait until tomorrow, and give the rest a note so it doesn't have to be held all night.
intro_md: A busy mind at bedtime is not a broken mind; it is a mind that has been handed too much to hold, with nowhere to put it down. This sheet gives it somewhere. You are not solving anything tonight, and there are no right answers. You are sorting what you are carrying into what can rest, what needs a note, and the small amount that truly needs you before morning — which is usually nothing.

fields.label: Everything on your mind right now, in whatever order it comes — tasks, worries, conversations, things you forgot, things you can't change. Don't tidy it
The one that keeps coming back most, the one your mind returns to when the others go quiet
What your body is doing while you hold all this — jaw, shoulders, stomach, breath
The things on your list that cannot be done tonight no matter how much you think about them
The things that only need a note — a name, a time, a reminder — so tomorrow's you finds them. Write the notes here
Anything that genuinely needs doing in the next hour. Be strict — most nights this box is empty
The things that are not tasks at all, just feelings wearing a task's clothes — and what the feeling underneath is
A sentence to say to the loudest worry, like “I've written you down. I'll come back to you at nine tomorrow.”
What is actually true about this moment — the bed, the dark, the quiet, the fact that nothing is required of you right now
One thing from today that went fine, or better than fine, that your busy mind skipped straight over
Where you'll look for tonight's notes in the morning, and the time you'll actually deal with the first one
What you'll notice about how you slept, and whether writing it all down made any difference

title: Small Joys, Savored
description: A seven-entry log for the small good moments that usually slide past — the first sip, the sun on the back of your neck — and how long you managed to stay with each one before moving on.
intro_md: Good moments happen more often than we register, and pass faster than they need to. Savoring is the simple practice of staying with a pleasant thing a few seconds longer than usual — not manufacturing happiness, just not rushing past what is already there. This is not a happiness score and there is nothing to achieve. Small is the point: a warm mug, a song, a patch of sun, a dog on the street.

fields.label: The kinds of small good things that already happen in your ordinary day, even if you barely register them — coffee, a joke at work, the walk home
What usually cuts them short — reaching for the phone, the next task, a habit of thinking “yes, but”
Seven small joys, one line each. Under “How long I stayed”, be honest — three seconds is a fine answer. Under “What I noticed”, use your senses
The kind of moment that appeared most often — taste, warmth, a person, something outside, something funny
The longest you stayed with any of them, and what let you stay that long
The moment you cut short fastest, and what pulled you away from it
Any change across the week in how quickly you spotted a good moment while it was still happening
One small joy you can count on tomorrow, and the extra few seconds you'll give it — a second breath before the first sip, eyes closed for the chorus
A short phrase to remind yourself to stay — “this, now”, “one more second”, or your own

title: A Week of Values in Action
description: Values are easy to name and hard to spot in an ordinary Tuesday. This seven-day log helps you catch one value a day actually showing up in something you did, however small.
intro_md: This is not a test of whether you are living up to your values, and there is no pass mark. Most days, what we care about shows up in small, unremarkable ways — a text answered, a corner cut on purpose, a door held. The point of a week like this is simply to start noticing those moments while they are still warm, so that your values stop being a poster and start being something you can see.

fields.label: Three or four values you'd like to see yourself living this week, in your own words — “being straight with people”, not the poster version
What usually crowds them out on an ordinary day — tiredness, hurry, other people's plans, the phone
One row per day: a value you care about, and one thing you did — however small — that expressed it
columns: One thing I did that expressed it

fields.label: Which value showed up most often, and which one you had to hunt for
The smallest thing on the table that still counts — something you would normally never have noticed yourself doing
A day where nothing seemed to fit. What was going on, and what might have counted if you'd looked harder?
Anything on the table that surprised you about what you actually care about, as opposed to what you thought you did
One value you'd like to give a little more room next week, and one ordinary moment where it could happen
A sentence to say to yourself on a day when none of it seems to show — something kinder than “I've failed again”

title: The Toasts at Your 80th Birthday
description: Imagining what three people might say about you at your 80th birthday is a quick way to hear what you actually value. You then bring one piece of it back into this month.
intro_md: This is an exercise in imagination, not a prediction and not a report card. Nobody is grading the life you have had so far, and there are no right answers about who should stand up to speak. Let it be as ordinary or as grand as you like. The useful part comes at the end, when you look at what the speakers said and notice what it implies about the next thirty days rather than the next thirty years.

fields.label: Picture the room at your 80th birthday. Who is there, and where is it — a kitchen, a garden, a hall? As ordinary or grand as you like
Three people who stand up to speak. Name them, or name their place in your life — a child, an old friend, someone you haven't met yet
What the first person says about you. Two or three sentences, written in their voice rather than yours
What the second person says about you — a different side of you than the first speaker saw, if you can
What the third person says. Let this be the person who knows you least well, or the one whose words you'd most want to hear
Read the three toasts back. What do they have in common — what kind of person do they describe?
What none of them mention. Notice what is missing — the job title, the tidy house, the things you worry about most
Which sentence would be hardest to earn from where you are right now, and what makes it hard
One thing you could do in the next thirty days that a speaker might mention — small counts, like calling your brother back or showing up to the thing
When you'll do it, and who might notice that you did
A line from one of the toasts to keep somewhere you'll see it — a mirror, a wallet, the lock screen

title: Mapping a Decision You Keep Circling
description: A decision you keep circling usually has more in it than the two options you argue about. This map lays out what each option costs and gives, hears what fear is voting for, and borrows your own advice.
intro_md: There is no right answer waiting at the bottom of this page, and nothing here will decide for you. Going round and round on a choice is not indecisiveness; it usually means something in it matters and you have not yet seen all of it laid out in one place. This map is for getting it out of your head and onto a table, where the costs, the gains and the fears can be looked at one at a time.

fields.label: The decision, in one plain sentence — what you are choosing between, and by when it has to be made, if it does
How long you've been circling it, and what happens each time you get close to deciding
Each option gets a row, including “do nothing for now” — what it costs, what it gives, and who else it touches
An option you left off the table because it seemed silly, selfish or impossible. Write it down anyway
If fear got a vote, which option would it choose, and what is it afraid will happen otherwise?
What the fear is trying to protect — your safety, your reputation, someone else's feelings, a version of yourself you're attached to
Set fear aside for a moment. Which option would you pick if you knew you could handle whatever followed?
A friend describes exactly this situation to you. What do you say to them — the actual words, not the tactful version
Imagine looking back at this a year from now. What do you suspect you'll wish you had known or trusted today?
One thing you'd need to find out, try or say before you could decide — a single thing, not a research project
The date you'll come back to this page and decide, or decide to wait on purpose

title: Where the Attention Goes
description: Seven areas of life rarely get attention in proportion to how much they matter. This balance sheet scores importance against attention for each, finds the biggest gap, and moves one area by a single point.
intro_md: This is not an audit of how well you are doing, and low numbers are not failures. Every life is lopsided in some direction, and often for good reasons — a new baby, a deadline, an illness, a season that simply looks like this for now. The aim is only to see the shape of it honestly, so that if one gap is bothering you, you can choose to move it a little instead of feeling vaguely guilty about everything at once.

fields.label: One row per area: health, relationships, work, play, growth, community, money. Score how much each matters to you and how much attention it actually got in the last month
Anything you'd add or rename — some people need “faith”, “creativity” or “the kids” as a row of their own
The biggest gap between mattering and attention. What is the honest reason it gets so little?
An area getting more attention than it matters to you. What would happen if you gave it a little less?
An area where the two numbers roughly match. What are you doing right there that could travel to another row?
Is the biggest gap a real neglect, or does this season of life just look like this for now? Say which, and how you know
What you tell yourself about the neglected area — “later”, “when things calm down”, “it's not that important really”
One area to move by a single point in the next two weeks — not a life overhaul, an extra hour or one conversation
Where that hour will come from, honestly — what gets a little less so this can get a little more
How you'll know, at the end of two weeks, that the point actually moved

title: What Your Regrets Are Pointing At
description: Regrets come in two kinds — things you did and things you didn't — and each is pointing at something you value. This helps you name one of each, find the pattern, and turn toward what's still repairable.
intro_md: Regret is uncomfortable, and it is also one of the clearest signals you have about what matters to you. This page is not a place to punish yourself or to relitigate the worst thing you have ever done. Choose regrets that still visit you but that you can look at without flinching too hard. The question throughout is not “how could I” but “what was I wanting, and what is this still pointing toward?”

fields.label: Something you did that you wish you hadn't. Not the worst thing you can think of — one that still visits you now and then
What you wanted in that moment, and what you got instead
What that regret is pointing toward — a value you crossed, a person you would rather have been
Something you didn't do — the call you never made, the move, the thing you didn't say while there was still time
What stopped you at the time. Fear, timing, someone else's opinion, tiredness, not knowing how to start
What that one is pointing toward — a wish that is still alive, or a value you'd rather have acted on
Which kind weighs more for you — the things you did, or the things you didn't? What might that say about how you make decisions?
A regret that has softened over the years. What softened it — time, repair, understanding, being forgiven, forgiving yourself?
Something you're doing or not doing right now that could become a regret later. Say it plainly
One regret that could still be partly repaired — an apology, a late start, a conversation. What would the repair look like?
If it can't be repaired, one way to honor what it taught you this month — a small act in the direction it points
A sentence of kindness for the person you were when it happened, who was doing the best they could with what they had

title: If It Didn't Have to Be Perfect
description: Some things never get started because they might not be done well or admired. This helps you take the audience away, count what waiting has cost, and do a deliberately unimpressive version this week.
intro_md: This is not about lowering your standards, and it is not a lecture about perfectionism. It is about noticing how many things you might enjoy that you have quietly filed under “only if I'd be good at it”. There is no score here and nobody watching. The only task at the end is to do one small thing badly, on purpose, and see what that is actually like compared with what you feared.

fields.label: Things you'd like to do but haven't, because you're not sure you'd be good at them — list as many as come, from learning guitar to hosting a dinner
Pick one. Who would you be trying to impress if you did it, and whose judgment are you most afraid of?
Imagine nobody will ever see it, grade it or ask how it's going. Does it still appeal? What changes about it?
The worst version you can picture — the wobbly first attempt, the awful draft. What actually happens in the hour after that?
A thing you already do badly and enjoy anyway — singing in the car, cooking without a recipe. What lets you do that one freely?
What waiting to be good enough has cost you so far — in time, in fun, in things that never happened at all
Where you learned that things were only worth doing if they'd be done well. A person, a classroom, a single comment that stuck
Design the deliberately unimpressive version — twenty minutes, no special equipment, nobody told beforehand
When this week, and what you'll do with the result — keep it, throw it away, or show one safe person
Afterwards: what it was like to do it, and whether it was as bad as you feared — a line or two is plenty

title: From Goal to First Step
description: A goal stays a wish until it has a done-when definition and a first action with a date. This breaks one goal into sitting-sized next actions and gets the first one done this week.
intro_md: This is not a productivity system and there is no score for how much you get done. A goal that has been sitting untouched is not evidence of laziness; usually it is just too big to pick up in one hand. The work here is to make it smaller and more specific until there is a first action so clear that the only thing left is to do it. Pick one goal, not five.

fields.label: The goal, as concrete as you can make it — not “get healthier”, but “walk to work three days a week by November”
Why this one, and why now. What would you have then that you don't have today?
Done when: the plain test that tells you it's finished — what you'd see, hold, or be able to do that you can't now
The next actions, each one small enough to finish in a single sitting — “find three routes”, not “sort out the walking thing”
The action you're least sure how to do. Who or what could show you, and how would you ask?
The most likely reason this stalls — the excuse you have used before, said honestly
If that happens, what you'll do instead of quietly dropping the whole thing
The very first action from the table, and the day and time you'll do it this week
Who you'll tell that you did it, and what you'll say to them
Afterwards: what happened when you did the first step, and what the next one is now

title: Moments That Felt Worth It
description: Meaning tends to hide in small moments rather than big achievements. This seven-day log helps you catch one moment a day that felt worth it, then see what those moments have in common.
intro_md: This is not a gratitude exercise and you do not have to feel thankful for anything. It is simply a week of noticing which moments, when you look back on the day, felt worth having been there for. Some days it will be obvious and some days you will struggle to find one; both are fine and both tell you something. There are no wrong answers and nobody will read this but you.

fields.label: Meaning is usually quieter than it sounds. Before the week starts, name one small moment from the past month that felt worth it for no obvious reason
At the end of each day, one moment that felt worth it — as small as the dog leaning on your leg or a joke that landed
columns: A moment that felt worth it

fields.label: A day when you couldn't find one. What was the day like, and does anything come back now that it's over?
Read the seven moments. What do they share — people, making things, being outside, being useful, being still?
What is absent from them. Notice if the things you spend most of your week on don't appear at all
How much any of them cost — in money, in planning, in effort. Notice if the answer is “almost nothing”
What the moments say you care about, in a sentence that starts “It turns out I…”
One moment on the list you could reasonably arrange to happen again next week, and how you'd make room for it
Something to say to a person who was there for one of them — a text, a word at dinner, nothing elaborate

title: The Same Every Day
description: When every day looks alike, wanting things quietly switches off. This helps you map the sameness, notice what you've stopped wanting and why, and make one small departure this week.
intro_md: A rut is not a character flaw and it is not laziness. Sameness usually settles in for good reasons — it is restful, it is safe, and it asks nothing of you. This page is not about blowing up your routine or becoming a different person by Friday. It is about looking honestly at the shape of your days, hearing what has gone quiet, and choosing one small departure to see what it stirs.

fields.label: Walk through an ordinary weekday from waking to sleep. Where does it go — the routes, the screens, the meals, the same words at the same times?
What has been exactly the same for longer than you'd like. Say how long, if you can
Which parts of the sameness are actually holding you up — the routines you'd keep even if you could change everything
Things you used to want or look forward to that have gone quiet — a hobby, a friend, a place, an ambition
Did they stop mattering, or did you stop believing they were possible? Those are different things, so say which
What the rut protects you from — surprise, effort, disappointment, being seen trying and falling short
If the rut could speak, what would it say it is waiting for before it lets go?
The one thing you'd change first if a stranger could change it for you, with no effort on your part
A departure small enough to make this week — a different route home, a phone call, a room rearranged, saying yes to the invitation
The day you'll do it, and what you expect to feel before and after
Afterwards: what happened, and whether the day felt any different from the others

title: The No List
description: Every yes needs room, and room comes from saying no to good things. This helps you name what you're choosing not to pursue this year, find the words to hold the line, and give the yes its first hour.
intro_md: This is not a list of things you have failed at or given up on. Choosing not to pursue something this year is a decision, and a generous one, because it leaves space for what you actually want. Some of the nos will be good things you would genuinely enjoy; that is what makes them hard, and also what makes the exercise worth doing. Nothing here is forever. It is only this year.

fields.label: The one or two things you most want this year to hold — the yes that needs room to breathe
What is currently sharing the calendar and the energy with it — commitments, half-finished projects, other people's priorities
Things you are choosing not to pursue this year. Not forever, just this year. Include good things you'd genuinely like to do
For each no, why it is a no for now — wrong season, someone else's dream, the price, what it would take from the yes
A no that is hard to write because someone else expects it of you. Whose voice is that, and what does it say?
A no that feels like relief. Sit with that for a moment and say what the relief is about
What you'll say when one of the nos is offered to you — a sentence you could actually get out, like “Not this year, ask me in the spring”
The person most likely to push back, and what you'll say to them when they do
Where you'll keep this list so it is still in sight in March, when the nos start looking tempting again
With those out of the way, the first thing the yes gets this month — an hour, a booking, a conversation
How you'll notice, a few months from now, that the no list did its job

title: Name It to Tame It: A Seven-Day Emotion Log
description: Putting a plain name on a feeling, and noticing the urge that rides in with it, takes some of the heat out of it. Over seven days you'll log the emotion, its intensity, the urge, and what you did.
intro_md: There is nothing to score here and no right way to feel. This is simply a place to notice. Feelings tend to arrive with an urge attached — to snap, to hide, to text, to eat, to go quiet — and the urge is not the same as what you do. Naming the feeling, and its size, and the pull that came with it, creates a small gap. That gap is where choice lives. One row a day is plenty; more is fine.

fields.label: A few feeling words you'd actually use — not a textbook list, but the ones that fit you, like fed up, flat, wired, tender, small
The urges you know well in yourself when a feeling gets big — going quiet, picking a fight, scrolling, leaving, saying yes too fast
Once a day, or whenever a feeling is loud enough to notice, fill in one row
Which feeling showed up most often this week, and was that a surprise to you?
Look at the urge column and the what-I-did column side by side. How often were they the same thing?
A row where you did something other than the urge. What made the gap possible that time?
The intensity number that seems to be a tipping point for you — the level at which the urge starts to win
One feeling you'd like to catch a little earlier next week, and the first small sign of it in your body
A sentence you could say to yourself at that moment, in your own words, that names it without judging it

title: Acting Opposite to the Urge
description: When a feeling doesn't fit the facts, or is bigger than the moment calls for, doing the opposite of what it urges can shrink it. You'll pick one feeling, plan the opposite action, and test it.
intro_md: This is an experiment, not a test, and there is no right answer. Every emotion comes with an action it wants: fear wants to avoid, anger wants to attack, shame wants to hide, sadness wants to withdraw. Sometimes that action is exactly right. But when the feeling is out of proportion, or acting on it would make things worse, doing the opposite — all the way, with your whole body — can turn the feeling down. You are not pretending. You are giving your body different information.

fields.label: The feeling you want to work with, and a recent moment when it showed up — the situation in a sentence or two
What the feeling urges you to do — avoid the call, slam the door, apologize six times, stay in bed, go silent
Does the feeling fit the facts, and is its size in proportion to what happened? Say honestly what you think
If you acted fully on the urge, what would probably happen next, for you and for anyone else involved?
The opposite action, spelled out — not just “don't avoid” but “walk in, say hello, stay ten minutes”
What the opposite looks like in your body: posture, face, tone of voice, where your eyes go, the pace you move at
Your prediction. What you expect to feel while doing it, and what you expect the feeling to do afterwards (1–10)
Each time you try the opposite action this week, note what happened
How the result compared with your prediction. Where were you right, and where did the feeling surprise you?
A time this week when the feeling did fit the facts and acting on it was the right call
The next situation coming up where you'll try this, and the first physical thing you'll do when the urge arrives

title: Checking the Facts Behind One Strong Reaction
description: A strong reaction often rests partly on what happened and partly on what you assumed. This helps you separate the two for one recent moment and see whether the size of the feeling fits.
intro_md: This is not about proving your feeling wrong. Feelings are real whether or not they fit the facts, and a big reaction usually has good reasons behind it, even if they belong to an older moment. The point is only to look. When you separate what actually happened from what you read into it, sometimes the feeling shrinks on its own, and sometimes it turns out to be exactly the right size. Either answer is useful.

fields.label: The moment, described like a camera would see it — who was there, what was said or done, in what order. No adjectives yet
The feeling that hit, and how big it was on a scale of 1–10
What your body did in the first few seconds — heat, tight chest, tears, a rush to speak, going blank
What you decided it meant, in the moment — about them, about you, about what happens next
The worst version of the story your mind told. Write it out in full, even if it sounds harsh on paper
Whose voice that interpretation sounds like, and whether you've felt this exact thing before in a different situation
Only the parts you could prove to a stranger. What did you actually see and hear?
Two other explanations that fit the same facts, including at least one that has nothing to do with you
Something you'd need to know before you could be sure, and whether there's a way to find it out
Given only the facts, how big would the feeling reasonably be (1–10)? Compare it with the number you wrote earlier
If the feeling fits the facts, what does it need from you? If it's bigger than the facts, what might the extra be about?
One thing you'll do or say in the next day based on what you know for certain, not on the story

title: Your Own Crisis Kit for Riding Out a Hard Hour
description: When a feeling is too big to solve right now, the job is to get through the next hour without making it worse. You'll build a kit of things that distract, soothe, and steady you, then test it.
intro_md: Some moments are not for fixing. They are for getting through. This kit is not a cure and there is no right answer for what belongs in it — only what actually works for you, which you'll find out by trying things. Build it on a calm day so it's ready on a hard one. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What a crisis hour looks like for you — the feeling, the urge, and the thing you're most likely to do that you'd regret later
Things that pull your attention somewhere else for a while — a show, a task with your hands, counting backwards, a walk to a specific place
One person you could contact just to talk about something ordinary, and what you'd say to open
Something for each sense that settles you: what to look at, listen to, smell, taste, and touch. Be specific — the gray blanket, not “a blanket”
A way to change the room, your body, or the thought — cold water on your face, a different chair, one sentence you'll repeat, a prayer, a breath count
A picture in your mind you can go to — a real place, a remembered day, a made-up one — described with enough detail to actually get there
Acting on the urge: what it gives you in the moment, and what it costs you tomorrow
Riding it out instead: what it costs you in the moment, and what it gives you tomorrow
Each time you use something from the kit, note what it was and how it went
The two or three things that actually helped, written out as the short list you'll reach for next time, in the order you'll try them

title: What Makes Feelings Harder to Hold
description: Short sleep, skipped meals, illness, alcohol, and stress don't cause feelings, but they thin the skin that holds them. You'll look at each, notice its effect on you, and choose one to tend this week.
intro_md: This is not a health audit and there is no passing grade. Bodies have limits, and when you're running on four hours of sleep or haven't eaten since breakfast, a small thing can land like a large one. That is not weakness — it's physics. Looking honestly at what's been wearing you thin lately, and picking one thing to tend, is a kindness to the version of you who'll have to feel things tomorrow.

fields.label: A moment in the past week or two when a feeling was bigger or faster than you'd have expected. What happened, briefly
What the previous 24 hours had been like — how you'd slept, eaten, whether you were sick, what you'd had to drink, what was piling up
One row each for sleep, food, illness, substances, and stress — how it's been lately and what it does to your feelings
The factor that shows up most often in the background of your hardest days
The one you tend to ignore or explain away, and the story you tell yourself about why it doesn't count
The factor you'll tend this week — pick the one that's most changeable, not the one you feel worst about
What tending it actually looks like, sized for a real week — lights out by eleven on three nights, lunch that isn't coffee, one alcohol-free evening
What will get in the way, and what you'll do when it does
At the end of the week: how did your feelings behave on the days you tended it, compared with the days you didn't?
The sentence you'd like to remember the next time a feeling is huge and you haven't slept

title: Emotion Mind, Reasonable Mind, Wise Mind
description: When you're stuck on a decision, the feeling side and the thinking side often pull in different directions. You'll give each a voice, then listen for the quieter one that holds both.
intro_md: There is no right answer here, and neither side of you is the enemy. Emotion mind is hot, fast, and knows what matters to you. Reasonable mind is cool, orderly, and knows the facts and the consequences. Wise mind is the place where they overlap — a kind of knowing that is calm and certain even when it's uncomfortable. You can't force it, but you can make room for it by letting both of the other voices finish speaking first.

fields.label: The decision you're facing, stated plainly, with the real options on the table — including the option of doing nothing
How long it's been sitting with you, and what it costs you to keep it undecided
Let the feeling side speak without editing. What does it want, what is it afraid of, what does it say in the middle of the night?
Which option emotion mind would pick if it were choosing alone, and what it's hoping that choice would give you
The facts, the numbers, the practical consequences of each option, as a careful friend with a spreadsheet might lay them out
Which option reasonable mind would pick if it were choosing alone, and what it's ignoring about how you'd feel living with it
Take a slow breath and ask the question inward, then wait. What comes back — not the loudest answer, but the one that feels settled?
Where the two sides actually agree, once you look. What do they both want for you underneath?
How you'd know a wise mind answer from an emotion mind answer dressed up in reasons — what it feels like in your body
The smallest step in the direction wise mind pointed, something you could do this week without committing to everything
When you'll check back in with yourself about it, and what you'll be watching for

title: Asking for What You Need Without Losing Yourself
description: Asking for something clearly, while keeping the relationship and your self-respect intact, is a skill rather than a personality trait. You'll build a script for one real request, one line at a time.
intro_md: This is a script, not a test, and you're allowed to change every word of it. Most of us either ask too softly and get nothing, or ask too hard and get a fight. There is a middle way: describe what's happening, say how you feel, ask for what you want, and give the other person a reason to say yes — all while staying calm, looking like you mean it, and being willing to meet partway. Write it here first so you're not improvising in the moment.

fields.label: Who you're asking, what you're asking for, and what usually happens when you try to bring this up
What matters most here: getting the yes, keeping the relationship warm, or keeping your self-respect? Rank all three honestly
Describe: the situation in plain facts the other person couldn't argue with — “The last three weekends I've done the school run alone”
Express: how it makes you feel, using “I” and a feeling word, without blame — “I feel worn out and a bit invisible”
Assert: the ask itself, in one clear sentence. Not a hint, not a question that's really a complaint
Reinforce: what's in it for them, or what saying yes would mean for both of you — the reason it's worth their while
Stay mindful: the thing they might say that would knock you off track, and the sentence you'll return to when it does
Appear confident: what your voice, posture, and eyes will do, even if inside you're shaking
Negotiate: what you'd accept instead of the full ask, and the line you won't go below
How you'll stay gentle with them even if they say no — an easy tone, curiosity about their side, no old scores
How you'll stay fair to yourself — no over-apologizing, no pretending it doesn't matter, no giving in just to end the discomfort
When and where you'll have it, and what you'll do for the ten minutes before to settle yourself
Afterwards: what they said, what you managed, and what you'd keep or change the next time you ask for something

title: Why This Feeling Makes Sense
description: Telling yourself you shouldn't feel something rarely makes it go away. This helps you take one feeling seriously, trace why it makes sense, and speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend.
intro_md: There is no right answer here and no feeling that's off limits. Validating a feeling doesn't mean agreeing with everything it says or doing what it wants. It means acknowledging that it's there and that, given what happened and who you are, it makes sense. Most of us are far better at this for other people than for ourselves. This is practice at turning that same fairness inward, one feeling at a time.

fields.label: The feeling, named as precisely as you can — not just “bad”, but hurt, envious, ashamed, lonely, furious, flat
What you usually say to yourself about having this feeling — “get over it”, “you're being dramatic”, “other people have it worse”
What happens to the feeling when you say that. Does it leave, or does it just go quieter and heavier?
What happened, and what about it would make almost anyone feel some version of this
What you were hoping for or needing that didn't come — being seen, being safe, being chosen, being left alone
Anything from your history that makes this particular thing land harder for you than it might for someone else
Imagine a friend told you all of the above. Write the first thing you'd say to them, word for word
Now the second thing — the part where you'd tell them why their feeling is reasonable, given everything
The tone you'd use with them: your pace, your face, whether you'd touch their arm. What of that could you give yourself?
Rewrite what you'd say to the friend as a short note to yourself, using your own name and “you”
Read it back. What is it like to hear it, and where in your body do you feel any resistance to it?
The next time this feeling comes, the one sentence from the note you'll try to say to yourself first

title: The Morning After a Big Feeling
description: After a night of tears, a blow-up, or a panic that ran its course, the next day has its own weather. This helps you tend to yourself, decide what to repair, and let the rest go.
intro_md: There is no verdict here about last night. Big feelings leave a residue — a tiredness, a wince, a wish to hide — and it's tempting to spend the whole next day replaying it. This is a different way to spend the morning: notice what you need, sort what actually needs mending from what only shame says needs mending, and put the rest down. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What happened, in a few plain sentences — the feeling, how big it got, roughly how long it lasted
How you feel this morning, in your body and your mood — heavy, raw, embarrassed, flat, relieved, all of the above
The thoughts that are circling. Write them down so they're on the page instead of on a loop
What your body needs today — water, a proper meal, a nap, a walk, fewer plans
What your mind needs — quiet, company, a distraction, someone to say it's okay
One thing you can do for yourself in the next hour, before you do anything about anyone else
Anything you said or did that actually hurt someone or crossed a line you care about. Only real harm, not everything you feel bad about
The repair, sized to fit — a short apology, a text, a conversation later this week — and what you'll say in it
What you won't do in the name of repair: over-explaining, groveling, promising it'll never happen again
The parts that shame wants you to keep chewing on but that don't need fixing — being seen crying, needing help, having feelings at all
A sentence that closes it — something like “That was a hard night, I got through it, and today is a different day” in your own words
Something from last night worth keeping — a thing you learned about what you need, or a person who showed up

title: Seven Days of Small Good Things on Purpose
description: Pleasant moments don't always arrive on their own, especially in a hard stretch. Over a week you'll plan one small good thing a day, do it, and notice how present you managed to be.
intro_md: This is not a happiness program and there's nothing to get right. It's a bank: small deposits of pleasant experience, made on purpose, that build up a little cushion for the harder days. The events can be tiny — a coffee outside, ten minutes of music, a phone call, a bath. The only extra ask is to be there while it happens, rather than planning the next thing or waiting for it to go wrong.

fields.label: Ten small things that reliably give you a little pleasure — cheap, quick, and possible on an ordinary weekday
Things you used to enjoy and quietly dropped, and which one you might be willing to pick back up
What usually gets between you and doing something nice for yourself — guilt, tiredness, “I'll do it when things calm down”
Plan one small good thing for each day, then afterwards note how it went and how present you were
Which one gave you the most, and was it the one you expected?
The days you were most present. What was different about them — the activity, the time of day, who was there?
A moment when you noticed your mind drifting to worry or to the to-do list, and what, if anything, brought you back
What happened to the rest of the day around a good thing — did anything feel a little easier, or not?
The three deposits you'll keep making next week, put into your calendar as real appointments with days and times
The sentence you'll say to yourself when guilt shows up about taking the time

title: A Field Guide to Thinking Traps
description: Most of us fall into the same handful of thinking habits when we are stressed or low. This helps you name the trap in a thought and write a fairer version beside it.
intro_md: Thinking traps are not signs that something is wrong with you. They are shortcuts every mind takes, and they get louder when you are tired, anxious, or hurt. This is not a test and there are no right answers. The point is simply to catch a few of your own thoughts in the act, give the pattern a name, and see whether a fairer sentence is available. Naming a trap does not make the thought disappear, but it does loosen its grip.

fields.label: Read these eight traps and note which two or three feel most familiar: all-or-nothing, mind reading, fortune telling, catastrophizing, should statements, labeling, discounting the positive, personalizing
Over the next few days, catch seven thoughts that carry a sting. Write each one down exactly, name the trap, and try a fairer version
Where you were and what was happening when the thoughts in the table showed up — a meeting, late at night, scrolling, after a text went unanswered
Which trap appears most often in your table, and what kind of situation seems to invite it
What that trap is trying to do for you — keep you safe, prepared, humble, ahead of disappointment
A person or a voice from your past who thought in the same shape, and how you learned it from them
Pick the thought that stung most. Read the balanced version aloud. What shifts, even slightly, and what stays the same
One question you could ask yourself next time this trap appears — for example, “what would I say to a friend who thought this?”
The trap you'll watch for over the next seven days, and where you expect to meet it
A small sign you'd accept as evidence that the balanced version was closer to the truth

title: Test a Belief in the Real World
description: Arguing with a belief in your head rarely settles anything. This helps you design one small, safe experiment — a prediction, a test, a result — so real life gets to weigh in.
intro_md: Some beliefs cannot be talked out of existence, but they can be tested. This is not an exam and there is no way to fail it: an experiment that proves your prediction right is just as useful as one that proves it wrong, because either way you learn something true. Keep the test small enough that you would actually do it this week, and write your prediction down before you start, so the result cannot be quietly rewritten afterwards.

fields.label: The belief you want to test, written as a plain sentence — for example, “if I say no to a favor, people will be annoyed with me”
