How much you believe it right now, in your own words — a little, mostly, completely
What you currently do to avoid finding out whether it is true
If the belief is true, exactly what will happen during the test. Be specific enough that you could check it afterwards
What you fear most about doing the test, and how likely that feels
What would count as the belief being wrong, or at least less true than you thought
The experiment itself: what you'll do, with whom, and where. Small enough to do this week
Day and time you'll run it, and anything you need to set up first
One way to make it a little safer without making it pointless — a shorter version, a kinder audience, a backup plan
What actually happened, described the way a reporter would — what was said, what people did, how long it lasted
How you felt during it, and how you felt an hour afterward
Put the prediction next to the result. Where did they match, and where did they differ
How much you believe the original sentence now, and one thing you'd like to test next

title: The Should Audit
description: The word “should” carries a lot of quiet pressure. This helps you collect a week of your shoulds, notice who they came from, and decide which ones you actually want to keep.
intro_md: “I should have known better.” “They should have called.” “I should be over this by now.” Shoulds sound like standards, but they often work more like a rulebook nobody agreed to. This is not a test, and you are not being asked to drop your values. You are being asked to look at each rule in daylight, find out where it came from, and rewrite the ones that mostly produce guilt without producing anything else.

fields.label: For seven days, write down one should each day the moment you notice it — about yourself, other people, or how the world ought to be
Which shoulds showed up more than once, and at what time of day or in what kind of moment
Pick the should that carried the most pressure. Whose voice does it sound like — a parent, a teacher, a former boss, the internet
What that rule was originally for. Most shoulds started as protection or care, even if they no longer feel that way
What happens, honestly, when you break this rule — the real consequence, not the imagined one
Shoulds you genuinely want to keep because they match what matters to you, rewritten as “I choose to” instead
Shoulds you want to soften. Try replacing “should” with “it would help if” or “I'd prefer to” and write the new version
Shoulds you're ready to retire, and a sentence thanking each one for the job it once did
One should you aim at other people — “they should know”, “he should have asked”. What do you actually want from them, and could you ask for it plainly
The one should you'll catch yourself saying this week, and the replacement sentence you'll say instead
What you'll notice about how you feel when the replacement lands, even if it feels awkward at first

title: The Mind-Reading Check
description: When you are sure you know what someone thinks of you, it is worth checking. This helps you separate what you assumed from what you saw, and find out for real.
intro_md: Mind reading is guessing what someone else thinks and then treating the guess as fact. Everybody does it, and anxious or tired minds do it faster and darker. This is not a test, and there are no right answers — you might even turn out to be correct. The point is to slow the guess down, look at the evidence, and work out whether there is a way to find out instead of assuming.

fields.label: What happened — who was there, what was said or not said, the look, the short reply, the unanswered message
What you decided they were thinking about you, in the exact words your mind used
How sure you felt at the time, and how your body reacted
What you actually saw or heard. Only things a camera would have recorded
What you filled in from your own head — tone, motive, what they “must” have meant
Three other explanations for what they did that have nothing to do with you — tired, distracted, worried about something else
When you believe this is what they think, how do you act toward them — pull back, go quiet, over-apologize, get sharp
How your reaction might look from their side, and what they might guess about you in turn
A way you could actually check, and the plain words you'd use — “you seemed quiet earlier, is everything okay between us?”
What stops you from asking, and what asking would cost compared with guessing
A short sentence to say to yourself the next time you catch a mind-reading thought — for example, “that is a guess, not a fact”
One person you'll check with this week rather than assume, and when

title: The Responsibility Pie
description: After something goes wrong, it is easy to hand yourself the whole thing. This helps you list every cause that played a part and work out your honest share.
intro_md: When something goes badly, a common trap is to take one hundred percent of the responsibility and leave nothing for anyone or anything else. This is not a test and it is not a way of letting yourself off the hook. It is a way of drawing the picture accurately. Picture a pie. Every cause gets a slice, and you get yours last, once the others have been given their honest size.

fields.label: The bad outcome, described in one plain sentence — the missed deadline, the argument, the friendship that faded
How much of it feels like your fault right now, as a rough percentage, and the sentence you say to yourself about it
List every cause that played a part, big or small, and give each a slice. Leave your own slice until the very last row
Causes people often forget: timing, luck, other people's choices, tiredness, money, what nobody could have known at the time. Add any you missed
Now that the other slices are drawn, the part that is honestly yours — a specific choice or action, not a character flaw
Whether that part was a mistake, a limit, or a reasonable decision that happened to go wrong
What you'd say to a friend who owned exactly this slice and no more
If your slice calls for a repair — an apology, a fix, a conversation — what is the smallest honest version
If it calls for nothing but learning, what you'd do differently in the same spot next time
A sentence to carry with you the next time your mind serves you the whole pie — for example, “I was one cause among several”

title: Follow the Thought Down
description: A small worry often has a bigger belief underneath it. This helps you follow one thought down, one “and what would that mean?” at a time, until you reach the belief — then answer it.
intro_md: An everyday thought like “I sent that email too late” can sit on top of something much older, such as “I let people down” or “I am not enough.” This is not a test and there is no right answer waiting at the bottom. You follow the thought down by asking, each time, “and if that were true, what would it mean?” — and you stop when the answer starts repeating. Then, gently, you reply to what you found.

fields.label: The thought that bothered you today, small and specific — “I said the wrong thing at lunch”, “I haven't texted back”
What feeling came with it, and how strong that feeling was
If that were true, what would it mean about you, your life, or other people
And if that were true, what would it mean
And if that were true, what would it mean
Keep going only if it hasn't started to repeat. And if that were true, what would it mean
Where the answers started repeating. Write the belief you landed on as one plain sentence
How old this belief feels, and the earliest memory you have of believing it
What it has cost you to carry it, and what it has tried to protect you from
Evidence from your actual life that does not fit this belief — moments, people, things you've done
A truer, kinder sentence you could put in its place. It doesn't have to be the opposite; “I sometimes let people down, like everyone, and I repair it” is fair
Return to the starting thought and read it with the new sentence underneath. What does it look like now, and what is the next ordinary thing to do

title: What a Belief Gives and Costs
description: A rule like “I must never let anyone down” gives you something, or you would not keep it. This helps you weigh what it gives against what it takes, honestly.
intro_md: Beliefs that hurt usually stick around because they also help, at least a little. “I must never let anyone down” might make you reliable and well liked while also keeping you exhausted and afraid. This is not a test, and no one is asking you to throw the belief out. It is a ledger. You write down both columns, look at the totals, and decide whether a slightly looser version would serve you better.

fields.label: The belief, written as the rule you actually live by — “I must never let anyone down”, “I have to be certain before I act”
How long you've held it, and where you think you picked it up
Fill in a row for each area of life the belief touches — work, friendships, family, rest, health, how you talk to yourself
The costs are often paid later, or by someone else — your sleep, your partner, your evenings. Any you didn't see at first
What the belief gives you in the next hour, and what it costs you over the next ten years
Who benefits from you holding this belief, and who pays for it
Rewrite the belief so it keeps what is worth keeping and drops the “never” or “must” — for example, “I care about people and I sometimes have to say no”
What the looser version gives, and what you'd have to tolerate to live by it
One situation this week where you could act on the looser version, and what you'll do
What you'll watch for afterwards — the reaction you feared, and what actually happens instead

title: Honest and Kind at the Same Time
description: Between the harsh thought and the falsely cheerful one there is a third voice, honest and kind. This helps you find it, sentence by sentence, for the things you're hard on yourself about.
intro_md: When you are low, the harsh voice says “you ruined it.” The cheerful voice, trying to help, says “it was fine, don't worry about it” — and you don't believe a word. Neither is telling the truth. This is not a test and there are no right answers. You are practicing a third voice, one that admits what actually happened and still speaks to you the way you would speak to someone you love.

fields.label: Something recent you've been hard on yourself about — a conversation, a mistake, a thing you didn't do
The harsh thought, in the exact words it uses. Let it be as unkind as it really is
The falsely cheerful thought — the thing a well-meaning friend or a poster might say, that you don't quite buy
What is actually true here — the parts of the harsh voice that are fair, and the parts that are not
Now the honest and kind version. Admit what happened, then say what you'd say to a close friend in the same spot
Try the same three voices on five more things your mind has been hard on you about lately
Read the honest, kind sentences aloud. What is different in your body compared with the harsh ones
What makes the kind voice hard to believe — does it feel like letting yourself off, or like a language you don't speak yet
One honest, kind sentence you'll keep for the week, for the moment the harsh voice starts up
Someone whose voice already sounds like this, and what they'd say to you tonight

title: Getting Out of the Loop
description: Going over the same thing again and again feels like problem-solving, but it rarely solves anything. This helps you see what the loop promises, what it delivers, and how to step out of it.
intro_md: Rumination is the thought that keeps circling — replaying the argument, rehearsing what you should have said, asking “why am I like this” late at night. It feels like work, which is why it is hard to put down. This is not a test and there is no right answer. You are stepping outside the loop to check what it really gives you. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: The thought you keep circling, in the words it uses — “why did I say that”, “what if I'd left earlier”, “what's wrong with me”
When it tends to start — in bed, in the shower, on the drive home — and how long a typical round lasts
What it feels like in your body while the loop is running, and afterwards
What the loop seems to be offering — an answer, a way to undo it, certainty, a guarantee you'll never do it again
Finish this: “If I just think about it hard enough, I'll…”
Honestly, what the last hour of looping actually produced — a decision, a plan, or the same three sentences and a headache
What you didn't do while the loop had you — sleep, the call, dinner, the thing you'd been looking forward to
Real problem-solving ends in a next step. What does the loop end in, and how is that different
Something you can do with your hands or feet for ten minutes — wash up, walk to the corner, water the plants, text one person
A sentence to mark the exit — for example, “I've noticed the loop. I'll give it ten minutes at six if it still wants attention”
If there is a real problem inside the loop, the one concrete step it needs, and when you'll take it
The earliest sign you'll watch for that the loop is starting — the phrase, the posture, the time of night

title: Evidence for a Kinder Belief
description: A new belief needs evidence before it feels true. This gives you a week to collect small, ordinary proof for a kinder sentence about yourself that you're trying out.
intro_md: An old belief like “I'm a burden” has years of evidence filed under it, while a newer, kinder belief has almost none — not because it is false, but because you haven't been collecting. This is not a test and there is nothing to score. For seven days you simply write down anything, however small, that fits the new sentence. Holding the door counts. Being thanked counts. The bar is deliberately low; the point is to start the file.

fields.label: The old belief you're tired of — “I'm a burden”, “I always mess things up”, “people put up with me”
The kinder belief you're testing, worded so it's believable rather than grand — “I contribute”, “I'm someone people are glad to see”
How true the new sentence feels today, in your own words
What will count as evidence. List small things in advance — a text answered, a job done, a laugh shared — so you recognize them when they happen
Each day, write down at least one thing that fits the kinder belief, however ordinary
Anything you nearly didn't write down because it seemed too small, or because your mind said “that doesn't count”
Read the whole table back. Which entries surprise you, and which would you have missed a month ago
How your mind tried to dismiss the evidence — “anyone would have”, “they were just being polite” — and what you'd say back
How true the kinder sentence feels now, compared with day one
Where you'll keep this log going — a note on your phone, a page by the bed — and the first thing you'll add tomorrow

title: What Sunday Night Is Dreading
description: The dread that arrives on Sunday evening is rarely about the whole job. This helps you name the specific parts of Monday it is pointing at, then sort each one into what you can change, prepare for, or accept.
intro_md: This is not a test of whether you like your job, and there are no right answers. Sunday-night dread is information: it usually has a few specific Monday moments in mind, and vague dread is heavier than named dread. Take fifteen minutes with it this evening. You are not deciding anything big here — just getting a clearer look at what tomorrow holds, and which small part of it is actually yours to move.

fields.label: When the dread starts — the hour, what you are doing, and what you notice in your body
What you have been doing to push it away — scrolling, planning tomorrow's outfit, staying up late so the evening lasts longer
List the specific Monday moments the dread is pointing at, and for each decide whether you can change it, prepare for it, or accept it
Which item on that list is carrying most of the weight, and what makes it heavier than the others
The things you could actually change — a meeting you could shorten, a task you could hand off, a boundary you could state out loud
The things you could prepare for tonight in ten minutes or less — laying out notes, drafting one email, deciding what you'll say first
The things you can only accept for now, and one sentence that lets you carry them without fighting them all evening
What the dread is saying about the whole job, or about you — and whether Monday's actual evidence supports that
A recent Monday that turned out easier than Sunday said it would, and what made the difference
The one preparation you'll do tonight, and the time you'll stop working on tomorrow and give the evening back to yourself
Monday evening: what actually happened with the thing you dreaded most, compared with what Sunday predicted

title: When You Feel Like a Fraud
description: Feeling like you're about to be found out is common in people who are actually doing fine. This helps you catch the moment it happens, open the evidence file you usually skip, and hear what a mentor would say.
intro_md: Feeling like a fraud is not proof that you are one. It shows up most in people who care about doing well and who have just been handed something new. Nothing here scores you or settles whether you are good enough. It gathers the facts you skip over when the fear is talking, and gives the fear a fair hearing rather than the last word. There are no right answers.

fields.label: The most recent time the feeling hit — where you were, who was there, and what was being asked of you
What you did in that moment: went quiet, overexplained, worked twice as long, said yes to something you had no room for
The exact sentence the fear says, in its own words — e.g. “they're going to realize I don't belong here”
What you imagine happening on the day you're “found out” — who says what, and what happens next
What you believe the people around you have that you don't — training, ease, confidence, a natural gift
Where you first learned that being good at something meant never struggling with it, and who taught you that
Things you have actually done in this role or place that a genuine fraud could not have done — be concrete, with dates or names if you can
Feedback you have received and discounted — the compliment you brushed off, the review you decided was just politeness
What you have learned in the last six months that you didn't know before. Not knowing it earlier wasn't fraud; it was the job of learning it
Picture someone who has watched you work and wants you to do well. Write what they would say about the moment in the first section
The one line from that which you could actually believe on a bad day
A sentence to say to yourself when the fear speaks next week — short enough to remember in the middle of a meeting
One thing you'll do differently the next time you don't know something: ask, say “I'll find out”, or let the silence sit

title: Money and the Feelings Around It
description: Spending, and not spending, are both often driven by a feeling that passes quickly. Over one week, this log helps you notice the feeling before and after money moves, so the pattern becomes visible without judgment.
intro_md: This is not a budget, and nobody is grading how you spend. Money carries feelings — relief, guilt, fear, a small lift — and those feelings often decide things before the numbers get a say. For seven days, jot down purchases you made and purchases you talked yourself out of, with the feeling on either side. The aim is to see the pattern, not to fix it. There are no right answers here.

fields.label: What you expect this week to show you about your spending — the story you already tell yourself about money and you
One row per day. Include at least one thing you spent on and one thing you avoided spending on, with the feeling before and after
The feelings that showed up most often before money moved, and the situations they came from — tired, lonely, praised, bored, rushed
The purchase that felt best afterward, and the one that felt worst — what was different about the two
The spending you avoided: was it relief, deprivation, or something else, and did the urge come back later
Anything you noticed that you'd rather not have noticed. Write it plainly; it is information, not a verdict
What money meant in the home you grew up in — safety, argument, secrecy, generosity, never quite enough
Which of those old meanings still shows up in the log above, and where
Next time the feeling before is strong, one thing you'll do first — wait ten minutes, name the feeling out loud, check the balance, text someone
A purchase or non-purchase next week you'll make on purpose, knowing the feeling ahead of time, and what you predict you'll feel afterward

title: Planning a Money Conversation
description: Talking about money with a partner or family member can go sideways fast. This helps you work out what you actually want to say, guess what they'll hear, and set things up so the talk stays a conversation.
intro_md: This is not a script for winning. Money talks go wrong when they arrive as ambushes — one person has been rehearsing for weeks and the other has had ten seconds. This gives you somewhere to do the rehearsing where it belongs, on paper before the talk, so that what you bring to the table is clear, fair, and small enough to actually discuss. There are no right answers, and no one is being judged.

fields.label: The money issue in one plain sentence — the credit card, the wedding cost, the loan to your brother, who pays for what
The feeling underneath the issue for you — fear of running out, feeling unseen, resentment, embarrassment, being the only one who worries
What you want to be different after this conversation. Not “for them to get it”, but a concrete change or decision
What money likely meant in their home growing up, and how that might shape what they hear when you raise it
The version of this conversation they are probably dreading, and what they would need to hear early on to relax
One thing they are right about, even if you don't like it
When and where you'll ask to talk — not late at night, not mid-argument, not when either of you is hungry or halfway out the door
How you'll open — one sentence that names the topic and says you want to work it out together, e.g. “I'm worried about the card and can't carry it alone”
The one request you'll make. Just one — a number, a decision, a shared look at the account together
The signs, in you and in them, that the conversation is turning into a fight — volume, old grievances, silence, leaving the room
What you'll say to pause it without abandoning it, e.g. “Let's stop here and pick this up Sunday morning after coffee”
The day and time you'll suggest for the talk, and the exact words you'll use to ask
After the conversation: what they said that surprised you, what got decided, and what still needs a second talk

title: Stay or Go: A Job Decision Map
description: A job decision rarely gets clearer by thinking harder in circles. This lays the two paths side by side — what you'd gain, lose, and fear on each — and asks what an ordinary day looks like a year on.
intro_md: This will not tell you what to do, and there is no right answer waiting at the bottom of the page. Most job decisions get stuck because gain, loss and fear are all talking at once. Putting them in separate columns turns the noise into something you can look at. Take your time; you can come back to it more than once before you decide, and changing your mind halfway through is allowed.

fields.label: Path A — staying where you are, or the current situation — described in two or three plain sentences
Path B — the change: the new job, the leave, the move into something else — in two or three plain sentences
Compare the two paths across the things that matter to you — money, hours, people, learning, health, pride, commute — one area per row
The fear that belongs to leaving, said plainly, e.g. “I'll fail somewhere new and won't be able to come back”
The fear that belongs to staying, said just as plainly, e.g. “I'll still be here in five years, wondering”
Which of those two fears you have been avoiding looking at, and why it is the louder one
It is a year later and you stayed. Describe an ordinary Tuesday — the morning, the work, the evening, how you feel at the end of it
It is a year later and you went. The same ordinary Tuesday, in the same detail
Reading both Tuesdays back, which one made your shoulders drop, and which one made your stomach tighten
The information that would actually change the decision — and how you could get it this month: a conversation, a trial day, a real number
Who you'll talk to before deciding, and what you'll ask them that isn't “what should I do”
The smallest next move on either path — an application, a conversation with your manager, a look at the numbers
The date by which you'll decide, and what you'll do if that date comes and you still don't know

title: Your First 30 Days Somewhere New
description: Starting a new job, school, or role is a stretch of not-knowing. This helps you decide what to learn, whom to meet, and what to give yourself permission not to know yet, one week at a time.
intro_md: Nobody expects you to know everything in the first month, though it can feel as if they do. This is not a performance review, and there are no right answers. It is a plan for how you'll spend the not-knowing — what to learn first, whom to meet, and what to leave alone until later — so that the days have a shape even while the role doesn't yet. Fill in what you can now and come back as the weeks pass.

fields.label: What you are stepping into — the role, the place, the start date — and the one thing you are most looking forward to
What you're most nervous about, said plainly: not knowing anyone, looking slow, the commute, the first question you can't answer
What you learned from the last time you started somewhere — what helped in the first weeks, and what you'd skip this time
One row per week: what you'll learn, whom you'll meet, one question you'll ask, and one thing you'll deliberately not worry about yet. Last row: what can wait
The people who could make the first month easier — the one who knows where things are, the one who started last year, the one everyone goes to
How you'll introduce yourself in a sentence or two, and the one question you'll ask each new person so you're not doing all the talking
Things you give yourself permission not to know or not to be yet — write them as permissions, e.g. “I'm allowed to ask the same question twice”
The signs that you're pushing too hard — skipped lunches, rereading emails at midnight, apologizing for things nobody minded
What you'll keep the same outside the new place — the run, the Sunday call, the show you watch — so not everything changes at once
Who you'll tell how it's going, and when, so the first weeks are not carried alone
On day 30, what you'll look back and check — not “did I nail it” but “did I learn what I set out to, and did I meet the people”
Day 30, filled in then: what turned out easier than expected, what was harder, and one thing you know now that day-one you didn't

title: When a Big Role Ends
description: Retirement and an emptying house both take away a role you were good at and a structure you never had to think about. This helps you name what is ending, what you'll miss, and what you'll build in its place.
intro_md: Retiring, or watching the last child leave, is often called a happy ending, which makes the flat or lost feeling harder to admit. This is a place to admit it. There are no right feelings here and no timetable. A role that shaped your days for decades does not end in an afternoon, and grief for it can sit alongside relief. Both are information about what mattered, not a sign that something is wrong with you.

fields.label: The role that is ending or has ended, named plainly — the job title, “the one who packed the lunches”, “the person people called”
What that role gave you that had nothing to do with money: being needed, a reason to get up, people to talk to, a way to introduce yourself
The parts of it you will honestly not miss, and are allowed not to miss
What an ordinary weekday looked like when the role was in full swing — from waking to sleeping, with the fixed points
What a weekday looks like now, or what you expect it to look like. Notice where the gaps are
Which of those gaps feel like freedom, and which feel like falling
The thing you'll miss most, and the last time you had it
The feelings that have shown up that you didn't expect — irritability, envy, relief, guilt about the relief, tears at odd moments
Things you did before the role took over, or always meant to do, that could fill an hour of a weekday
One fixed point you'll put into each weekday — a walk, a class, coffee with someone, a shift somewhere — so the day has a spine
Who you'd like more of now, and how you'll ask for it without making it their job to fill the gap
One thing from the list above you'll do this week, with the day and the time
A new way to answer “so what do you do?” that you would be comfortable saying out loud

title: Settling Into a New Place
description: Moving house or city uproots the small routines that made life feel like yours. This helps you notice what the move took, rebuild the anchors one at a time, and keep a record of the place becoming home.
intro_md: A move is counted as one event, but it is dozens of small losses at once: the route you walked without thinking, the barista who knew your order, the friend across town. Feeling unmoored months later is not failing at the move. This is not a checklist to complete, and there are no right answers. It is a way to notice what is missing and start putting anchors down, one at a time.

fields.label: The small, ordinary things you lost in the move — the walk, the store, the neighbor, the light in the old kitchen
The person or people you miss most, and what specifically you did with them that you have no replacement for yet
What you were hoping the move would fix or bring, and how that hope is holding up so far
The moment in the week when the new place feels least like home — Sunday afternoon, the commute, walking into an empty apartment
What you have been doing with that feeling — calling home constantly, not unpacking, saying yes to everything, saying no to everything
For each routine or place you lost, the closest new version you could try and when — it doesn't have to be as good, just a start
Where people who'd be your kind of people might already be gathering — a class, a run club, a volunteer shift, a place of worship, the dog park
The one line you'll use to turn a nod into a conversation, e.g. “I just moved here — is this place always this busy?”
Who from the old place you'll keep on a regular call, and how often, so those friendships don't depend on you remembering
One spot in the new place — a bench, a cafe, a corner of the apartment — you'll claim as yours this week, and when you'll go
A month from now: what feels more like home than it did today, and what still doesn't

title: The Week After a Layoff
description: Losing a job knocks out income, routine, and a piece of how you introduce yourself, all at once. This helps you look at the story you're telling, plan a practical week, decide whom to tell, and keep one routine going.
intro_md: This is not a job-search plan or a pep talk. A layoff is a loss, and the first days are often shock, anger, relief and shame in any order. None of it says anything about your worth. This is a place to get the story straight, do the practical things that matter this week, and keep one piece of your day the same. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: What happened, in the plainest version you can write — the date, who told you, and what they actually said
The version you have been telling yourself since, especially the sentences that start with “I should have” or “this proves”
What is actually known about why this happened, and what is guesswork filling in the gap
The version you would tell if it had happened to a friend. Notice the difference between the two
Money: what you know and what you need to find out this week — severance, final paycheck, health coverage, unemployment filing, which bills can wait
The three or four practical things that genuinely need doing in the next seven days, and the day each one will happen
The things that feel urgent but can wait two weeks — updating every profile, telling everyone, deciding what comes next
Who needs to know soon, and one sentence you're comfortable saying to each — it can be short, e.g. “My role was cut. I'm okay, and I'll be looking”
Who you're dreading telling, and what you're afraid they will think
Who you'd like to be around this week, whether or not you talk about it
One ordinary thing you'll keep doing at the same time every day — dressed by nine, the walk, the gym, dinner at the table
At the end of the week: which day was hardest, what helped, and whether the story in the first section has shifted at all

title: Getting Ready for a Big Change
description: Any large transition is easier to walk into when you know what will stay the same, what you're leaving, what you're taking with you, and who is coming along. This maps all four, whatever the change is.
intro_md: This works for any change big enough to make you nervous — a new baby, a separation, a career shift, a graduation, a change in your health. It is not a test of readiness, and there is no score at the end that says go or don't go. Big change feels as if everything is moving at once. Sorting it into what stays, what goes, what comes with you and who comes along makes it a size you can hold.

fields.label: The change, in a sentence, and roughly when it happens
How you feel about it today — it is fine if several feelings sit side by side, e.g. excited and dreading it
The parts of your life this change does not touch — the people, the habits, the places, the parts of you
Which of those you'll deliberately protect through the change, and how
What ends with this change — name it plainly, even if you chose it
What you'll miss, and what you're relieved to put down
Something you'd like to do to mark the ending — a last visit, a note, a meal, a photograph
What you learned from the last big change you went through — the thing that helped, and the thing you'd do differently
The strengths, habits and people who come with you no matter where the change lands you
Something you're carrying that you'd rather set down before you go — an old story about yourself, a grudge, a role you've outgrown
The people who will be there on the other side, and what each can actually offer — a couch, a listening ear, a spare key, a laugh
One of them you'll tell this week that the change is coming and how you feel about it, and what you'll ask them for
The first morning after the change: one small thing from your “stays the same” list that you'll do, so the day begins with something familiar

title: Noticing Hunger and Fullness
description: Hunger and fullness are signals, not instructions to obey or override. This log helps you notice what your body was saying before, during, and after seven eating moments — with curiosity and no rules.
intro_md: This is not a food diary and nothing here gets counted. There are no portions to measure and no right way to eat. Over seven eating moments — a meal, a snack, a handful of something on the way out the door — you simply notice what your body seemed to be saying and what else was happening around you. Some entries will be blank or vague. That is fine. Noticing is the whole practice.

fields.label: Seven eating moments, filled in when you remember rather than when you think you should
How you usually decide when to eat — the clock, a plan, a rumble, a feeling, whoever else happens to be eating
Words your body uses for hunger — a headache, a hollow feeling, irritability, a thought about food that keeps coming back
Which moments you noticed hunger clearly, and which ones you ate for another reason — company, habit, availability, comfort
What fullness felt like when you noticed it, and whether you caught it during the meal or only afterwards
The “what else was going on” column — any pattern in stress, tiredness, rushing, or who was there
A moment you ate past fullness or skipped hunger. What made sense about that, given everything else in that hour?
Any old rule about eating you heard in your head this week, and whose voice it sounded like
One eating moment next week you'd like to slow down for — which one, and what would make that easier
A sentence to say to yourself when a rule about eating shows up in the middle of a meal

title: What Food Was Giving You
description: Eating for comfort is not a failure of willpower; it is a way of meeting a need. This sheet helps you name the feeling, what the food offered, and what else might offer it too.
intro_md: Nothing here is about stopping, fixing, or controlling. Eating when you are sad, bored, anxious, or lonely is one of the most ordinary things a person can do, and it often works, at least for a while. This is a curious look at one recent moment: what you felt, what food gave you, and what else might sometimes give you the same thing. No verdicts, no rules, no right answers.

fields.label: A recent time you ate when you weren't especially hungry — where you were, what time it was, what you ate
What had happened in the hour before — a conversation, a long stretch of nothing, a piece of news, a deadline
The feeling that was there, as best you can name it — bored, flat, lonely, tense, wired, sad, angry, nothing at all
Where you felt it in your body, and whether you noticed it before eating or only afterwards
What eating actually did — a pause, a taste, warmth, something to do with your hands, a reason to stop working, company
How long that lasted, and what came next once it wore off
Other things that have ever given you the same thing — a walk, a call, a bath, lying down, a show, telling someone
What was in the way of those this time — too tired, too late, nobody around, didn't think of it
What you would say to a friend who described this exact evening to you
Next time the feeling shows up, one thing you might try alongside food — not instead of it, alongside it

title: Movement You Might Actually Enjoy
description: Movement that feels like punishment rarely lasts. This finder helps you try out ways of moving your body, rate how each one felt before and after, and keep the ones that leave you better off.
intro_md: This has nothing to do with burning anything off, changing your shape, or hitting a number. Movement here means anything that gets your body doing something — a stretch in bed, dancing in the kitchen, walking to the mailbox, swimming, gardening. The only measure that matters is how you feel afterwards compared with before. There are no right answers, and “I hated it” is useful information too.

fields.label: What “exercise” has meant to you so far — gym class, a program you quit, something a doctor said, something you loved as a kid
Ways of moving that you have ever enjoyed, even briefly, even a long time ago
Six ways of moving to try over the next couple of weeks, rated on how you felt before and after, where 10 is best
Which ones left you feeling better than before, and what specifically was better — mood, energy, sleep, a quieter head
Which ones felt like a chore or a punishment, and what made them feel that way — the setting, the pace, someone watching, an old memory
Anything that surprised you about how your body or your mood responded
The thoughts that show up right before moving — “it won't count unless…”, “I'll look silly”, “I should be doing more”
What would make the enjoyable ones easier — a friend, a podcast, a time of day, lower expectations
The one or two you want to keep, and the smallest version of each — five minutes counts, so does one song
When you'll do the next one. Day, time, and where.

title: When the Mirror Gets Loud
description: A harsh thought in front of a mirror or a photo can take over a day. This sheet helps you slow one of those moments down, find whose voice it was, and remember what your body did for you.
intro_md: This is not about learning to love how you look, and it is not a test of your confidence. It is about one moment — a mirror, a changing room, a photo someone tagged you in — and the thought that arrived with it. Thoughts about our bodies are often borrowed from somewhere else. This sheet helps you look at where this one came from and what was actually true about your body that day.

fields.label: Where you were and what you were looking at — a mirror, a shop window, a photo, a video call
What you were doing just before, and how you were already feeling
The exact words of the thought, as harsh as they were
What the thought told you to do or not do — change clothes, skip the event, hide, delete the photo, eat differently
How much of the rest of the day it followed you around
Whose voice the thought sounds like — a parent, a coach, an ex, a magazine, a comment at school, your own from years ago
When you first learned that this part of your body was a problem, and who was there
What that person or source was gaining, needing, or afraid of when they said it
What your body did for you today, before and after that moment — carried bags, digested lunch, laughed, kept you warm, got you here
Something your body let you do this week that you would have missed without it
A sentence to say back to the voice — not a compliment, just a fact, like “this body got me through today”
One small thing you'll do next time the mirror gets loud — look away, name the voice, touch something solid, go outside

title: What My Body Needs Today
description: A short morning check-in that asks your body, not your to-do list, how the day should go. It helps you notice sleep, hunger, pain, and mood before deciding anything else.
intro_md: This takes about five minutes with your first cup of something. It is not a plan for being productive and there is nothing to get right. You simply check in with the body you woke up in — how it slept, what it is asking for, what it is already carrying — and let that shape one or two choices today. Some mornings the honest answer is “not much.” That counts.

fields.label: How you slept, in plain words — how many times you woke, how you feel in the first minute, whether you're already tired
Where your body is stiff, sore, tense, or heavy right now, and where it feels okay
Hunger and thirst this morning, and what would actually appeal — not what you think you should have
What your body seems to want in the way of movement — to stretch, to stay under the covers, to walk, to be outside, nothing
What it wants in the way of contact — people, quiet, touch, space, a phone call, a closed door
Anything from yesterday still sitting in your body — a conversation, a late night, a worry, a long shift
The mood you woke up with, without needing to explain or justify it
What the day is asking of you, and where it and your body disagree
One thing you'll give your body today because it asked — a real lunch, a nap, a slower pace, a walk, an early night
One thing you'll let go of or shrink today so there's room for that
At the end of the day, one line on whether your body got what it asked for, and how that went

title: Pacing Through Pain and Fatigue
description: When pain, fatigue, or a body that tires quickly limits your energy, every day is a budget. This sheet helps you decide what to spend on, what to protect, and what rest really looks like.
intro_md: This is written for days when your body sets the limits, whether that is pain that doesn't leave, tiredness that sleep doesn't fix, or recovery from something. It is not about pushing through, and it is not about giving up. It is a way of spending a limited amount of energy on purpose rather than by accident, and of treating rest as part of the plan instead of what happens when you crash.

fields.label: How much energy you seem to have today, in your own units — a percentage, a battery, a number of spoons, “a half-day”
What already spent some of it before you got here — a bad night, pain, getting dressed, getting the kids out the door
The things asking for your energy today, each with a rough cost and how necessary it truly is
Which of those can be dropped, shrunk, handed to someone else, or moved to another day without the world ending
What real rest is for you — lying down in the dark, a show, sitting outside, a bath, silence — and what only looks like rest but drains you
When rest will happen today, put in before you need it rather than after
What you tell yourself when you stop before the job is done
What happens in your body over the next day or two when you push past the budget
What you actually spent energy on, and whether it was roughly what you planned
One thing to do differently tomorrow, and one thing you got right today

title: What Your Body Did for You
description: A body-neutral thank-you that has nothing to do with how you look. It helps you notice what your body did today — carried, digested, healed, felt, breathed — even on days you're not fond of it.
intro_md: You do not have to like your body to fill this in, and you do not have to feel grateful. This is not about appearance at all. It is a plain list of what your body has been doing, mostly without being asked, while you were busy thinking about other things. Function, not looks. If some parts hurt or don't work the way you want, that goes here too, honestly.

fields.label: What your body did between waking up and now — the ordinary things, like getting you down the stairs, keeping your temperature steady, healing a paper cut
Something it let you feel today — warm water, a hug, cold air, a song, the taste of something
Something it did while you were asleep or not paying attention
Things your body has carried you through — fevers, births, moves, long shifts, grief, a hard year
A part of your body you rarely think about, and what it quietly does — feet, eyelids, liver, the small muscles in your hands
Parts that hurt, are tired, or don't work the way you'd like, named without blame
What those parts are still managing to do, despite that
A way you've been treating your body as if it were a picture rather than a place you live
If you spoke to your body the way you speak to a hardworking friend, what would you say?
One thing your body did today that you'll mention to it, out loud or silently, before you sleep

title: A Meal Without a Screen
description: An experiment, not a rule. You predict what eating one meal a day without your phone or a show will be like, try it for a week, and see what actually happened.
intro_md: This is a small experiment and you are the only person who sees the results. Screens at meals are not bad, and you are not being asked to give them up. The idea is to eat one meal a day without one for seven days, predict what it will be like first, and then compare. Whatever happens — boredom, calm, giving up on day three — is a result, not a failure.

fields.label: What you expect a meal without a screen to feel like — restless, lonely, peaceful, pointless, long
What you think you'll notice about the food, if anything at all
Which meal you'll choose and why — the one that's easiest, or the one you're most curious about
Seven days, one screen-free meal each, filled in right after eating if you can
How the actual week compared with what you predicted
What the screen was doing for you at meals — company, distraction from thoughts, a break, a way to not feel rushed
Anything you noticed about hunger, fullness, taste, or pace that you don't normally notice
Days you skipped it or gave up halfway, and what made sense about that
Whether you'll keep any of this, and in what form — one meal, weekends only, none at all
One thing you might try at the table next week that isn't a screen — a window, a person, music, nothing

title: Rest Is Not Earned
description: If you only rest once everything is done, you never rest, because everything is never done. This sheet looks at where that rule came from and helps you take one rest before it's earned.
intro_md: This is for people who sit down only when the last dish is washed and the last email answered, and who feel a small guilt even then. There is nothing wrong with you for doing this. Somewhere you learned that rest has to be paid for. This sheet is not a lecture about self-care; it is a look at that rule, what it costs, and one unearned rest this week.

fields.label: Finish this sentence honestly: “I'm allowed to rest when…”
What actually happens when you try to rest before that — the guilt, the list running, getting up again
How often the condition is actually met. When was the last time everything was done?
Who you watched rest, and who you watched never rest, growing up
What rest was called in your house — lazy, idle, deserved, a reward, a weakness
What you're afraid would happen, or what people would think, if you rested without earning it
What your body and mood are like by the time you finally do stop
Something you've missed, cut short, or resented because rest had to wait
Someone you know who rests without earning it. Do you think less of them?
What you'd say to a friend who told you they were only allowed to sit down once everything was finished
One rest you'll take this week before the list is done — when, for how long, and what you'll do
What you'll say to the guilt when it shows up, in one sentence
Afterwards: what actually happened, and whether the undone things were still there and still fine

title: Seven Days of Mood and Movement
description: A week-long log of what you moved, for how long, your mood before and after, and where you were. Not for burning anything off — just to see what movement does for how you feel.
intro_md: Nothing in this log is about distance, steps, or effort. It is a week of noticing whether moving your body — a walk, stretching, dancing, carrying groceries, gardening — changes your mood at all, and under what conditions. Rain, sunshine, indoors, alone, with someone. There is no minimum, no target, and a day with no movement is a valid entry too. You are collecting information, not proof.

fields.label: Your honest guess about what movement does to your mood right now — nothing, a little, a lot, depends on the day
What usually stops you moving — time, pain, weather, energy, embarrassment, nowhere to go
Seven days, filled in on the day if you can, including days with no movement at all
The days your mood changed the most between before and after, and what those days had in common
Whether the setting mattered — outdoors, indoors, alone, with someone, daylight, evening
Whether length mattered, or whether five minutes did about as much as thirty
Any day your mood went down after moving, and what you think was going on
Days with no movement — what was happening, and what those days felt like, without judgment
One kind of movement, setting, and time of day you'll try again because of what the week showed
The smallest version of it you'll accept on a bad day

title: Repairing It After You Lost Your Temper
description: Every parent shouts, snaps, or slams a door sometimes. What matters most is what happens next. This sheet helps you look at what happened, work out what your child saw, and plan a repair that is honest and short.
intro_md: This is not a test of whether you are a good parent, and there are no right answers. Losing it is information about how much you were carrying, not a verdict on you. Children do not need parents who never get it wrong. They need parents who come back afterward. Take your time here, and be as honest about what you needed as you are about what you did.

fields.label: The moment itself, described plainly — what your child did, what you did, what you said. No softening, and no piling on either.
What the hour before looked like — how tired, rushed, hungry, or already stretched you were when it started
The exact point it tipped. What was the last small thing before you lost it?
Picture it from their height and their age. What did they see on your face and hear in your voice?
What they might have made it mean — about themselves, about you, or about whether they are safe with you
How they have been with you since — clingy, quiet, angry, or acting like nothing happened
Underneath the anger, what were you actually needing in that moment — quiet, help, to be listened to, five minutes alone?
Who or what could have met that need earlier, and what got in the way of asking for it
What you will say, in your child's language. Short, no excuses, no lecture — for example, “I shouted. That was not your fault. I'm sorry.”
What you will not say — the “but you made me” or “if you had just listened” you can feel wanting to come out
When and where you will say it — at bedtime, in the car, on the floor next to them
Afterward: how it went, what they said or did, and one thing you will do differently the next time you feel it tipping

title: Seven Days of Caregiver Check-Ins
description: Caring for someone can quietly empty you while everyone, including you, looks the other way. This week-long log tracks what you gave, what came back, how depleted you feel, and one thing each day that is only for you.
intro_md: This is a log, not a test, and nothing here is a right or wrong answer. Caregiving often goes unmeasured, which is part of why it wears people down. Writing it down for one week does not mean you are complaining or keeping score against the person you care for. It is a way of noticing what the week actually costs you, so that the cost stops being invisible, at least to you.

fields.label: Who you care for, and what a typical day of caring involves — the visible tasks and the invisible ones like worrying, planning, and being on call
How depleted you feel right now, before the week starts, on a scale of 1 to 10, and what that number feels like in your body
Fill in one row each evening. “What I got back” can be a thank-you, a moment of ease, a laugh, or honestly nothing at all.
Which day was heaviest, and what made it heavy — the tasks, the emotions, or something someone said
What came back to you across the week, if anything. Was it more or less than you expected?
The “one thing for me” column — how many days did it actually happen, and what got in the way when it didn't?
Something you gave this week that nobody else knows about
Finish this: “If I let myself want something for me this week, it would be…”
The voice that says you shouldn't need anything. Whose voice is it, and what would you say back to it?
One thing for you that you will protect next week — write the day and the time, and who you will tell so it is harder to skip
One person you could ask for a specific hour of help, and the exact sentence you would use to ask them

title: What Was Normal in Your House
description: Every family has rules that were never said out loud. This sheet helps you name what counted as normal where you grew up, then choose deliberately what you are keeping and what ends with you.
intro_md: There are no right answers here and no verdict on your family or on you. Every household has a way of doing things that felt like simply how life is, until you met people who did it differently. Some of what you learned is worth keeping. Some of it you may decide ends with you. Both are allowed, and you can change your mind. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: How anger was handled in your house — shouting, silence, slammed doors, jokes, leaving the room, or something else
How affection and praise were shown, or not shown, and who in the house got them
What happened when someone was sick, sad, or struggling. Who noticed, and what were they told?
The things nobody talked about — money, a relative, a drinking habit, a death, a feeling
What you had to do or be to stay in good standing — be quiet, be funny, be the achiever, be the easy one
The first time you noticed another family did it differently. What did you see, and what did you feel?
A pattern from your house that you have caught yourself repeating with a partner, a child, or a friend
What you are keeping — the traditions, phrases, and ways of caring that you want to carry on, and why they matter
What you are ending — the pattern, rule, or silence that stops with you. Name it as plainly as you can.
What ending it will cost you, and what it might cost the people who still live by it
One moment next week where the old pattern would usually show up, and what you will do instead
Who you could tell about this — a sentence you could say to a partner, sibling, or friend

title: Getting Through the Family Gathering
description: Holidays and family gatherings can undo months of steadiness in an afternoon. This before, during, and after plan names the people and topics you expect, gives you an exit line, and makes sure you are not alone.
intro_md: This is a plan, not a test, and there is no right way to do a family gathering. Dreading one does not make you ungrateful or difficult. It usually means you know exactly what tends to happen there. Planning for it is not the same as expecting the worst. It is a way of walking in with some choices already made, so you have more of yourself left by the end of the day.

fields.label: The gathering — where, when, how long, and who will be there. Include how you are getting there and, more importantly, how you can leave.
What usually happens that you dread. Be specific — the comment, the seating plan, the question about your life.
What you actually want from the day, if anything — to see one person, to eat well, to leave by four, to not fight
One row per person or topic you expect trouble from. An exit line is a short sentence that ends the conversation, like “I'm going to check on the food.”
Where you will go for five minutes alone when you need it — the porch, the car, a walk with the dog
The signal you will notice in your body that says it is time to use an exit line or take a break
Your ally — what you will ask them to do, in one sentence, and when you will ask them before the day
The one thing you decide in advance you will not do — argue about that topic, explain your choices, stay past a certain time
How you will get home, and what you will do that evening to come back to yourself
Afterward: what actually happened, which parts of the plan you used, and what surprised you
One sentence you want to remember for the next gathering, whenever it comes

title: Dividing the Invisible Load
description: Households run on work nobody sees — remembering, planning, noticing, worrying. This sheet maps who carries what with a partner or co-parent, then helps you plan a conversation about it that is not a fight.
intro_md: This is not a scorecard and there are no right answers. The invisible load is the remembering, tracking, and worrying that keeps a family running, and it is often carried mostly by one person without anyone ever deciding it should be. Naming it is not an accusation. Fill this in for yourself first, and if it helps, invite your partner or co-parent to fill in their own copy before you compare.

fields.label: The things you are keeping in your head right now — appointments, birthdays, school forms, the thing that needs fixing, who is low on socks
The things you believe your partner or co-parent keeps in their head. Be fair, and guess honestly.
One task per row. Noticing, planning, and doing are three different jobs — a task can be done by one person and carried by another.
Which rows surprised you, and which ones felt exactly as you expected them to
The task you most resent carrying, and what the resentment is really about — the task itself, or not being seen
A task you have been holding onto that you could genuinely hand over completely, including the noticing and the planning
How you will open it, in a sentence that describes rather than accuses — for example, “I've noticed I'm the one tracking the school stuff and it's wearing me out.”
What you will ask for, specifically — one task, handed over whole, by a date you both agree
What you will do if they get defensive, and what you will do if they simply agree
When you will have the conversation, and where — not at bedtime, and not in the middle of an argument
Afterward: what was said, what changed, and the one task that now lives somewhere else

title: When Your Parents Start Needing You
description: When a parent starts needing care, the roles you have known all your life begin to turn over. This sheet helps you name that shift, sort what you can carry from what you can't, and ask siblings for specific help.
intro_md: This is not a test of whether you are a good son or daughter, and there are no right answers. Watching a parent become someone you look after can bring grief, guilt, tenderness, and old resentment all at once, sometimes in the same hour. None of that is a flaw. You are allowed to have limits, and you are allowed to ask for help from the people who share the responsibility.

fields.label: What has changed — the specific things your parent used to do that you now do, or check on, or worry about
The moment you first realized the roles had shifted. Where you were, and what you felt.
What it stirs up from earlier in your life — what they were like as a parent, and how that makes this harder or easier
What you can genuinely carry right now — the tasks, visits, calls, and money, and how much of each
What you cannot carry, or cannot carry alone, however much you feel you should be able to
What it costs you to keep carrying the things in the last answer — your job, your partner, your children, your sleep, your health
One need per row. Ask for something specific — “take the Tuesday appointment” lands better than “help more.”
The sibling you will talk to first, and the sentence you will open with. Describe your situation before you ask.
What you expect them to say, and what you will say if it is “I can't” or “you're better at it than me”
What you will accept as good enough from them, even if it is not the way you would do it
One thing that is yours and not your parent's that you will protect this month, and the day you will do it
Afterward: what you asked for, what you got, and what you will ask for next time

title: Family Rules You Make Together
description: Rules that are handed down get argued with; rules that are built together get kept, mostly. This sheet plans a short family meeting about screens and the other things you fight over, and records what you agree.
intro_md: This is not a test, and there is no correct set of rules. Every family is different in what it can live with. The point of building rules together is not to give children the final say. It is to let them be heard, so the rules make sense to them and to you. Expect it to be imperfect. A rule that gets kept most of the time is doing its job.

fields.label: What you are fighting about right now — screens at the table, bedtime, homework, chores. Name the top two or three.
The rule you would impose if you could, and honestly, why that has not worked so far
What you think each child would say they want, if asked. Guess now, then check later.
Your own screen habits, honestly, and what your children see you doing with your phone
When and where you will hold it, how long it will be, and what you will do to make it feel like a conversation rather than a lecture
The questions you will ask, in your children's words — for example, “What feels unfair right now?” or “What would you change?”
The things that are not up for discussion, said in advance so nobody feels tricked — safety, sleep, being kind to each other
Write the rules as the family agreed them, in plain words a child can read. “If it slips” is what happens next, not a punishment to be dreaded.
Where the rules will live so everyone can see them — the fridge, a shared note, a drawing
The first rule to try, and what you will notice this week about whether it is working, for them and for you
One thing you will say when a rule slips, instead of the thing you usually say

title: The Good Enough Parent
description: The standard many parents hold themselves to would exhaust anyone. This sheet helps you write out that standard, trace where it came from, and check it against what your child actually needs from you.
intro_md: There are no right answers here and no verdict on the parent you are. Children do not need a perfect parent; they need one who is present enough, kind enough, and steady enough, most of the time. If the bar you hold yourself to feels impossible, that is information about the bar, not about you. This sheet is for looking at it closely enough to decide whether it is really yours.

fields.label: The parent you feel you should be — write it out as a job description: how patient, how present, how organized, how cheerful
The moments this week when you fell short of it, and what you said to yourself afterward
What you never let yourself do because a good parent wouldn't — sit down, say no, be bored, ask for a break
Whose voice the standard sounds like — a parent, a relative, a book, a feed full of other people's kitchens
What your own parents got wrong that you are determined to get right, and how that shapes the bar
Who benefits from you holding this standard, and who pays for it — including you
Picture your child at their happiest with you this month. What were you actually doing? It is often something small.
What your child would say they need from you, in their words. If they are old enough, ask them.
One thing on your job description that your child has never asked for and would not notice if it stopped
One thing you will deliberately do less than perfectly this week — store-bought cake, a movie so you can rest, a plain no
Your prediction: what you expect to happen, and how you expect to feel about it
The result: what actually happened, what your child did, and what you noticed about the bar afterward

title: The Distance You Keep From Family
description: Low contact or no contact with a family member is a decision people rarely make lightly. This sheet helps you look at what the distance protects, what it costs, and what would genuinely have to change for it to shift.
intro_md: This is not a test, and there is no right answer about how much contact to have with your family. Nobody else gets to grade this. Distance from a parent, sibling, or child is usually protecting something real, and it usually costs something real too. Holding both at once is the work here. You do not have to decide anything today. If you are in danger or cannot keep yourself safe, please reach out now — in the US you can call or text 988 at any time.

fields.label: Who you have distance from, what the contact looks like now, and how it got here — a decision, a drift, or a door that closed
What people around you say about it, and what you feel when they say it
What happens to you when you are in contact — what gets said, what you do afterward, how long it takes to recover
What the distance protects — your peace, your children, your sobriety, your sense of who you are
The part of you that the distance was built for. How old is that part, and what did it need?
What you miss, honestly — the person, the version of them you hoped for, the rest of the family, the holidays, the story you tell about yourself
What the distance costs other people — your children, your partner, a sibling caught in the middle
The grief in it, if there is any, and where you put that grief
What they would need to do, specifically, for you to consider more contact — not “be different,” but the actual behavior
What you would need to be true in yourself — steadier, less afraid, more supported, less alone
What is not going to change, and what it means to accept that for now
The right amount of contact for the next three months — none, a card, a call, a visit with a plan — and one sentence for anyone who asks

title: Adjusting to a New Family Member
description: A new baby, a stepchild, a foster placement, or a parent moving in changes everything at once. This sheet checks in on sleep, identity, partnership, and support so the strain has somewhere to go.
intro_md: There are no right answers here and no verdict on how you are adjusting. Loving someone new and being flattened by their arrival happen at the same time, and feeling the second does not cancel the first. Most families do not talk about how hard the first months are until they are over. This sheet is somewhere to say it now, before it turns into something you carry alone.

fields.label: Who has joined your family, when, and what the arrival was like — planned, sudden, longed for, complicated
What you imagined this stage would feel like, and how the real thing compares
How much sleep you are actually getting, in hours, and how it is affecting your patience, your mood, and your memory
One thing that could give you more rest this week — a swapped night, a nap, a limit on visitors — and what stops you asking for it
What has fallen away from your life since they arrived — work, friends, your body, time alone, a version of yourself
What you miss most, and whether you have said so out loud to anyone
Something that is still yours — a habit, a friendship, a place — and how you will keep it this month
How you and your partner, if you have one, are talking to each other now — as a team, as shift workers, as strangers passing
One thing you appreciate that they have done, and one thing you need from them that you have not asked for
The sentence you will use to ask for it, and when you will say it
Who has actually shown up, and who you expected to show up and hasn't. What has that felt like?
One specific ask you will make of one person this week — a meal, an hour, a ride, a phone call at a bad time
One thing you will notice next week about how you are doing, so you know whether it is getting lighter or heavier
